questions.evidence: Compare the headline and underlying inflation decompositions and the change in local-currency import assumptions.

questions.question: What share of bank funding now trades close to the policy rate?
questions.evidence: Use the report’s charts and subsequent alternative funding, repo and overnight market data.

questions.question: Which forecast components are most sensitive to longer energy disruption?
questions.evidence: Use the full report’s alternative risks with updated local fuel prices, exchange rates and expectations.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
title: Fatih Karahan’s briefing on Inflation Report 2026-IV
locator: Prepared remarks, the domestic economic outlook and medium-term projections, pp. 9–11. Scope excludes Q&A and the separate full report.
summary:
Governor Fatih Karahan described an improvement in underlying inflation, including services categories with historically persistent inflation, as tight policy dampened demand. He pointed to weakness in industrial activity and domestic demand alongside a drag from elevated global energy, food and freight costs. The balance of risks differed by channel: more persistent costs could spread into prices and expectations, while weaker-than-expected demand would reduce inflation.

The end-2026 inflation forecast was raised to 29.5%. The new interim path is 21% at end-2027, 13.5% at end-2028 and 9% at end-2029, converging towards the medium-term 5% objective. Karahan attributed the upward revisions to more persistent war and energy effects, updated food assumptions, administered-price measures and a slower improvement in expectations. He committed to a tight stance until the disinflation path was on track. The revisions describe the bank’s forecast and interim targets rather than a rate decision.

questions.question: Which inputs account for the forecast revision?
questions.evidence: Quantify the contributions from energy, food, administered prices and expectations in the full report’s revision decomposition.

questions.question: Is the fall in core services broad enough to persist?
questions.evidence: Review the distribution of monthly changes across sticky service categories and changes in wage and rent growth.

questions.question: How much does a weaker-demand scenario change the reaction function?
questions.evidence: Read the risk scenario, credit and activity indicators, and compare the projected inflation path against the interim targets.

title: Farm bankers cautiously optimistic despite a tough few years
summary: The Minneapolis Fed’s agricultural credit survey shows pressure from farm operating costs in the Ninth District. Around 29% of lenders reported greater loan demand than a year before and 34% reported more renewals or extensions. Repayment weakened on balance and 22% required more collateral. Land values were more resilient than farm income, with nonirrigated cropland up 2.5% year over year. Fourth-quarter lender views on farm income leaned modestly positive, although repayment expectations and planned capital spending were weaker. These are reported survey responses for the district.
locator: Loan demand, cash rents and land values, outlook and state survey tables

questions.question: Does the gap between land values and farm income point to a collateral risk?
questions.evidence: Compare rent-to-value ratios, farm income, leverage and renewal rates.

questions.question: How much of rising borrowing reflects operating costs rather than investment?
questions.evidence: Review loans by purpose and reported capital spending by state.

questions.question: Are repayment pressures concentrated in weather-exposed areas?
questions.evidence: Compare late-season crop and moisture indicators with local lender responses.

title: Economic Bulletin Issue 7, 2026
summary:
The ECB’s economic update described the energy shock as a two-sided problem for policy: greater pass-through could lift inflation, while the loss of purchasing power and tighter financing conditions could depress demand. Upside inflation risks included broader energy spillovers and winter gas supply pressures. A lasting geopolitical resolution, weaker pass-through or a further tightening of financial conditions could reduce inflation instead.

The financing data distinguish changes in credit prices, standards and volumes. In August, the cost of market-based debt for firms rose to 4.1% while their bank borrowing rate remained 3.8%. Corporate bank lending growth slowed from July, while growth in corporate bond issuance accelerated through September. The lending survey reported tighter corporate credit standards and weaker loan demand despite greater working-capital needs. These indicators describe transmission and do not identify a single reason for the change in financing mix. The policy section restates the October hold.

questions.question: Which firms can substitute bond issuance for bank lending?
questions.evidence: Compare credit growth, issuance and costs by firm size, rating and country to test whether the transmission burden falls on bank-dependent borrowers.

questions.question: How sensitive is inflation to a further gas shock?
questions.evidence: Use the Bulletin’s energy discussion with storage, wholesale forward prices and national pricing rules.

questions.question: How do changing financing conditions alter the expected rate path?
questions.evidence: Compare contemporaneous OIS, credit volumes and the ECB’s financing condition measures.

locator: Economic, financial and monetary developments: Overview, Risk assessment and Financial and monetary conditions.
coverageLimitation: Overview and financing sections reviewed here. The separate articles and boxes in the issue are outside this summary.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Reserve Money (October 2026)
locator: Release paragraphs on level, composition, drivers and annual growth.
summary:
The CBC reports that October daily average reserve money declined NT$76.5 billion to NT$7,610.1 billion. Currency in circulation rose NT$10.5 billion while reserves deposited with the bank fell NT$87.0 billion. The release attributes much of the net movement to tax remittances, bond issuance and government borrowing offsetting expansionary items such as debt repayments and a decline in the bank’s negotiable certificates of deposit outstanding. The annual rate slowed to 6.80% from 8.03% in September, while the first ten months still averaged faster growth than in the same period of the previous year.

The composition makes a difference for interpretation. More currency in circulation can coincide with lower bank reserves. The net change in reserve money combines shifts in government cash balances, monetary operations and currency demand. The release does not record a change to the policy rate or identify unexplained financing stress.

questions.question: Were reserves temporarily lower around tax and bond settlement dates?
questions.evidence: Combine a daily balance series with fiscal disbursements, bond settlements and central bank operations.

questions.question: Did lower deposited reserves affect short market rates?
questions.evidence: Test whether changes in effective overnight rates and dispersion accompany the reserve moves.

questions.question: Is the change in annual growth driven by base effects?
questions.evidence: Compare seasonally aligned levels and component contributions against the same months in previous years.

institution: Banco Central de la República Argentina
title: Informe Monetario Mensual – October 2026
summary:
The October monetary report records a 0.4% fall in real, seasonally adjusted private transactional M2 while time deposits increased for a third month. The broader private M3 aggregate grew by an average of 0.9% per month in real terms from August to October. This split stems partly from a fall in transactional deposits relative to currency and time deposits.

The monetary base increased 1.1% in October after adjusting for prices and seasonality. The BCRA says it supplied money through FX purchases and absorbed excess liquidity through market operations and repos. Private credit across both currencies expanded 0.4% in real, seasonally adjusted terms, with growth concentrated in pesos. Credit card financing continued to contract more slowly. The report identifies the figures as provisional.
locator: Executive summary, monetary aggregate and balance-sheet descriptions

questions.question: Is growth in time deposits a change in money demand or a reallocation into yield?
questions.evidence: Compare deposits by holder and maturity, nominal rates, and subsequent real transactional balances.

questions.question: How much of FX buying fed into the monetary base after sterilisation?
questions.evidence: Reconcile the balance sheet, open market operations and repo flows with the report’s monetary base components.

questions.question: Is peso lending growth broad and durable?
questions.evidence: Track new credit by segment, especially credit cards, alongside rates and bank funding.

coverageNote: Executive summary and its main aggregate figures reviewed. Full tables and spreadsheet are linked in the original.

title: Increased risk of serious events that could weaken financial stability
summary:
Norges Bank saw a resilient financial system but judged the likelihood of severe adverse events to have increased. Solid bank capital and liquidity, low losses and improvements in household debt servicing capacity provided buffers. Household debt had grown more slowly than incomes and liquid buffers showed signs of recovery. Vulnerability from household debt had therefore declined somewhat in the bank’s assessment.

Commercial real estate offered a different balance of risks. The share of highly indebted firms with weak servicing capacity had declined, but financing and construction costs were weighing on valuations and new development. Developers’ bankruptcies had increased and banks reported higher default risk. The countercyclical buffer was held at 2.5%. The release describes resilience at the current point and identifies external shocks and property exposures that could test it.

questions.question: Which commercial property borrowers face the largest refinancing step-up?
questions.evidence: Compare maturity walls and rate resets with rent coverage, refinancing spreads and bank credit exposures.

questions.question: Are improving household buffers concentrated in lower-risk cohorts?
questions.evidence: Use the underlying Financial Stability Report and household microdata on liquidity and debt servicing.

questions.question: How much could a global risk sell-off feed into Norwegian bank funding?
questions.evidence: Monitor covered bond and senior funding spreads alongside cross-border funding dependencies.

locator: Press release sections on households, property and capital requirements.

title: Financial Stability Report 2026 H2
summary: The committee judged Norwegian banks and borrowers resilient while warning of a higher probability of adverse events. Household debt-to-income ratios were down across groups and most households could service their loans. Bank buffers and low losses also supported resilience. Commercial property and developers remained exposed to higher financing costs and weaker valuations. The countercyclical capital buffer stayed at 2.5%. External shocks could simultaneously affect asset quality and funding, making property and counterparty exposures relevant despite the aggregate assessment.

questions.question: Which property loans combine weak interest coverage with early refinancing?
questions.evidence: Compare maturities, rents and collateral values.

questions.question: Could unemployment offset stronger household balance sheets?
questions.evidence: Stress household debt service by income and liquidity.

questions.question: What funding channels could amplify shocks?
questions.evidence: Track covered bond and wholesale spreads and maturities.

locator: Executive summary and sections on borrowers, markets and the capital buffer
coverageLimitation: Headline risk assessment reviewed. Full report scenarios are pending.

title: Edited Minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee Meeting No. 5/2026
summary:
The minutes released 11 November cover the October meeting and explain why the MPC retained accommodation amid stronger activity in some sectors. The committee attributed much of the stronger outlook to technology-linked manufacturing exports and investment and judged the distribution of gains narrow. The minutes note that revised manufacturing coverage affects estimates of recent momentum and that historical GDP revisions could affect year-on-year comparisons.

For inflation, energy subsidies reduced the forecast compared with the previous projection despite higher global oil prices. The committee identified the Oil Fuel Fund’s financial capacity as a risk to future cushioning and watched for higher input costs passing through to core prices. External reserves were cited as a buffer against funding volatility. Domestic credit remained uneven: rising loans to larger borrowers coexisted with weak SME credit. Members discussed targeted interventions because an aggregate policy rate cannot directly resolve structural barriers to credit.

questions.question: How sensitive is the inflation forecast to the Oil Fuel Fund’s ability to cushion energy costs?
questions.evidence: Compare the minutes’ assumptions with the fund’s financial statements and retail fuel price schedules.

questions.question: How much of the growth revision survives methodological changes?
questions.evidence: Reconcile old and revised output and manufacturing vintages, keeping growth rates and levels distinct.

questions.question: Which targeted measures can reach borrowers facing credit rationing?
questions.evidence: Track eligible SME borrowing, risk grades and arrears before and after changes in guarantee or lending programmes.

locator: Edited minutes pp. 1–4, especially the inflation outlook, financial conditions and monetary policy considerations.

title: China Monetary Policy Report, Q3 2026
locator: PBOC original report on Shanghai government host. See executive summary, Part II §1 and the policy outlook. The original report was disseminated 11 November, before Shanghai’s republication.
summary:
The PBOC retained a moderately loose stance and described a recovery with first-three-quarter growth of 4.6% year on year, but with supply still stronger than demand and uneven sector performance. It set out three channels: ample system liquidity, lower all-in financing costs and targeted support to selected activities. Among targeted changes were a 25 basis point reduction in the pledged supplementary lending rate and additional lending capacity for technology and small businesses. An authorised programme ceiling is a facility parameter rather than evidence that funds were drawn.

The operating chapter explains why the switch to a daily fixed-rate overnight reverse repo matters. It narrows the distance between the policy instrument’s maturity and overnight traded funding. The report describes a 1.25% overnight operation rate from the new daily framework and a separate seven-day tender principally around liquidity pressure points. It reports earlier injections through several longer tools to offset drains including tax and bond issuance. The policy outlook emphasises stronger countercyclical adjustment, flexible timing and a managed RMB float with protection against overshooting. These are the bank’s outlook and reported operations as of publication.

questions.question: Does the overnight framework reduce liquidity dislocations?
questions.evidence: Compare DR001, DR007 and their dispersion during matched tax dates and month-ends, adjusting for government cash flows.

questions.question: Does cheaper or targeted funding reach businesses facing weak demand?
questions.evidence: Check tool drawdowns, effective rates and fee disclosures for borrowers rather than programme limits alone.

questions.question: Is credit formation broadening beyond policy-supported sectors?
questions.evidence: Review the composition of aggregate financing and private loan demand alongside quarterly data on private investment and household spending.

coverageLimitation: Analysis covers the executive summary, main operations and policy outlook. Detailed tables and appendices were not independently checked.

title: Abigail Ng: From Execution to Impact, Financing Asia’s Transition and Resilience
locator: Transition taxonomy, FAST-P deployment, and adaptation and resilience sections
summary:
Ng argues that financing depends on clarity about viable projects, their underlying economics and how risk is allocated. She discusses guidance on transition-enabling activities, financing platforms, carbon-market capabilities and an example of a US$50 million financing announcement for distributed solar and storage. The projected emissions reductions in the speech describe estimated future effects from the projects.

She says adaptation and resilience are at an earlier stage of measurement and financing than mitigation. Benefits can be specific to a location or risk, making them harder to compare than a standard emissions measure. Her concluding questions concern how broadly frameworks are used, whether catalytic finance reaches otherwise overlooked projects and whether deployed capital produces measurable effects. The relevance is to financing channels, project economics and risk allocation, without a monetary policy signal.

questions.question: Which projects depend on catalytic capital to proceed?
questions.evidence: Review investment mandates, financing terms and credible counterfactuals for projects already funded.

questions.question: Do expected emissions savings survive operating and financing assumptions?
questions.evidence: Compare project verification and generation data with stated forecasts over time.

questions.question: How can adaptation investors compare financial resilience outcomes?
questions.evidence: Use measures tied to asset loss, financing or recovery prospects across hazards and locations.

title: AI and Regional Labor Markets
locator: Official English research summary and linked BOK Issue Note 2026-25; Korean edition appeared in September.
summary:
The staff study estimates occupational and regional exposure separately for generative, agentic and physical AI. It finds more concentration of generative and agentic exposure in metropolitan Seoul and other centres for knowledge services, while several manufacturing and agricultural regions have relatively higher exposure to physical AI. In early observations, employment grew faster in occupations with higher generative or agentic exposure, driven by the metropolitan area. Occupational composition both determines measured exposure and can explain different regional employment outcomes. The authors explicitly caution that early regional associations do not establish that AI caused changes in employment.

The distinction is useful when assessing whether a technology-led upswing in output is broadly shared. Regional purchasing power, migration and occupations can respond differently even if nationwide productivity improves. The November posting is the English-language edition and should not be dated or treated as newly released Korean evidence without checking the original publication.

questions.question: Does exposure translate to realised adoption and productivity?
questions.evidence: Track uptake and measured output by occupation and region, allowing for task and firm composition.

questions.question: Are regions following different pre-existing growth paths?
questions.evidence: Test pre-trends in regional hiring before AI adoption and compare the same occupations across regions.

questions.question: How do gains in knowledge occupations compare with pressures in production jobs?
questions.evidence: Compare vacancies, worker flows and wage growth by AI category exposure rather than using employment stocks alone.

coverageLimitation: Analysis uses the official web summary. The detailed charts and statistical specifications in the attachment were not verified.

title: The low-gear labour market — Clare Lombardelli
summary:
Lombardelli argued that UK labour demand had cooled mainly through lower hiring while dismissals stayed relatively low. Incumbent workers were relatively protected while new entrants faced fewer openings. This cyclical adjustment comes on top of a longer decline in job turnover. Chart 10 shows the quarterly job-to-job switching rate running just over 2% in the preceding year, compared with more than 3% three decades earlier. The age breakdown also shows a disproportionately large contribution from young people to the rise in unemployment since mid-2022.

The policy question is whether job seekers can fill the roles employers have available. If matching has weakened, unemployment can increase without producing the usual restraint on wages. Lombardelli did not infer a material change in equilibrium unemployment from the moderate increases seen so far. Lower mobility could weigh on productivity and slow the reallocation needed to capture AI gains, but the size of those effects remains uncertain.

questions.question: How much of the rise in unemployment reflects weaker matching?
questions.evidence: Decompose job-finding and separation rates by age and sector, and measure vacancy duration and skill mismatch.

questions.question: Have softer hiring conditions moderated pay in occupations that are still recruiting?
questions.evidence: Compare pay settlements and vacancy wages for switchers and stayers by sector rather than relying on aggregate earnings.

questions.question: Where could mobility constraints delay AI-related productivity gains?
questions.evidence: Compare firm adoption and productivity data with occupations’ hiring, retraining and reassignment patterns.

locator: Charts 10, 14–15 and 18, with the discussion of equilibrium unemployment.

title: The Swiss National Bank, its monetary policy and the Swiss economy — Antoine Martin
summary: Martin compared the Swiss and US monetary policy frameworks. The SNB’s rate is its main tool, supplemented by foreign exchange interventions. The importance of the franc reflects Switzerland’s openness and safe-haven status. The inflation forecast serves as a guide to the setting of policy. The presentation illustrates how different mandates and economic conditions can lead to different instruments and balance-sheet exposures. On current conditions, it highlights elevated energy costs, interest-rate differentials and continued expected Swiss growth. The inflation assessment referred back to September, when the conditional outlook had risen slightly since June.

questions.question: How might the franc respond when rate differentials widen and risk appetite falls?
questions.evidence: Compare CHF exchange rates with relative yields and risk measures.

questions.question: Which price pressures are imported?
questions.evidence: Compare energy and exchange-rate measures with Swiss domestic services prices.

questions.question: What would shift the September assessment?
questions.evidence: Compare newer price and activity data with the projections.

locator: Presentation slides 19–32
coverageLimitation: Official slide deck reviewed. No separate transcript was available.

title: Summary of Opinions at the Monetary Policy Meeting on October 29 and 30
locator: Footnote on preparation and §§I–III, especially §II on monetary policy.
summary:
The edited summary shows different assessments of the costs of waiting. Some views support the hold while the Board assesses earlier tightening, soft spots in activity and weaker consumption momentum. Others favour further accommodation withdrawal because underlying inflation is broadly at the objective and stimulus remains in place. One argument stresses being able to act promptly by bringing the policy rate toward neutral; another stresses several months of observation after each move. The report gives individual opinions without assigning them to named members or establishing a numeric distribution of policy preferences.

Evidence discussed includes rising wages and prices, a labour shortage and uncertainty around the persistence of oil, semiconductor and other cost shocks. Some participants favoured watching the next spring wage bargaining cycle and firms’ pass-through behaviour. Broader AI demand helps exports and investment, but its industrial concentration limits what can be inferred for household spending. This document was published on 10 November and describes the October policy meeting.

questions.question: How would we detect whether disagreement narrowed after the meeting?
questions.evidence: Use the decision’s published vote, subsequent named speeches and future vote records to distinguish documented dissent from unattributed views.

questions.question: Which data separate weak consumption from restrictive rate transmission?
questions.evidence: Compare real consumption, corporate funding and new mortgage conditions against timing of earlier hikes and energy-cost changes.

questions.question: Are inflation expectations anchoring near target?
questions.evidence: Compare household and business survey distributions with wage settlements, realised services prices and inflation compensation.

title: Summary of Governing Council deliberations: Fixed announcement date of October 28, 2026
summary:
The minutes explain why Governing Council tightened even with core inflation near 2% and slack remaining. Members saw direct energy effects in headline CPI but judged that prolonged high fuel and materials costs could affect a wider set of prices. Surveys suggested firms expected to pass on more of their costs. Longer-term expectations remained anchored, while near-term expectations had risen.

Members differed on the timing and extent of pass-through. Higher expected inflation and a modestly stronger growth outlook supported the October increase to 2.50%. The minutes place particular weight on the duration of the shock and whether costs broaden beyond energy-sensitive components. These are deliberations for the October decision, published in November.
locator: Canadian economy, inflation and considerations for monetary policy

questions.question: What evidence would show that the energy shock is becoming persistent inflation?
questions.evidence: Compare wage-setting, CPI diffusion and cost pass-through in business surveys with historical episodes.

questions.question: Can tighter credit offset the improved growth outlook?

questions.question: Did the minutes alter pricing beyond the original decision?

title: Sticky-Price CPI: October 2026 release
summary: The Atlanta Fed separates CPI items by how often prices typically change. Its slow-adjusting basket grew 4.7% at an annualised rate in October following 3.4% in September, and 3.1% over twelve months. Core sticky CPI also rose 4.7% annualised in October and 3.1% year over year. Flexible CPI grew 3.0% annualised in October and 6.2% over twelve months. The two horizons therefore rank the baskets differently. The release offers a measure of price adjustment frequency without isolating how persistent this month's movement will be.
locator: Release text and charts for sticky, core sticky and flexible CPI

questions.question: Which slow-adjusting items account for the October pickup?
questions.evidence: Use component weights and prices in the associated data download.

questions.question: Is October's increase unusual after averaging three months?
questions.evidence: Compare recent annualised rates across the chart's horizons.

questions.question: Does the pickup persist when shelter is excluded?
questions.evidence: Compare alternative sticky and underlying inflation measures with the same timing.

title: Paul Conway: How is the New Zealand economy tracking?
locator: Speaking notes, slides 2–5 and discussion of the outlook
summary:
Conway explained his own October vote for a 25 basis point hike while the committee held the OCR at 2.75%. He and the other dissenters put more weight on high core inflation and rising breadth than the hold voters, who wanted time to see the effect of previous increases on an uneven domestic recovery. He characterised the vote as a difference about the timing and risk management of a shared, conditional tightening direction.

He noted that subsequently released labour data were relatively weak and that oil prices and regional AI-related equity valuations had fallen. This matters for interpreting an earlier affirmative hike vote: the new evidence could change the balance between persistence and weaker demand, and the speech does not promise the next vote. Conway’s presentation also makes clear what is extrapolation: the previous 4.4% fourth-quarter inflation projection used oil futures at the time of the October review.

title: Minutes of the Monetary Policy Meeting of 3 November 2026
summary: The minutes discuss the increase from 1.75% to 2% against firmer activity and a rising risk of energy costs spreading into broader inflation. They include a 1.6% September reading excluding energy and temporary fiscal effects, below the 1.8% projected in September. Lower-than-anticipated travel inflation helped explain the surprise. Several members discussed a risk that stronger demand would facilitate pass-through while weaker activity could contain it. The minutes were published on 10 November after the rate decision was announced.

title: Minutes of the Monetary Policy Board Meeting (October 2026)
locator: Official release abstract. The published PDF attachment was not accessible for the member-by-member discussion.
summary: The release abstract confirms all members considered it appropriate to leave the rate at 3.00% until the next meeting at the 22 October meeting. This was a backward-looking publication on 10 November. The abstract attributes the unanimous judgement to domestic and international conditions taken together. title: Minutes of the 282nd Copom meeting
summary:
The minutes explain the 3–4 November decision to keep the Selic target at 13.75%. Copom described a sharper slowdown in cyclical activity and early cooling in the labour market, alongside accelerating headline and underlying inflation above the tolerance range. The external backdrop, including higher energy costs and tighter policy in advanced economies, added to uncertainty.

In the reference scenario the committee projected IPCA inflation at 5.6% for 2026, 4.7% for 2027 and 3.5% at the policy-relevant horizon in the second quarter of 2028. The interest-rate assumption comes from Focus survey paths. Separately, Focus respondents expected 5.2% and 4.8% inflation in 2026 and 2027. The committee’s risk balance skewed upward because of potentially de-anchored expectations, services persistence and supply or currency effects, while sharper activity deterioration remained a downside risk.
locator: Sections A–C, paragraphs 1–18 and Table 1

questions.evidence: Compare services IPCA, labour costs and credit-sensitive consumption against the minutes’ assessment.

questions.question: How dependent is the inflation projection on the assumed Selic path?
questions.evidence: Re-run the projection under less easing than the Focus path and monitor subsequent committee forecasts.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: Michelle Bowman · The U.S. Economy and Considerations for Monetary Policy
locator: October FOMC review, Inflation, Financial Conditions, Energy Markets, AI Buildout and The Path Forward
summary:
Bowman backed the October hold at 3.75–4.00% but described persistent and potentially broadening price pressure against a more stable labour market. From that morning’s CPI data she inferred that October core PCE inflation was likely near 3.3% year over year, an estimate made before the PCE release. Low hiring and low layoffs complicated her reading of labour resilience. Her forecast for inflation to move closer to target the next year depended partly on tariffs, energy and AI-related price pressures easing.

She described how near-term AI investment competes for limited inputs while adoption could raise productivity and lower costs over a longer horizon. Greater external financing, including contingent obligations, increases the potential spillovers if revenues disappoint. She said higher private borrowing costs, wider spreads and lower equity valuations had tightened financial conditions somewhat, a consideration when weighing additional rate increases. Identical remarks appeared at more than one event on the same day.

questions.question: Is inflation broadening beyond the categories Bowman identifies?
questions.evidence: Check PCE component contributions, diffusion and inflation expectations.

questions.question: Could low hiring become falling employment if layoffs increase?
questions.evidence: Compare claims and job-finding rates with the November labour release.

questions.question: How much could rising spreads slow the AI buildout?
questions.evidence: Review capex funding disclosures and issuer spreads. For an event study verify the first public release and account for the same-day CPI report.

title: MAS launches central-bank gold vaulting and announces wholesale gold tax changes
locator: Paragraphs 1–7, gold custody, GST treatment and expected rollout
summary:
MAS announced a gold custody offering aimed at official institutions and an enhanced GST framework with the Ministry of Finance for wholesale investment precious metal gold activities. It plans to use the national currency vault, which the announcement says can hold up to 500 tonnes, and offer custody accounts to selected bullion banks. MAS frames the package around physical settlement, sovereign custody options and better Asian-hours access to trading liquidity.

The stated timing is for live trading and operations to begin in the first quarter of 2027, with an exchange-listed physically deliverable kilobar futures contract targeted for the second quarter. The capacity figure describes storage potential. The figures and timelines do not establish take-up, announced allocation shifts, or how prices will respond. The research value lies in how infrastructure and tax treatment could affect transaction costs and regional liquidity if participants migrate trading and settlement.

questions.question: Does the new framework reduce the cost of physical arbitrage?
questions.evidence: Compare clearing, storage and tax costs across Asian hubs once the rules take effect.

questions.question: Could deeper liquidity improve Asian-hours price discovery?
questions.evidence: Measure venue-specific turnover, basis, spreads and price leadership after live trading begins.

questions.question: Will reserve managers actually use the new custody service?
questions.evidence: Look for official usage disclosures and distinguish transfers of existing holdings from new demand.

institution: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
title: Labor Market Conditions Indicators: October 2026
summary: The Kansas City Fed’s level-of-activity indicator rose from 0.29 to 0.37 in October, above its historical average, while momentum was little changed at 0.27. The most important positive contribution to the improvement came from an increase in the share of small firms reporting positions they could not fill, which rose from 32% to 36%. An increase in involuntary part-time work was the largest drag. The level and momentum indices give different readings and combine indicators that can move in opposite directions.
locator: Dated release, both index charts and the contribution table on p. 2

title: Economic Outlook
summary: Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson reports stronger growth and more broadly distributed job creation than she had expected. She says September headline PCE inflation reached 3.6% year over year and that measures of underlying inflation remained in a 2.5–3% range. She identifies energy, tariffs and AI-related demand as price pressures and sees more uncertainty around energy and AI than around fading tariff effects. She judges monetary policy should be somewhat restrictive. She supported the September hike and October hold and indicates further action is likely, without specifying an unconditional path.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: Christopher Waller · The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism
locator: Opening account of October vote, labour-market flows and figures 1–2, concluding policy discussion
summary:
Waller supported the October hold in part because communication had already led markets to price in some tightening. He argued that credibility would erode and financial conditions would loosen if the expected hikes were indefinitely delayed. Compared with his October 8 remarks, he gave a more explicit next-meeting preference: he leaned toward 25 basis points and said a 50 basis point increase could warrant consideration if the forthcoming inflation data were weak on disinflation.

His labour discussion separates stable net employment from low hiring and low separations. The two charts show that both rates were depressed relative to historical experience used in the speech. He considered competing explanations, including better matching versus reduced mobility, and saw the downside of longer unemployment spells if low hiring persists. The speech preceded that day's CPI release, so its market window needs to end before the release or otherwise account for it.

questions.question: Was the larger move already priced after the October meeting?
questions.evidence: Use pre-speech futures or options around December and distinguish its release window from CPI.

questions.question: Does lower churn reflect better matches or weakening demand?
questions.evidence: Compare worker flow, quits and job-finding data and track unemployment duration.

questions.question: What drove the last several core CPI readings?
questions.evidence: Use the component-level releases available to Waller and compare the subsequently published print as a separate event.

title: Sarah Hunter: What Happens to the Economy as ‘Intelligence’ Gets Cheaper?
locator: Diagram of economic channels, Inflation section, neutral rate estimates and Conclusion
summary:
Hunter examines the timing mismatch between AI investment, which raises demand immediately, and broader productive gains, which take time and vary widely across studies. Near-term investment runs into limited capacity in data centres, technology goods and complementary inputs. The speech’s cross-country price charts show stronger increases in several exposed goods, especially in the United States, while the theoretical framework allows rising supply to relieve those bottlenecks over time.

The speech also distinguishes the effects of AI on the level of real activity, inflation and the neutral rate. Stronger investment demand could raise the neutral rate, but the range is wide and depends on diffusion, the labour market and households’ response. Stronger demand can eventually accompany stronger productive capacity, so favourable productivity is compatible with a broadly neutral longer-run effect on inflation. Hunter presents channels and uncertainties rather than a short-term rate call.

questions.question: Which bottlenecks are visible in Australia’s prices today?
questions.evidence: Compare affected CPI components with import unit values, domestic construction costs and investment plans.

questions.question: What would demonstrate a persistent productive-capacity gain?
questions.evidence: Look for output per hour and adoption changes outside technology producers and early adopters.

questions.question: Would a higher neutral rate alter interpretation of long yields?
questions.evidence: Compare model estimates and investment scenarios against the neutral-rate range in the speech.

institution: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
title: Inflation Expectations Stable; Labor Market Expectations Mixed
summary: The October Survey of Consumer Expectations found unchanged median inflation expectations of 3.9%, 3.3% and 3.0% at the one-, three- and five-year horizons. The labour picture was mixed. The mean estimated probability of higher unemployment a year later rose to 45.3%, the highest since April 2020, with respondents without a college degree driving the increase. Expectations of finding a job conditional on a layoff also improved. Income and spending expectations were broadly stable while delinquency expectations worsened. The release measures households’ reported expectations rather than realised outcomes.
locator: Survey field dates and sections on inflation, labour markets and household finance

questions.question: Does stable median inflation conceal changes in uncertainty or the tails?
questions.evidence: Compare the report’s disagreement measures and underlying respondent distributions.

questions.question: Why did unemployment and conditional job-finding expectations increase together?
questions.evidence: Examine respondent groups, measures of layoff risk and actual hiring data.

questions.question: Does expected delinquency predict deterioration in credit?
questions.evidence: Compare the next household credit report with the survey’s expectations.

title: Consumer Survey October 2026: Consumer Confidence Increasing
summary:
Bank Indonesia reported that October consumer confidence rose from 118.1 to 119.9. The survey uses 100 as its threshold for optimism. Its Current Economic Condition Index rose from 107.5 to 109.1, while the Consumer Expectation Index increased from 128.7 to 130.7.

The decomposition shows improvement in both readings, with expectations higher than the current-conditions measure. Survey sentiment can inform a consumption outlook. It takes data on actual purchases and household income to judge how far the improvement is carrying through to demand.

questions.question: Which households and spending categories account for the improvement?
questions.evidence: Review the survey breakdown by income, spending and region.

questions.question: Is the confidence improvement visible in spending?
questions.evidence: Compare retail sales, payment data and durable goods purchases in the same window.

questions.question: Does confidence hold as external and funding conditions change?
questions.evidence: Track later confidence and spending readings alongside real income and loan rates.

locator: Release 28/245/DKom, main two paragraphs.

title: Kazuo Ueda: Japan’s Current Account Surplus and Corporate Adjustment
locator: Official posting dated 7 November; lecture delivered 6 November. §§II–VI and charts 6, 9 and 12–13.
summary:
Ueda’s central argument is that corporate balance-sheet repair, weak expected domestic returns and outward investment explain Japan’s sustained external surplus better than a simple story about labour scarcity. Firms cut domestic investment after the bubble and prioritised debt reduction, then accumulated buffers or invested overseas. As the stock of foreign assets grew, overseas investment income became more important to the current account than the earlier merchandise-surplus story. Some overseas profits remain abroad despite being counted in Japan’s income and savings statistics.

Demographics matter in this explanation through expectations of a smaller market, even before workers became scarce. For the earlier decades, Ueda points to unused domestic capacity and elevated unemployment as evidence against a simple binding labour-supply explanation. More recently, actual labour shortages are encouraging automation and investment at home. This could narrow excess saving, although large foreign-asset stocks and the return differential could sustain primary income. These are structural channels; the lecture does not announce an imminent rate or exchange-rate decision.

questions.question: Will higher domestic investment persist enough to reduce net corporate saving?
questions.evidence: Compare sector funding balances, firms’ expected domestic returns and realised capital outlays across vintages.

questions.question: How much does primary income translate into FX demand?
questions.evidence: Compare reinvested and repatriated earnings against outward investments and FX hedging activity.

questions.question: Could labour shortages change both the expected return on capital and scale of investment abroad?
questions.evidence: Distinguish domestic labour-saving capex from cross-border acquisitions by firm size and industry.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Summary of Interbank Call Loan and Commercial Paper Markets (October 2026)
locator: Sections I–II and tables 1–4; commercial paper averages marked preliminary.
summary:
The CBC reports a monthly average weighted overnight call rate of 0.811%, down 0.006 percentage points, even as daily interbank turnover and daily outstanding balances rose. In contrast, preliminary averages for one- to thirty-day commercial paper increased to 1.95% in the primary market and 1.75% in the secondary market. The respective increases were 3 and 23 basis points. That divergence matters for financing analysis, because overnight borrowing among banks and paper issued or traded by companies differ in tenor, counterparties and composition.

The release describes October averages. It records funding outcomes and no new policy rate vote. A change in absolute differences between market segments may reflect a change in issuer or maturity mix. It can justify a closer look at financing conditions, but does not itself identify a change in the credit premium for fixed issuer, tenor and date.

questions.question: Does the secondary paper increase survive matching by tenor and credit quality?
questions.evidence: Separate observations by issuer, residual maturity and credit rating in official transaction or dealer data.

questions.question: What drove the sharp rise in interbank volumes?
questions.evidence: Look at reserve positions, calendar effects and volumes by lender and borrower alongside the turnover tables.

questions.question: Is the month’s average representative of a persistent move?
questions.evidence: Compare higher-frequency observations with previous and subsequent month-end patterns.

title: Pan Gongsheng’s Report to the National People’s Congress Standing Committee on Financial Work
locator: State Council report delivered by PBOC Governor on 3 November, official PBOC-sourced republication dated 6 November. Sections II.1–2 and III.1, III.3, III.5.
summary:
Reporting to the legislature on State Council financial work, Pan described continued moderately loose policy alongside greater use of rates and structural facilities. He pointed to liquidity management through reverse repos, medium-term lending and bond operations, with targeted measures in January and September. September weighted rates on new corporate lending and personal mortgages were 2.96% and 3.05%, respectively. The report presents these as low financing costs during the reporting window, alongside favourable aggregate measures for bank resilience.

Its forward agenda combines low-cost financing and RMB stability with reforms to transmission and financial regulation. It highlights liquidity support for large nonbank redemptions and the role of capital-market instruments in supporting market functioning. It also describes risks from property, local financing and particular institutions. This is a report of actions and policy objectives by the governor on behalf of the State Council. References to previous yields and currency performance describe longer windows and cannot measure the reaction to delivery or publication.

questions.question: Which borrowers actually received the decline in headline rates?
questions.evidence: Compare weighted and borrower-level new lending rates and financing fees against mix shifts by loan type.

questions.question: How might open-market and nonbank liquidity support transmit during stress?
questions.evidence: Compare eligible participants, collateral, utilisation and spreads across the rescue and broader funding channels.

questions.question: Are local financing and property risks receding at similar rates?
questions.evidence: Compare cash-flow coverage, loan rollovers and collateral performance by sector with central supervisory data.

title: NBP November Inflation Report – inflation and GDP projection
locator: NBP-authored Polish Inflation Report reviewed via an accessible copy because the official page returned HTTP 403. Scope covers chapter 4: methodology, table 4.2, charts 4.24–4.27 and table 4.3.
summary: NBP staff’s NECMOD projection holds the reference rate at 3.75% and uses data through 15 October. It raises 2027 CPI inflation to 4.2% from July’s 2.7%, led by energy with contributions from food and core inflation. The 2027 real GDP forecast remains 2.8%. More persistent input costs weaken projected consumption and investment while stronger starting activity offsets part of that drag. These are conditional projections.

questions.question: How much of the inflation revision depends on administered energy prices?
questions.evidence: Check the forecast revision decomposition and compare its energy assumptions with actual tariff decisions.

questions.question: Does unchanged annual GDP growth hide different drivers?
questions.evidence: Use the contribution charts and quarterly paths to trace the drag on private consumption and investment against the stronger starting point.

questions.question: How symmetric are the forecast risks?
questions.evidence: Read the fan charts and compare alternative energy and ETS2 scenarios with the central assumptions and forecasting horizon.

title: Gabriel Cuadra · Crecimiento económico en México: retos y perspectivas
locator: Investment and productivity exhibits, pp. 16–22
summary:
Cuadra’s growth presentation separates recent investment outcomes from long-run productivity. The exhibits include aggregate productivity, a cross-industry comparison and a plot of annual investment and productivity changes. The industry exhibit shows substantial variation, which matters if improvements in a few large sectors are treated as an economy-wide supply shock.

The AI adoption slides report survey results for establishments with more than 100 employees. Reported adoption and intended future use are separate measures, and firms’ perceived impact on employment or sales per worker cannot establish a causal productivity effect. The research question is whether diffusion leads to measured efficiency gains outside the firms already at the frontier.

questions.question: How broadly distributed are productivity improvements?
questions.evidence: Use industry productivity data, sector weights and firm-level adoption evidence.

questions.question: Does faster capital formation coincide with later productivity gains?
questions.evidence: Check capital measurement, lags and possible reverse causality in the investment relationship.

questions.question: Can adoption gains be extrapolated to smaller firms?
questions.evidence: Seek comparable surveys that include establishments below the EMAER size threshold.

coverageLimitation: Analysis covers the named slides in the official deck. The archive date is the date Banxico lists for the presentation.

title: Weathering the Storm: The Importance of Trust and Time for Operational Resilience
summary: The article uses a June settlement delay to show how problems in central clearing can affect the implementation of monetary policy. The delay raised clearing utilities’ balances at the Fed for a day, reducing reserve balances held by banks. The authors explain why a sufficiently large reserves drain could raise demand for market funding. Market rates did not move in this episode. The article suggests the ample-reserves cushion was one possible reason that the reserve shift did not translate into higher short rates. Its stylised reserve supply and demand chart describes how the same kind of incident could have different effects if reserves became scarce.
locator: June case study and Figures 1–2, based on 5 November seminar remarks

questions.question: What reserve conditions would make a similar delay matter for repo and fed funds?
questions.evidence: Compare reserve levels and money-market sensitivity around past settlement disruptions.

questions.question: Do relevant clearing entities experience mismatched payment timing?
questions.evidence: Use public settlement calendars and balance-sheet categories to trace flows.

questions.question: Which funding measures are most informative during operational stress?
questions.evidence: Compare intraday moves across repo and fed funds alongside settlement information.

title: Transmission and conduct of monetary policy in Switzerland — Martin Schlegel
summary:
Schlegel argued that exchange rates are central to Swiss policy transmission because they affect import prices directly and export competitiveness and demand indirectly. The SNB’s policy rate is its main instrument, with foreign-exchange intervention available where needed. A June 2022 hike that exceeded market expectations was followed in his example by higher longer-maturity rates, a stronger franc and lower equities. The speech separately presents estimates in which higher rates reduce inflation and output after a year. The chart evidence relates to the historical event and estimated transmission, with no claim about the price reaction to this speech.

The speaker contrasted purchases of foreign exchange during crisis-era appreciation pressure with foreign-currency sales alongside rate increases during the post-pandemic inflation surge. That history illustrates how the direction of intervention depends on what the exchange rate is doing to the price stability outlook.

questions.question: How large is exchange-rate pass-through for the current mix of imported goods?
questions.evidence: Compare the SNB’s cited transmission estimates against observed changes in import prices and exchange rates by product.

questions.question: When has the SNB preferred intervention to a further rate change?
questions.evidence: Map dated policy assessments and disclosed FX transactions to inflation forecasts and changes in the effective franc.

questions.question: What changes the asset response across policy cycles?
questions.evidence: Compare high-frequency rates, CHF and equity reactions to prior surprises and account for safe-haven flows.

locator: Sections 1–3 and Slides 6–10.

title: Rate decision November 2026
summary:
The committee held the policy rate at 4.5% after the September increase. It still expected rates to stay elevated for a time and retained the option to raise them if the inflation outlook warranted. It did not prepare new forecasts because developments had not materially changed the September outlook. September CPI inflation was 3.4% and CPI-ATE 3.0%, with domestically produced goods and services inflation stronger than expected and imported consumer goods inflation weaker. The committee judged capacity use slightly below normal, and registered unemployment stayed at 2% in October.

A stronger krone could damp inflation while higher energy costs worked in the opposite direction. The decision reports that the market priced an increase by the end of the first half of 2027. The September forecast had envisaged rates remaining around 4.5% for a period before edging down. This is a comparison between a contemporaneous market reading and an earlier projection. It does not establish any announcement surprise.

questions.question: Is domestic inflation persistent enough to trigger the option to hike?
questions.evidence: Track CPI-ATE composition, wage settlements and business costs relative to the September projections.

questions.question: Will the krone appreciation offset higher energy prices?
questions.evidence: Compare the effective exchange rate, imported goods prices and domestic power and fuel prices using the bank’s assumed paths.

questions.question: How large was the gap between market pricing and the September path?
questions.evidence: Retrieve NOK OIS or FRA pricing around release and compare the market-implied distribution with the September projections.

locator: Decision, Governor’s statement and Summary of the Committee’s deliberations.

title: October policy meeting minutes: hold at 12.25%
summary:
The minutes show why four directors paused and three favoured another 25 basis point hike. The majority thought the decline in core inflation and slower domestic demand might be reducing excess demand. It preferred to observe more data and limit the risk of overtightening while the effects of El Niño remained uncertain.

The dissenters judged another hike necessary to regain credibility and contain second-round effects. They argued that letting inflation remain high would make it harder to respond countercyclically once the output gap turns negative. The two sides agree that inflation is too high and differ on the weight to give preliminary signs of slowing demand versus the cost of waiting.
locator: Sections giving the majority and dissenting arguments

questions.question: Which of the October vote groups best anticipated subsequent core inflation?
questions.evidence: Track the categories the majority pointed to and compare them with the dissenters’ second-round risk indicators.

questions.question: What combination of fiscal restraint and higher rates would generate the largest activity drag?
questions.evidence: Look at updated spending plans, credit growth and the report’s output-gap trajectory.

questions.question: Does the market view the disagreement as front-loaded hiking risk?
questions.evidence: Compare short and intermediate swaps and bond-derived inflation expectations around the minutes release.

coverageNote: Main minutes text reviewed. Statistical appendix and separate capital-markets attachment are outside this card.

title: Navigating stormy waters: reflections on monetary policy — Isabel Schnabel
summary:
Schnabel argued for preserving policy flexibility when shocks are large, overlapping and persistent. She emphasised that a supply shock can spread through indirect costs, wages and inflation expectations, so the inflation outlook and economic context matter for the response. In this instance, the ECB’s staff scenarios explored different degrees of persistence and pass-through. She pointed to a rise in medium- to longer-term household inflation expectations in the wake of the latest energy shock, while identifying other shocks to demand and capacity linked to AI investment and fiscal spending.

She also linked monetary autonomy to fiscal and financial resilience. With greater public debt, the reduction in central bank portfolios leaves a larger role for price-sensitive private holders. Financial leverage and liquidity mismatch can then amplify stress in sovereign markets. These observations identify vulnerabilities and policy trade-offs rather than a meeting-specific rate recommendation.

questions.question: Which expectation measures show persistent de-anchoring?
questions.evidence: Compare the household measures highlighted in Slide 8 with wage settlements, professional surveys and inflation-linked market prices adjusted for premia.

questions.question: How sensitive are outcomes to the duration and pass-through of the energy shock?
questions.evidence: Compare staff scenario assumptions to firm pricing and the evolution of gas and oil forward curves.

questions.question: How much sovereign duration is held by leveraged intermediaries?
questions.evidence: Check supervisory data on non-bank leverage, bond and repo positions, and changes in dealer capacity.

locator: Takeaways one to three, including Slide 8 and the discussion of sovereign-market vulnerabilities.

title: Monetary Policy Statement
summary:
Bank Negara Malaysia held the Overnight Policy Rate at 2.75%. The MPC judged the setting consistent with its growth and price stability outlook. It expected 2026 growth above 5%, attributing the strength to exports and sustained domestic demand. For 2027 it pointed to technology shipments and tourism alongside investment, labour market conditions and support to consumption from Budget 2027.

The statement reported year-to-date headline and core inflation averaging 1.8% and 1.9%, respectively. The MPC expected both to rise modestly in 2027 as energy and commodity costs, geopolitical risks and weather fed through, with domestic measures and stable demand tempering the effect. A prolonged Middle East conflict could also weigh on activity, as could lower commodity production. The statement gives a decision and conditional outlook with a published 15:00 local embargo time, which offers a starting point for measuring any market repricing.

questions.question: How much of the 2027 inflation risk depends on domestic fuel policy?
questions.evidence: Compare budget measures and administered-price assumptions with CPI components and pass-through estimates.

questions.question: How much of the growth outlook depends on technology demand?
questions.evidence: Break exports and investment into technology-sensitive and other components, with imports separated from domestic value added.

questions.question: Was the communication a surprise even if the hold was expected?
questions.evidence: Compare OPR expectations and timestamped ringgit and short-tenor rate moves around the embargo.

locator: Policy decision, domestic economy and inflation outlook paragraphs; embargo heading.

title: Monetary Policy Report — November 2026
summary: The Bank’s November projections put the peak in UK inflation at around 5% in the second quarter of 2027. September’s 3.5% reading was 0.4 percentage points above July’s projection, with fuel and utility prices accounting for much of the overshoot relative to target. Chart 1.1 shows actual CPI and successive projection vintages. Some measures of services inflation and wage growth had stopped falling. The report attributes limited indirect effects so far partly to hedges and fixed-price contracts, with some firms absorbing costs in margins. Alternative scenarios explore how persistent energy prices, demand and pricing behaviour could produce different inflation and policy outcomes.

questions.question: When would existing energy hedges roll off?
questions.evidence: Compare businesses’ contracts with forward rates and input price surveys.

questions.question: How weak would demand need to be to contain price spillovers?
questions.evidence: Compare scenario assumptions against household spending, business margins and slack.

questions.question: How much of the new outlook was priced?
questions.evidence: Compare inflation swaps and SONIA before publication and after the briefing.

locator: Charts 1.1–1.3 and Sections 3.1–3.3
coverageLimitation: Central projection and policy scenarios reviewed. Separate report boxes and annexes are outside this summary.

title: Minutes of the Monetary Policy Meeting on September 17 and 18
locator: Voting and statement sections, plus the attached September decision and named dissent.
summary:
The full minutes document September’s 7–2 vote to move the overnight guideline to about 1.25%. The dissenters were Asada and Sato. The debate included different views about the resilience of current activity, recent measured inflation and the cumulative effect of tightening. Some members wanted to act proactively as the underlying inflation trend approached 2%. Those favouring waiting gave more weight to an economy that was not clearly strong and price data that had not decisively accelerated. The decision also changed facility rates and agreed to a floating rate for a climate-related operation.

The policy statement was approved unanimously as a communication after the majority policy vote. Those are two distinct votes. The longer minutes, published 5 November, can reveal reasoning that was absent from the headline September decision. They cannot be treated as a new rate increase in November, and provide no observed market pricing as of their own publication.

questions.question: Did release of the detailed debate add information beyond the September statement and October summary?
questions.evidence: Compare the three texts and identify which arguments were new to markets on 5 November.

questions.question: Could the dissenters’ concerns constrain further tightening?
questions.evidence: Check published speeches and later votes alongside consumption, wages and survey inflation.

questions.question: How broad was implementation of the overnight-rate change?
questions.evidence: Compare facility balances and realised rates with the accompanying implementation decisions and bank price adjustments.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Foreign Exchange Reserves as of the End of October 2026
locator: Release paragraph, three drivers and portfolio exposure note.
summary: The CBC reported end-October reserves of US$596.44 billion, US$4.31 billion lower than September. Its explanation identifies returns on reserves, valuation from non-dollar currencies and operations to smooth capital flow volatility. The release does not break out those components, making the gross change unsuitable as a measure of intervention size. It also reports that foreign portfolio investors’ securities and New Taiwan dollar deposits were worth US$1.743 trillion. That stock is an exposure indicator rather than an estimate of a future flow.

questions.question: How much of the change was transactional?
questions.evidence: Compare published net FX purchases and sales with reserve disclosures and account for valuation and accrued investment returns.

questions.question: Was capital flow volatility associated with foreign equity flows or hedging?
questions.evidence: Compare exchange-level foreign net purchases, spot and deliverable forward activity over the month.

questions.question: Did reserves move in tandem with currency pressure after adjustment for valuation?
questions.evidence: Compare the decomposed series against same-period changes in the TWD spot rate and available liquidity indicators.

title: CNB Bank Board raises the two-week repo rate to 4.00%
locator: Board statement, Monetary Department forecast and assessment of inflation risks.
summary:
The Bank Board voted 4–3 to raise the two-week repo rate by 25 basis points to 4.00%, with the other key rates raised by the same amount. The board cited persistent core inflation, especially services, strong wage growth in a tight labour market, and continued credit and money growth. It framed the decision as protection against a second round of the global energy shock feeding expectations, wages and broader prices. Higher longer-term rates were already exerting some restriction.

The Monetary Department forecast reduced expected 2026 GDP growth from 2.2% to 1.7% and projected 2.5% for 2027. The Board nevertheless assessed inflation risks as tilted upwards, including possible fiscal expansion and continued growth in housing-related prices. Subsequent action depends on the koruna, labour conditions, fiscal plans, demand and price pass-through. The close vote shows disagreement about immediate action. Market expectations and any actual price response require separate evidence.

questions.question: Was the 25 bp increase expected, and did the statement change the path afterwards?
questions.evidence: Compare CZK front-end forwards and the koruna around the decision and briefing windows separately.

questions.question: Have energy costs passed into broader inflation?
questions.evidence: Use price indices by category, labour settlements, household expectations and firm pricing surveys.

questions.question: Is private demand strong enough to offset long-end tightening?
questions.evidence: Compare mortgage and corporate lending volumes and rates with credit conditions and activity.

title: Bank Rate increased to 4% — November 2026 Monetary Policy Summary and Minutes
summary:
The MPC raised Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4%. Eight members supported the move and Catherine Mann preferred 50 basis points. The majority considered the scale and duration of the energy shock sufficient to warrant tightening even though evidence of broader price and wage effects was limited. Recent activity had also been stronger than expected. In September, CPI was 3.5% and the direct energy contribution was about one percentage point. The committee projected inflation near 5% by mid-2027 and a subsequent decline as the energy contribution faded and restrictive policy weighed on demand.

The minutes show different views within the majority on underlying demand and what further action could be needed. Bailey identified a case for another increase if inflation risks did not soften. Mann emphasised the possibility of inflation persistence becoming more difficult to reverse. The vote establishes the decision and distribution of preferences, while realised market surprise requires pre-release pricing.

questions.question: Did the decision or the vote split move the expected Bank Rate path?
questions.evidence: Compare intraday SONIA pricing around the release and subsequent press conference with pre-event prices.

questions.question: Are costs being absorbed temporarily or reaching underlying prices?
questions.evidence: Check firms’ margin, hedge and repricing data, services inflation and pay settlements. See the associated Monetary Policy Report’s discussion of second-round effects.

questions.question: How sensitive was projected inflation to the energy futures assumption?
questions.evidence: Review the Monetary Policy Report’s alternative scenarios and the UK gas and Brent curves used to condition the forecast.

locator: Monetary Policy Summary and minutes paragraphs 2–4 and 19–23.

title: Anuncio de Política Monetaria
summary:
Banco de México lowered its overnight interbank target by 25 basis points to 6.25%, effective on 6 November. Three board members supported the cut and two voted for a hold. The decision rests on continued disinflation, expected economic slack and an assessment that existing restraint still limits demand and currency pass-through.

Headline inflation rose from 3.42% to 3.62% between the first halves of September and October as non-core prices increased. Core inflation edged down from 3.79% to 3.78%. The table raises the fourth-quarter headline forecast from 3.5% to 3.7% and core from 3.6% to 3.7%, while keeping headline convergence to 3% in the fourth quarter of 2027. The board describes a discrete adjustment and expects maintaining the new level for an extended period to support convergence. The peso depreciation and yield moves discussed in the release predate the announcement.
locator: Statement, voting paragraph, forecast table and table footnotes

questions.question: Does the easing represent a one-off adjustment in market pricing?
questions.evidence: Look for divergence between the near-term and medium-term TIIE swap curve after the statement.

questions.question: Does continued peso weakness threaten the core forecast?
questions.evidence: Track imported core goods, FX and survey inflation expectations against the board’s pass-through assumption.

questions.question: What would drive the two hold voters to change their view?
questions.evidence: Compare the next published minutes and individual policy remarks with the current statement.

title: Andrew Hauser: Trust, Expectations and Monetary Policy
locator: Graphs 1–3, evidence on trust and concluding discussion
summary:
Hauser argues that trust changes how strongly and quickly monetary policy affects expected future conditions and spending today. In Graph 1, the model holds the realised cash-rate path fixed. Output and inflation fall sooner and further when the tightening is anticipated. Graph 2 turns the question around: after a temporary foreign cost shock, achieving the same inflation path can require less tightening and a smaller GDP loss if people expect the central bank to return inflation to target promptly.

He cites firm survey responses linking expectations of timely disinflation to intended restraint in cost pass-through. Graph 3 presents an association between household trust in the RBA and lower near-term inflation expectations. The surveys and simulations show different kinds of evidence and do not establish a realised causal effect for a particular speech. His conclusion is that clarity, accountability and demonstrated delivery matter for credibility, especially after a prolonged period of elevated inflation.

questions.question: Which expectations measure best tracks the pass-through mechanism?
questions.evidence: Match firm-level planned price increases to their inflation and trust answers and check for composition effects.

questions.question: Can communication alter expectations without a rate move?
questions.evidence: Compare changes around communication events across market pricing and survey waves, accounting for simultaneous news.

questions.question: Is the trust relationship stable in large cost shocks?
questions.evidence: Test the survey relationships across industries with different exposure to input costs and demand.

title: Policy rate raised to 2 per cent
summary:
The Riksbank increased its policy rate by 25 basis points to 2%, effective 11 November. The bank cited an economy moving towards normal levels of activity and rising cost pressures from the conflict in the Middle East. It projected inflation above 2% the following year. The communication made the possibility of further tightening conditional on the inflation and activity outlook holding. That distinguishes the current increase from the uncertain path beyond it.

The mechanism is the interaction of recovery and costs. Greater demand can make energy and other input costs easier for firms to pass through, while an increase in the policy rate acts with a lag to reduce demand. The decision and guidance establish the bank’s assessment at publication. The analysis would need contemporaneous measures of market pricing to establish the announcement surprise.

questions.question: Is current inflation broadening as the recovery strengthens?
questions.evidence: Compare current CPIF excluding energy, sector price diffusion and wage measures against the November update.

questions.question: How much additional tightening was priced?
questions.evidence: Check matched-maturity SEK OIS around the announcement and compare with the bank’s conditional path.

questions.question: Does the krona amplify or cushion imported costs?
questions.evidence: Compare import prices and the trade-weighted krona with the November update’s assumptions.

locator: Decision press release and published decision in brief.

title: NBP Monetary Policy Council communiqué, 3–4 November 2026
locator: Source checked against the original communiqué reproduced by the NBP in its November Inflation Report, chapter 3, pp. 30–31. The direct release page returned HTTP 403 during review.
summary: The Council kept the reference rate at 3.75%. October flash CPI fell to 3.5% from the revised 4.1% September rate, mainly because fuel became cheaper. The Council also saw signs of lower core inflation and slower Q3 GDP growth. Its staff projection under unchanged rates nevertheless shifted the 2027 inflation range upwards. The hold therefore sat alongside weaker recent data and higher projected inflation.

questions.question: Would the 2027 projection shift survive less persistent commodity prices?
questions.evidence: Compare the projection’s energy assumptions and risks with commodity forwards and regulated prices.

questions.question: Is the fall in core inflation broad-based?
questions.evidence: Check next releases for services, housing and other persistent components, alongside wages.

questions.question: What explains the timing of any repricing?
questions.evidence: Separate the 4 November announcement, governor communication and full report publication in the event study.

title: Informe de Política Monetaria – octubre de 2026
summary:
The October report, released in November, says inflation continued to rise in the third quarter as labour costs, demand above capacity, El Niño and service-price indexation affected the CPI. The technical team projects inflation at 7.1% at end-2026 and 4.8% at end-2027, moving toward 3% in 2028. Its path depends on the effects of restrictive policy and the reversal of adverse price pressures.

The staff’s projection shows GDP growth slowing to 2.0% in 2026 and 1.7% in 2027. It puts the slowdown in the context of the August earthquake, moderating labour indicators and weaker agricultural output, following stronger second-quarter consumption and investment. It also flags the consequences of possible fiscal changes for activity and the exchange rate. The projections represent the technical team’s views.
locator: Institutional overview and published inflation and GDP figures

questions.question: How sensitive is the projected inflation path to food and regulated prices?
questions.evidence: Compare weather and agricultural scenarios with component-level CPI and published technical assumptions.

questions.question: What are plausible fiscal and reconstruction effects on growth and FX?
questions.evidence: Compare budget execution and reconstruction plans to the forecast and test how a changed exchange rate affects CPI.

questions.question: Could activity weakness arrive while prices are still rising?
questions.evidence: Track the monthly activity indicator alongside wages and services inflation to assess how the mix evolves.
