title: Forecasting the post-COVID inflation surge in Switzerland
summary: Beyeler tests whether statistical models using contemporaneously available data would have recognised the 2021–23 Swiss inflation surge as persistent. Both an aggregate CPI model and a model using 22 expenditure groups attribute much of the shock to persistent trends, with seasonal effects explicitly modelled. The disaggregated model gives a greater role to sector-specific trends than to the common trend. This retrospective model exercise depends on how persistent components are specified and estimated.

questions.question: Would the model improve forecast errors outside this episode?
questions.evidence: Compare real-time forecasts against simpler benchmarks.

questions.question: How sensitive is the result to the choice of sectors and priors?
questions.evidence: Review alternative groupings and volatility assumptions.

questions.question: Which categories give early evidence of persistence?
questions.evidence: Compare release vintages and subsequent changes in forecast errors by sector.

locator: Abstract and model design
coverageLimitation: Headline results reviewed. Full sensitivity checks are pending.

title: Abridged minutes of the Monetary Council meeting on 20 October 2026
locator: Publication date on cover; section 1, pp. 2–4, including the vote. Analysis covers the decision discussion.
summary:
The minutes, released on 4 November, show that maintaining the base rate at 5.50% was the only option discussed at the October meeting. All ten members present backed the existing rates. Members acknowledged below-band September inflation and domestically stable risk premia while highlighting high foreign yields, volatile energy and food costs and potential inflation effects of domestic budget measures.

The discussion adds detail about what was still unresolved at the meeting. Members could not fully assess the fiscal plans or their market reception at that point. The Council saw exchange-rate developments as disinflationary, with some members emphasising the positive real-rate differential and the importance of FX stability. Those observations give reasons for the unanimous hold without assuming that any particular future rate path was agreed.

questions.question: Did later fiscal details increase or reduce the scope for easing?
questions.evidence: Read the December Inflation Report’s fiscal scenario and revisions to domestic demand and inflation.

questions.question: How broadly shared was the concern about the exchange-rate channel?
questions.evidence: Compare attribution in successive minutes against the unanimous vote and changes in HUF and import prices.

questions.question: Was there a distinct reaction when the minutes were published?
questions.evidence: Use the 4 November publication timestamp to compare intraday local rates and HUF, accounting for concurrent news.

title: The Impact of Global Financial Conditions on Debt Choice and Firm Performance: Evidence from the Philippines
locator: BSP Discussion Paper 2026-08, manuscript dated October and featured online on 3 November. Selected read of §§ IV–VI, Tables 5.1 and 5.3, Figure 5.1 and the external-debt proxy footnote.
summary:
The authors find that tighter global financial conditions are associated with Philippine firms shifting their funding mix towards domestic currency. Their indicators capture different forces: the US federal funds rate measures a funding-cost channel, dollar movements and volatility capture exchange-rate risks, and the VIX measures market volatility. The analysis combines an aggregate lag model for external debt with firm-level panel estimates of debt composition and local projections for firm performance. External debt is an imperfect proxy for foreign-currency debt. The paper’s footnote describes the prevalence of foreign currency within measured external debt.

The estimated funding shift varies across firms. For example, the paper reports a greater propensity to shift towards domestic currency among several globally oriented and manufacturing firms, with globally oriented firms starting from greater foreign-currency exposure. The authors treat firm size and access to local funding as possible explanations for uneven adjustment. Those patterns matter because the ability to refinance in pesos may vary substantially across borrowers.

Higher US policy rates are associated with larger interest expenses and weaker net income. Dollar volatility is associated with lower interest expense and stronger net income for some firms. The authors view those results as consistent with firms adapting their financing, while recognising uncertainty and limited firm coverage. Figure 5.1 presents estimated responses with confidence intervals for separate income measures and levels of FX debt. The panels use different vertical scales. The estimates do not establish that realised funding changes caused later performance outcomes. These are research findings attributed to the authors rather than a BSP policy decision.

questions.question: How much of the funding adjustment depends on debt maturities and bank access?
questions.evidence: Use currency-by-maturity loan and bond data and compare firms with similar initial FX exposure.

questions.question: Would exchange-rate hedges change which firms are vulnerable?
questions.evidence: Combine currency-matched revenues and derivative positions with debt schedules and financing terms.

questions.question: Can a domestic funding buffer help smaller or unlisted firms?
questions.evidence: Seek broader administrative loan data to test whether the sample’s adjustment is representative.

questions.question: Can the Fed funding-cost channel be separated from other global shocks?
questions.evidence: Compare higher-frequency identified surprises with the authors’ proxy specifications and test lag and sample sensitivity.

title: Statement on Monetary Policy, November 2026
locator: Overview and Outlook, especially Graph 3.1, the conditioning assumptions and forecast tables
summary:
The November Statement revises the inflation outlook upwards and delays the forecast return to the target band. Its outlook combines persistent domestic capacity pressure with higher oil and refined-product prices and resilient global demand connected to AI investment. Restrictive financial conditions are expected to keep growth below potential for a period, creating spare capacity and allowing inflation to fall. The forecast uses data through 28 October.

The staff’s oil assumptions illustrate the extent of the shock: the December-quarter level is 35% higher than in the August forecast, and by end-2028 it is 11% higher. Graph 3.1 compares the paths as assumptions. The cash-rate assumption is a market path, which rises by 35 basis points by mid-2027 and then eases a little before levelling near 4.8% in 2028. Its higher level than in August is part of the forecast conditioning, rather than a Board pledge. Staff also note that higher long real yields could mean less policy restraint if they signal higher neutral rates, or tighter conditions if they mainly reflect higher term premia. This entry focuses on the forecast and its assumptions.

questions.question: How far would a persistent fuel-cost shock delay disinflation?
questions.evidence: Use the RBA’s risk scenarios and compare dated crude and refined-fuel curves with its conditioning assumptions.

questions.question: Can we disentangle neutral-rate repricing from term premia?
questions.evidence: Compare short-rate expectations, longer real yields and term-premium estimates, acknowledging model uncertainty.

questions.question: Does restrictive policy transmit as forecast?
questions.evidence: Track mortgage resets, credit growth and business investment with an August-to-November forecast comparison.

title: Rashad Cassim on the Jibar to ZARONIA transition
locator: Opening remarks, paragraphs on the revised cessation date, legacy contracts and clearing.
summary:
Deputy Governor Rashad Cassim announced that Jibar cessation would move from 31 December 2026 to 31 May 2027. He described the main obstacle as contracts that cannot be amended through ordinary transition mechanisms and need a legislative solution. The SARB also wants the dates for benchmark cessation and clearing-house conversion to line up. Different conversion dates would risk basis, hedge, valuation and operational mismatches across markets.

The remarks concerned the reference-rate transition for ZAR contracts. Cassim described ZARONIA as a near risk-free benchmark drawn from overnight wholesale deposits and asked market participants to continue their transition work. Existing and new benchmarks may therefore coexist for longer than previously planned. The speech contains a change in market infrastructure timing and no new policy-rate decision.

questions.question: Which contracts are most exposed to the delayed transition?
questions.evidence: Inventory legacy loan, bond and derivative references and map them to applicable fallback provisions.

questions.question: How much hedging risk comes from conversion dates diverging?
questions.evidence: Compare clearing timetables, hedge reference rates and the maturity profile of outstanding cash and derivative contracts.

questions.question: Is the delay already reflected in traded basis?
questions.evidence: Inspect timestamped Jibar and ZARONIA derivative quotes around the speech, with an explicit measure of liquidity.

title: Monetary Policy Board decision: cash rate raised to 4.85%
locator: Media release, opening paragraphs and Decision
summary:
The Board raised the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85%, by six votes to three. The three preferred 4.60%. The statement judged inflation broad-based and the forecast materially worse than before. Higher fuel and commodity prices mattered, alongside tighter-than-estimated domestic capacity, higher AI-related technology goods prices and business reports of continuing cost pass-through. The Board said inflation was now expected to reach the top of the 2–3% target band in late 2027, roughly three quarters later than previously forecast.

The decision tightens the current setting, while the split shows the Board did not agree on the need for another move at this meeting. The statement makes further decisions conditional on incoming data, the outlook and risks. The investment question is whether incoming evidence will require more restraint than the future path markets already price. The release provides the policy decision and forecast revision, while price observations around publication are needed to assess the surprise.

questions.question: What drove the first change in short-rate pricing?
questions.evidence: Compare AUD overnight-indexed swaps and bills immediately around publication. The November forecast was released at the same time.

questions.question: Are weak labour conditions beginning to limit pass-through?
questions.evidence: Compare local services inflation, vacancies, unemployment and liaison evidence on selling-price plans.

questions.question: Which oil assumptions are most important for the forecast timing?
questions.evidence: Compare the Statement on Monetary Policy’s conditioning assumptions with Brent and refined-product futures on 3 November.

title: Michele Bullock: November monetary policy media conference
locator: Opening statement and Q&A on policy lags, housing and aggregate demand
summary:
Bullock said the Board raised the cash rate to 4.85% because domestic capacity pressures and inflation persistence required more restraint. She distinguishes the direct rise in global oil prices from domestic demand and the effect higher costs could have on expectations and firms’ selling prices. She points to weak productivity and unexpectedly strong data-centre-related investment. Earlier tightening had already slowed spending, reduced housing prices and eased the labour market, but she expected further moderation to be needed.

In the Q&A, Bullock discusses a policy transmission lag of around a year or potentially more and describes housing as one channel whose interpretation is complicated by other policy changes. She said the RBA takes public demand as given in assessing aggregate demand. The press conference starts after the concurrent decision and projections, giving a distinct period in which to look for incremental information in her explanation.

questions.question: Did the Q&A move pricing after the initial decision?
questions.evidence: Align market data with the decision at 2.30 pm AEDT and press conference at 3.30 pm AEDT, then isolate material remarks.

questions.question: How much do revisions to domestic capacity matter relative to fuel?
questions.evidence: Compare the forecast changes, trimmed-mean inflation and activity indicators with earlier releases.

questions.question: Is the latest tightening already affecting housing beyond other policy changes?
questions.evidence: Compare credit, prices and household cash flows across regions and cohorts with different rate sensitivity.

title: Die Schweizer Wirtschaft im globalen Umfeld — Martin Schlegel
summary: Schlegel described an economy that had held up in a difficult external environment. Exports supported growth, with important contributions from pharmaceuticals and chemicals. The real trade-weighted franc had been relatively stable since 2020, but currency exposure differed across industries and export markets. Company consultations suggested improving confidence. After a particularly strong second quarter, Swiss GDP was expected to grow more moderately. A rise in inflation was largely attributed to petroleum products. This discussion referred to the SNB’s September decision to hold its policy rate at 0% and its assessment of slightly greater inflation pressure than in June.

questions.question: How much of the growth strength reflects pharmaceutical exports?
questions.evidence: Compare national accounts and export value and volume by sector.

questions.question: Which firms are most exposed to a given bilateral exchange rate?
questions.evidence: Compare export destinations and industry-specific real exchange rates.

questions.question: Are higher petroleum prices spreading to broader inflation?
questions.evidence: Track domestic services and imported core prices alongside energy.

institution: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
title: The Impact of El Niño on the U.S. Economy
summary: The researchers estimate that the current El Niño may have raised U.S. headline price levels by about 0.3 percentage point between April and July, an effect expected to dissipate by year-end. Their historical model points to a potential renewed lift in prices in 2027 as well as higher employment. The authors say the estimate should be read as an upside risk, given the small number of very strong past episodes and uncertainty around forecasts. Changes in weather forecasting and exposure to global supply chains also limit historical comparisons.
locator: Model and results discussion, caveats and conclusion

questions.question: Which price categories and geographies carry the largest historical effect?
questions.evidence: Examine regional and component outcomes across past El Niño episodes.

questions.question: How robust is the estimate to excluding the strongest outlier episodes?
questions.evidence: Re-estimate the paper’s relationship across alternative historical samples.

questions.question: How would simultaneous energy and fertiliser disruptions affect pass-through?
questions.evidence: Compare joint historical episodes and sector input exposures.

title: Texas Economic Indicators: September 2026
summary: The Dallas Fed readout reports softer Texas employment in September and mixed sectoral performance. The dashboard shows 0.2% annualised job growth for June–September, unemployment at 4.4%, and smoothed annual hourly earnings growth of 5.3%. The release says headline inflation had risen and October business surveys signalled increased price pressure, while export values were higher than a year before. Labour growth and reported pricing pressure therefore send different signals in this regional update. The 0.2% figure summarises three months at an annual rate and is not the September employment change.
locator: Dashboard and labour market, price and trade sections

questions.question: Which industries account for the weaker employment reading?
questions.evidence: Compare industry payroll revisions and exposure to export and energy conditions.

questions.question: Are higher reported input costs being passed to customers?
questions.evidence: Compare Texas Business Outlook price-paid and price-received series.

questions.question: Do stronger exports support a broader regional rebound?
questions.evidence: Break export gains down by industry and compare them with activity and hiring.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey · October survey
locator: Summary, C&I and CRE loan questions, household credit and special questions on nonbank lenders; publication date from the Fed release listing
summary:
Banks reported that third-quarter commercial and industrial lending standards were broadly steady for larger and middle-market firms but tighter for small firms. Domestic banks also saw weaker C&I demand across firm sizes and attributed some of it to reduced investment and stronger competition from other sources of finance. Standards tightened across commercial real estate categories as demand weakened. In household credit, standards were broadly unchanged across the main consumer categories, with tightening in some terms and thresholds. Respondents reported tighter standards for bank loans to all surveyed classes of nondepository financial institutions.

Net responses represent the share tightening less the share easing. For analysis, the survey indicates both selectivity in bank supply and weaker demand in key credit channels. The survey does not establish their relative contribution to actual credit volumes.

questions.question: Is weak bank loan demand a credit slowdown or substitution?
questions.evidence: Reconcile bank lending data with corporate issuance and nonbank origination for comparable borrower groups.

questions.question: How does small-firm lending restraint affect investment?
questions.evidence: Track small-firm capex surveys, utilisation of bank credit lines and investment outturns.

questions.question: Where do tighter bank standards compound nonbank funding pressure?
questions.evidence: Check maturities and liquidity needs for the intermediaries in the survey's special questions.

title: Outlook for Economic Activity and Prices (October 2026, full text)
locator: Executive summary and Boxes 1–6, especially underlying inflation and the financial conditions assessment.
summary:
The full report supports the October policy outlook with work on the size and distribution of the AI-related acceleration, supply constraints on capacity, household spending during the price rise and pass-through from producer to consumer prices. Its baseline combines slower domestic growth in fiscal 2026 with relief from the energy drag and a stronger income-spending link from fiscal 2027. The central policy distinction is between a near-term CPI path lifted by energy, the yen and goods prices, and a more durable underlying trend associated with the wage-price mechanism and expectations.

The report’s box on anchoring inflation examines underlying measures rather than treating reported CPI as sufficient. The financial-conditions box considers the effects of rate changes through corporate finance, bank lending and asset prices. The boxes and forecasts expose where the path can change. AI demand can improve exports and investment but also feed input prices or reverse abruptly. A deteriorating terms of trade can weaken households at the same time as it lifts the CPI. The 2 November publication provides the fuller supporting analysis for the Board view issued 30 October.

questions.question: Are firms bottlenecked by orders, equipment or labour?
questions.evidence: Compare the capex box’s machinery and construction indicators using their respective data vintage and sector coverage.

questions.question: How persistent is price pass-through after the initial cost shock?
questions.evidence: Check the evidence in Boxes 4–5 against the distribution of price changes and wage settlements.

questions.question: Do bank lending and asset prices point to the same degree of accommodation?
questions.evidence: Compare the components of the financial conditions framework with subsequent financing, quantity and household indicators.

coverageLimitation: The summary draws on the Bank’s View and thematic boxes. The full set of 2026 forecast exhibits and appendices was not independently checked.

title: Bank lending survey – fourth quarter of 2026
locator: Official Polish PDF. Executive summary, methodology, corporate lending and household lending sections. NBP calendar gives the release date as 2 November.
summary:
The NBP’s October survey of 23 banks found a split between corporate and household credit in the third quarter. Responding banks reported easing business lending standards, mainly because of competition, and reducing margins, non-interest charges and some collateral requirements. They saw stronger demand for financing inventories, working capital and investment. At the same time, household lending standards tightened, particularly for consumer loans. Mortgage demand fell while demand for consumer loans rose by less than business lending demand.

Banks expected corporate and consumer loan demand to increase in Q4 while mortgage demand would remain weak, with limited changes in overall lending policy. The respondents represent about 90% of the sector’s exposures to businesses and households. Responses are weighted by segment market share and describe survey balances and expectations. The reported direction of easing in business credit is evidence about the lending channel rather than a change in the policy rate.

questions.question: Did easier corporate credit conditions result in more new lending?
questions.evidence: Compare new loan volumes and weighted pricing, distinguishing large firms from SMEs and working capital from investment.

questions.question: Why did mortgage demand fall despite some lower margins?
questions.evidence: Compare application data, mortgage availability, house prices and total borrowing costs with the survey’s housing section.

questions.question: Does the corporate-household split predict different spending responses?
questions.evidence: Link realised investment and household consumption to the sectoral loan series, accounting for income, fiscal and rate developments.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
title: Summary of the Monetary Policy Committee Meeting (2026-47)
locator: Financial conditions, inflation paragraphs 21–24 and monetary policy paragraphs 25–28. Meeting held 22 October.
summary:
The 22 October meeting summary explains the 100 bp cut alongside mixed evidence on demand, lending and inflation. It describes declines in many Turkish lira deposit and loan rates between the weeks ending 11 September and 16 October, with vehicle loan rates moving in the other direction. It also records recent reserve-requirement changes affecting selected forms of credit, so financing conditions reflect several instruments.

The Committee saw underlying inflation slowing even as energy and food were expected to lift monthly headline inflation in October. It identified a temporary mechanical effect from the timing of university tuition increases in September, with a rebound in monthly services inflation expected as that effect unwound. September expectations still differed sharply: 32.5% for firms and 45.6% for households at the 12-month horizon. The minutes thus provide evidence for the Committee’s distinction between a slowdown in underlying inflation and continued vulnerability to persistent shocks.

questions.question: Does the disinflation signal survive a consistent tuition adjustment?
questions.evidence: Reconstruct monthly core and services measures excluding changing education timing.

questions.question: Which groups are seeing looser effective borrowing conditions?
questions.evidence: Compare sector loan origination and pricing before and after the rate and reserve-requirement changes.

questions.question: Which expectation measure best explains pass-through?
questions.evidence: Compare firm and household survey horizons with subsequent prices and firms’ wage and sales plans.

title: Statement on Monetary Policy
locator: Sections 1–2, note on the dissent, ETF implementation footnotes and meeting reference.
summary:
The Bank of Japan kept its overnight call-rate guideline around 1.25% by an 8–1 vote and separately agreed unanimously to raise the pace of ETF sales. The dissent was for tighter policy: Hajime Takata proposed around 1.50%, arguing that underlying CPI had reached the target and the bank should move closer to neutral more quickly. His proposed rate differs from the decision actually adopted.

The new ETF pace is about ¥860 billion a year at book value starting January 2027, up from about ¥330 billion. The choice was linked to higher market turnover and the early experience of orderly sales. The bank estimated ¥2.46 trillion at market value using the observed conversion ratio, with scope to adjust timing in response to conditions. The pace of J-REIT sales remains about ¥5 billion a year at book value. The rate vote and the change in balance sheet flows are separate policy decisions. The statement provides no intraday quotes or pre-decision expectations for either.

questions.question: Was future overnight policy repriced around the release?
questions.evidence: Measure the change in yen OIS across maturities around the verified statement release, separating the later press event.

questions.question: How concentrated might ETF sales be relative to executable liquidity?
questions.evidence: Use actual sales, trading volumes, market-to-book ratios and dates when operations are temporarily adjusted.

questions.question: What would tell us whether Takata’s rationale is gaining support?
questions.evidence: Compare subsequent named remarks and vote records with survey inflation expectations and wage measures.

title: Savings in a changing society — Fabio Panetta
summary:
Panetta discussed how energy costs, higher yields and technological change affect savings and financial markets. He saw energy disruption as the main macro risk, with the AI investment cycle supporting production, trade and equity values but exposing the economy to a revision in expected returns. Figure 1 reports a rise in ten-year sovereign yields across six economies from spring 2026. He pointed to expected inflation and policy, fiscal concerns and competition for long-term funding from private issuance. The chart shows yields across markets and does not isolate the effects of those drivers.

He argued that further policy increases could be needed if energy inflation persisted and spread into expectations and behaviour. He also judged that higher long yields were already tightening conditions, which matters for the size of the appropriate response. He left room to adjust if geopolitical conditions improved or financial stress weakened demand.

questions.question: How much of the long-end move reflects term premia and issuance pressure?
questions.evidence: Compare sovereign curves against swaps, auction concessions and corporate duration supply.

questions.question: Could an AI earnings or financing repricing materially reduce demand?
questions.evidence: Track capex intentions, financing costs, equity valuations and bank exposure to firms dependent on those projects.

questions.question: What signal would distinguish a temporary energy rise from second-round effects?
questions.evidence: Follow euro area core inflation, wage contracts and inflation expectations across horizons.

locator: Global economic outlook, Figure 1 and the monetary policy discussion.

title: Quarterly Schedule of Outright Purchases of Japanese Government Bonds: Update
locator: Maturity buckets and footnotes 1–4, bilingual schedule.
summary: The BoJ revised its quarterly purchase schedule for coupon-bearing JGBs. The table groups planned offers by maturity and shows the size per auction, monthly amount and scheduled dates. Its figures are in units of ¥100 million and subject to change. The Bank says actual amounts will be announced at operation time and dates beyond the listed November schedule will be announced later. It also intends generally to avoid offering purchases in the overlapping maturity segment on a Ministry of Finance auction date. The figures are planned gross purchase amounts and should be read against actual tenders and maturities of existing holdings.

title: Outlook for Economic Activity and Prices: The Bank’s View
locator: Summary, §§II–IV, Policy Board projections and risk-balance annex.
summary:
The Board projects slower but still positive expansion in fiscal 2026, with high costs for imported energy and materials eroding real incomes and firms’ terms of trade. Government relief, accommodative conditions and AI-related export demand support activity. The bank expects growth to improve moderately from fiscal 2027 if the commodity drag eases and the link between incomes and spending strengthens. Real growth projections are broadly unchanged from the previous round.

The forecast separates CPI excluding fresh food from underlying inflation. Oil, semiconductor costs and the weaker yen are expected to raise the former above 2% before it returns toward 2% later in the projection. The fiscal 2027 CPI forecast is somewhat higher than in July. Tight labour markets, wage pass-through and expectations around 2% underpin the Board’s assessment that underlying inflation is broadly in line with the target. Risks are generally balanced for activity and skewed upward for CPI. Conditioning assumptions include oil eventually falling and Board forecasts taking account of financial-market policy views. Those inputs and the rate outlook remain contingent.

questions.question: How dependent is the moderation in CPI on the oil assumption?
questions.evidence: Re-estimate the baseline under alternative Dubai crude, yen and subsidy paths, using the projection footnotes and published CPI weights.

questions.question: Has the underlying measure become durable across sectors?
questions.evidence: Compare services inflation and wage pass-through with distribution-based indicators of underlying inflation.

questions.question: How broad is the income-to-spending recovery?
questions.evidence: Compare payroll, real disposable income and household spending by income group, alongside sector-level Tankan data.

title: October MPC follow-up interviews: Carl Hansen and Karen Silk
locator: Official public comment summaries in the October 2026 Monetary Policy Review section
summary:
Hansen and Silk describe different reasons for their October votes. Hansen supported holding after earlier tightening and wanted more evidence on household spending and what it meant for margins, wage growth and inflation. He expressed confidence in the export-led recovery while being cautious about extrapolating to households, and he described his near-term policy choice as finely balanced and conditional. He discussed using expected inflation to interpret the real policy rate.

Silk preferred a 25 basis point rise, arguing that policy normalisation could proceed while the recovery remained uneven and price pressures warranted attention. She said another rise would place the OCR near the midpoint of the stated neutral range and described the disagreement as mainly one of timing. Sustained NZD weakness could matter to import costs and activity, but she said it did not decide her vote. The official page gives selected interview summaries, with its coverage limited to the members’ individual views.

questions.question: Which household data best resolve the difference in emphasis?
questions.evidence: Compare short-run consumption, real income measures and price-setting updates before the next review.

questions.question: Are markets repricing the pace of policy or the starting point for neutral?
questions.evidence: Compare meeting-dated OIS with longer forwards and the neutral range cited by Silk.

questions.question: Has exchange-rate weakness persisted enough to affect costs?
questions.evidence: Track trade-weighted FX and retailer pricing and compare against import values.

title: Economic and Monetary Conditions for September and Q3 2026
summary:
The Bank of Thailand reports that activity improved in September and over the third quarter. Technology-related merchandise exports and the flow of equipment for data centres supported investment and manufacturing. Tourism arrivals fell, particularly on short routes, although longer stays supported foreign tourism receipts. Services consumption softened in September amid cost-of-living pressures.

The September and quarterly inflation pictures differ. In September, higher retail energy prices raised headline inflation while fresh food and core inflation were broadly stable from the previous month. Looking across Q3 as a whole, headline inflation fell relative to the prior quarter as energy prices declined, while prepared-food prices contributed to firmer core inflation. The current account was in deficit in September but in surplus over the quarter. The release flags rising unemployment-benefit claims for monitoring despite broadly stable labour conditions.

questions.question: Will technology exports lead to a broader improvement in domestic demand?
questions.evidence: Compare import content, investment volumes and employment in the sectors benefiting from data-centre activity.

questions.question: Are recent price increases reversing or spreading?
questions.evidence: Check monthly CPI changes across energy, prepared food and other services, and use the same comparison periods.

questions.question: Can tourism receipts remain stable with fewer arrivals?
questions.evidence: Compare nights stayed, daily spending and the composition of long- and short-haul groups.

locator: September detail and “Quarterly Review of the Thai Economy”; covers the release text.

title: Board holds the policy rate at 12.25% by majority vote
summary:
Four directors voted to retain the 12.25% policy rate and three preferred a 25 basis point increase. Annual September headline inflation edged up to 6.3%, while core inflation excluding food and regulated prices fell to 6.0% from 6.1%. Analyst expectations for the end of 2026 edged higher to 6.9%, and two-year expectations remained near 4.0%. Measures inferred from government debt remained away from the 3% target.

The release describes the rate as restrictive and consistent with declining inflation in 2027. Recent activity data pointed to weaker growth, partly related to lower consumption growth and the earthquake. El Niño and the fiscal outlook remained material risks. The vote leaves a live policy split over whether the current level suffices and does not establish the market surprise.
locator: Decision, voting split and inflation and activity bullets

questions.evidence: Check whether lower core inflation persists alongside the food and regulated components highlighted in the statement.

questions.question: Is weaker activity broad or driven by temporary events?
questions.evidence: Compare national activity data with geography and sector exposure to the earthquake.

questions.question: Could fiscal changes affect the yield curve independently of policy expectations?

institution: Banco Central de la República Argentina
title: Santiago Bausili’s opening remarks at the Q3 Monetary Policy Report press conference
summary:
BCRA President Santiago Bausili presents monetary-quantity control and the consistency of fiscal and exchange-rate policies as the basis for disinflation. He describes the exchange-rate regime as a buffer against a more adverse external setting. He cites second-quarter GDP down 0.6% quarter on quarter after seasonal adjustment but up 2.0% year on year, showing why a quarterly setback can coexist with positive annual growth.

Bausili says the bank bought over USD 15.8 billion in the FX market through 28 October, including USD 3.4 billion in the third quarter. The change in reserves was smaller than gross purchases. He describes liquidity management and growing foreign-currency intermediation alongside the purchases. The inflation figures he cites from the REM and breakevens reflect survey and market measures, while the assessment of policy discipline is the speaker’s.
locator: Opening remarks sections II–IV; slides and Q&A linked by the bank

questions.question: How do gross FX purchases translate into reserve accumulation?
questions.evidence: Reconcile intervention flows, other public-sector transactions, valuation and the BCRA balance sheet.

questions.question: What portion of the monetary impact of FX purchases is sterilised?

title: Monetary policy statement and Q&A — Christine Lagarde and Boris Vujčić
summary: Lagarde said the October hold was unanimous after a discussion of whether to tighten immediately. The Council balanced inflation risks from higher energy costs against a tightening of financing conditions and chose to wait for another round of data. Lagarde indicated that the policy direction was broadly clear absent a major development, while leaving open when to act. The press conference also considered the effect of policy and inflation expectations and longer-duration bond issuance on global long yields. She described the need to monitor effects on fiscal planning and sovereign transmission.

title: Monetary policy decisions
summary:
The Governing Council left the deposit facility rate at 2.50%, the main refinancing rate at 2.65% and the marginal lending rate at 2.90%. Higher energy prices were seen as damaging growth while raising inflation risk. The Council noted that the duration and size of the shock increased the chance of pass-through, though underlying inflation remained broadly stable and wages had yet to show a material response. Financing conditions had tightened since the previous meeting, which could damp both growth and inflation.

The Council made its next decision contingent on the inflation outlook, underlying inflation and monetary transmission. APP and PEPP portfolios continued to run down without reinvestment. The Transmission Protection Instrument remained available if disorderly market dynamics threatened transmission across member states. The release contains the decision and policy rationale but does not quantify market expectations or the realised announcement response.

questions.question: Are stronger energy price pressures spreading to wages or core prices?
questions.evidence: Track wage settlements, services HICP and price-setting surveys alongside energy futures.

questions.question: How much does additional credit restraint offset inflation pressure?

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Minutes of the Monetary Policy Meeting (2026 Q3)
locator: Attached minutes, §II.3 votes and §III press release with Appendix Tables 1–2.
summary:
The minutes of the 17 September meeting, published on 29 October, show how directors weighed rapid export-led growth against the inflation outlook and remaining housing imbalances. The Board held the discount rate, secured refinancing rate and temporary accommodation rate at 2.00%, 2.375% and 4.25%, respectively. Two listed directors voted against the hold. Separately, directors agreed to adjust selective credit controls, with one recorded dissent on that proposition. The discussion describes less concentrated property lending alongside a case for giving creditworthy borrowers somewhat more flexibility on second homes.

The Bank’s September baseline put growth at 11.48% in 2026 and 5.82% in 2027, helped by technology demand and subject to a high base. The forecasts for 2026 CPI and core CPI were 2.03% and 2.16%, with both projected below 2% the next year if oil and other pressure softened. The press statement discusses financing needs, foreign portfolio outflows and continued liquidity management. The minutes record what was known in September. They do not turn the publication date into the decision date.

questions.question: How concentrated is the growth outlook in the AI supply chain?

title: Liquidity against collateral: the SNB’s approach — Petra Tschudin and Thomas Moser
summary:
Tschudin and Moser described collateral policy as part of the infrastructure that lets the SNB implement its rate, support settlements and supply liquidity in stress. With reserves abundant and the policy rate non-negative at the time, open market operations absorbed liquidity. This contrasts with occasional provision during negative rates to contain upward pressure on short rates. Intraday payment needs and emergency support have separate purposes.

The SNB General Collateral Basket is also a standard for private repo transactions. The speakers emphasised both usable breadth and protection against losses, supported by high ratings, minimum issue sizes and pre-positioning for some facilities. Chart 3’s ratings distribution showed just under 60% AAA and about 40% AA and reflected the large share of sovereign issuers. The operational implication is that available, mobilisable collateral matters for a counterparty’s funding capacity alongside headline reserves. The speech does not signal a change in the SNB policy rate.

questions.question: Are eligible securities available to the counterparties that would need them in stress?
questions.evidence: Compare GC Basket eligibility and holdings against pledged assets and pre-positioned buffers.

questions.question: How does collateral composition affect Swiss repo-rate dispersion?
questions.evidence: Consult the companion Economic Note and trade-level repo volume and spread data by issuer and currency.

questions.question: How would a change in eligibility affect short-rate control?
questions.evidence: Compare prior rule changes with volumes, settlement failures and SARON deviations around the change dates.

title: Lesetja Kganyago on low growth and the role of monetary policy
locator: Sections on the growth diagnosis, policy responsibilities and recent reforms.
summary:
Governor Lesetja Kganyago argued that durable growth depends on how fiscal stability, operational reforms and government capacity reinforce each other. He identified electricity, logistics and labour-market constraints as persistent limits on productive capacity. He viewed lower and more stable inflation as supportive of investment through greater certainty and lower hurdle rates, while arguing that interest-rate policy primarily affects cyclical demand.

He described the 3% target and its one percentage point tolerance as an anchor while discussing an energy shock that could pass into expectations and wages. Following a cumulative 50 bp rise since March, he said the SARB’s modelling then indicated that prevailing settings could return inflation to target after the shock had passed, and that it would act if inflation threatened to become entrenched. His account of lower long-term costs and a resilient rand is commentary on conditions at the time, rather than an event-window result.

questions.question: Is improvement in fiscal credibility passing through to funding costs?
questions.evidence: Compare sovereign spreads and issuance costs around fiscal announcements with global benchmarks.

questions.question: How stable are inflation expectations under another fuel shock?
questions.evidence: Compare expectation surveys and wage settlements with energy-price scenarios and the latest MPC projections.

questions.question: Which structural reforms contribute most to current growth?

institution: Banco Central de la República Argentina
title: Informe de Política Monetaria (IPOM), third quarter of 2026
summary:
The Bank’s quarterly report overview links Argentina’s disinflation to fiscal balance, the end of monetary financing of the Treasury, changes in relative prices and repair of the central bank balance sheet. It also explains how the bank uses monetary aggregates and FX operations within its stabilisation programme. The report presents these links as the Bank’s assessment of its programme. They identify mechanisms to test against inflation, reserves and liquidity data.

The report was published as part of the fourth phase of the stabilisation programme. Its policy discussion is therefore most informative about control of money and the operation of the FX regime, alongside the evolution of expectations.
locator: Official IPOM overview and linked report

title: OCR held at 2.75%: October Monetary Policy Review
locator: Media release and summary record, especially the conditional outlook and vote
summary:
The MPC voted 4–3 to hold at 2.75%. September-quarter annual CPI eased to 3.7% from 4.1%, a slightly better outcome than expected, while core measures were near the top of the 1–3% target range and increases had broadened. The December-quarter forecast was 4.4%, largely on fuel futures at the time of the review. The export recovery contrasted with weak domestic demand. The lower trade-weighted currency could add to imported costs, while weak demand limited how easily firms could pass these through.

The majority put more weight on subdued wage growth, anchored medium-term expectations and allowing time for two previous increases to work. The minority preferred a 25 basis point increase to 3%, pointing to inflation persistence and sufficient overall resilience to act. All members judged tighter policy likely, conditional on the outlook. The record explicitly leaves room to hold if domestic pricing cools and to ease if a severe global downturn materially changes the outlook. The divergence was about timing and risk, alongside agreement on the central direction.

questions.question: Does domestic pricing broaden after accounting for imported fuel?
questions.evidence: Compare core and non-tradables subindices with wage growth, margins and business pricing intentions.

questions.question: How much of the decision was in NZD rates before publication?
questions.evidence: Check dated OIS or bank-bill quotes around the confirmed 2 pm New Zealand release and verify other overlapping news.

questions.question: Is export strength reaching households?
questions.evidence: Track regional employment, consumption and confidence alongside trade and tourism receipts.

title: Monetary Policy Report—October 2026
summary:
The October outlook projects inflation above 3% through much of 2027 and near 2% by mid-2028. The Bank judged that sustained oil and refinery pressures were affecting Canadian firms’ costs, with broader consumer-price effects expected as those costs passed through. The same energy shock supports investment and exports through Canada’s commodity sector while reducing purchasing power for households and raising costs for energy users.

The Bank forecasts 1% annual growth in 2026 and 2% in both 2027 and 2028. Stronger midyear activity improved the growth outlook versus July. Tariffs and uncertainty still constrain exports and investment in affected sectors, while housing remains weak. The report’s outlook is conditional on its trade, energy and pass-through assumptions.
locator: Overview and report chapters on outlook and risks

questions.question: How exposed is the growth upgrade to tariffs?
questions.evidence: Track trade by industry, capital spending plans and US demand in the sectors identified by the report.

questions.question: Is housing the main source of downside growth risk?
questions.evidence: Compare mortgage renewals, resale activity and residential investment with the report’s projected path.

title: Monetary Policy Committee’s Decision 5/2026
summary:
The participating MPC members unanimously held the policy rate at 1.00%; one member was absent. The committee said an accommodative setting and targeted financial measures supported an uneven recovery. It expected the technology and AI cycle to support exports and investment, with GDP growth of 2.4% in 2026 and 2.1% in 2027. It judged output growth still below potential and benefits concentrated in the sectors most exposed to the cycle.

The bank expected temporary supply-driven inflation from energy and El Niño. Its projections put headline inflation at 2.1% in 2026 and 1.3% in 2027, while core inflation was 1.2% and 1.3%. The committee noted a weaker baht and somewhat higher government yields, while private loan costs remained broadly steady. Larger borrowers drove the pickup in loans as SME credit continued to contract. The combination explains why broader credit measures could look firm while some borrowers still faced financing constraints.

title: Michele Bullock’s opening statement to Senate estimates
locator: Opening statement, discussion of inflation and policy, housing and payments passages
summary:
Bullock told the Senate that recently realised upside risks would probably push inflation above the RBA’s August base case even as aggregate growth slowed. She distinguished energy costs and pass-through from inflation in domestically exposed goods and services. Although unemployment had risen somewhat more than expected, she judged the labour market still a little tighter than previously assessed and weak productivity continued to limit how fast output could grow without price pressure.

She argued that a further period of weak demand growth was necessary and framed the coming meeting around whether tightening to date was sufficient. Higher rates can affect housing values, but the relevant channel in the testimony was their effect on spending, employment and inflation. The latter portion discusses payments and cash distribution as separate responsibilities. The investment relevance is the information available to markets before the November decision: Bullock indicated a less favourable inflation outlook without precommitting the Board’s vote.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: FOMC statement · October rate decision
locator: Release time, policy decision, activity and inflation paragraphs, voting record
summary: The FOMC held the federal funds target at 3.75–4.00% by a 10–2 vote. Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack preferred a quarter-point increase. The statement characterised activity as strong, spending as resilient, investment as robust, and unemployment as little changed. It flagged elevated inflation and framed further information as useful to assessing the stance needed to return to 2%. The dissents establish a debate over whether to tighten immediately. institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: FOMC press conference · October meeting
locator: Transcript opening remarks and Q&A on the hold, expectations, strategy and the 2027 schedule
summary:
Warsh described real activity as improving while inflation remained too high, with a risk that sector-specific price changes could spread. In response to questions about the hold, he framed policy around the broader strategy and incoming information. He defended the 2% target and discussed anchoring expectations, while his responses left the timing of the next decision contingent. The Q&A contains the reporters’ descriptions of market and household expectations, which should be read as questions unless separately supported.

He also announced a planned format change in 2027, with one of eight meetings devoted to strategy and no rate vote or statement anticipated for that meeting. That institutional change is distinct from the October decision. The value of the press conference for event analysis is the clarification delivered after the statement at a separate time.

title: Economic Resilience, Thinner Buffers, Emerging Risks Globally: Where Does India Stand?
summary:
Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta argues that global growth has so far weathered repeated shocks, while fiscal room has narrowed and inflation has led some central banks to tighten. She distinguishes the IMF forecasts she cites from the RBI’s MPC forecast of 7.1% growth in India in fiscal 2026–27. She points to strong consumption and investment in the first quarter and describes September CPI released after the October meeting as broadly in line with its quarterly forecast.

Gupta describes how temporary supply shocks can produce more durable inflation through expectations, wage setting and wider price increases. She discusses pre-emptive moves when waiting for complete evidence is costly and cites October’s 25 basis point hike as an example of the Indian policy response. She also draws out two time horizons for AI. Near-term investment can boost demand, while wider use can improve productivity; persistent investment demand could raise the neutral rate. The debt discussion contrasts the projected global loss of fiscal room with India’s projected decline in the debt ratio, which depends on nominal growth staying above the effective borrowing cost.

questions.evidence: Compare diffusion, wages and surveyed price expectations across releases around the speech.

title: Bank of Canada raises the policy rate by 25 basis points to 2½%
summary:
The Bank raised the overnight-rate target to 2.50%, with the Bank Rate at 2.75% and the deposit rate at 2.45%. Persistently high energy prices and refinery margins had kept headline inflation near 3% since April. The Bank saw signs of broader cost pressures, including transport and imported industrial and electronics inputs. Core measures remained near 2%, but its surveys indicated more firms expected to pass through higher input costs.

The Canadian economy also entered the second half of 2026 stronger than the Bank had forecast in July. The Bank nevertheless projected a tariff-related slowdown in the fourth quarter and described some excess supply. The decision addresses the risk of persistent inflation as activity recovers, with the next steps contingent on incoming data. The release describes recent rates and currency conditions without providing an event-window market response.

Net corporate loan demand came in at −6%, against +4% expected. Higher rates and weaker fixed investment demand weighed on borrowing while inventory and refinancing needs offset part of the decline. Banks also saw potential demand for data centre finance. Mortgage demand dropped to −27% net versus −12% expected, mainly owing to higher rates. These net balances describe how many banks reported changes in each direction, rather than the growth rates of loan balances.

title: Brad Jones: Panel at the AFR Super and Wealth Summit
locator: RBA transcript on early withdrawals, superannuation cash flows and FX hedging
summary:
Jones discusses the liquidity consequences of changes in Australian superannuation. He distinguishes an unexpected opening of early withdrawals during a financial-market crisis from a predictable reform that funds could prepare for in advance. He cites work on experience during COVID while clarifying that the RBA had not modelled the precise inflation scenario posed by the moderator. As a larger share of members moves from accumulation to withdrawals, he expects the sector to become less self-contained and its demand for liquidity from FX hedging to grow.

The market question is whether superannuation funds’ cash, collateral and market-making arrangements can accommodate stress while continuing to hold and hedge international portfolios. His discussion concerns market structure and potential flows, with no guidance on the cash rate.

title: An Assessment of Recent Youth Labor Market Conditions: Causes and Policy Implications
locator: Bank of Korea Issue Note 2026-27, the official summary and the linked research note.
summary:
The Bank of Korea staff note argues that weak youth employment since the pandemic is more evident in job quality and segmentation than in headline unemployment. Stagnant hiring for preferred, more stable positions can push jobseekers into secondary jobs rather than recorded unemployment. The authors connect this to a shift toward IT manufacturing, which creates relatively few regular jobs, to emerging AI effects on demand for young workers and to rigidity in the transition between job segments.

The paper’s implication is that an aggregate rebound in hiring may leave an important part of youth labour slack unresolved if secondary workers cannot move into primary jobs. The finding is a staff structural assessment, conditional on the links it identifies. It is relevant for reading labour market breadth and income growth in Korea alongside export performance, rather than choosing a near-term rate path mechanically from one employment statistic.

questions.evidence: Compare entry, tenure and transitions by age, job type and industry in labour panel data.

questions.evidence: Examine exposure by occupation and watch for pre-existing trends and changes in composition.

title: Sarah Hunter: Interview on 60 Minutes
locator: Broadcast 25 October, recorded 21 October. Discussion of supply, demand, cost of living and the decision process
summary:
Hunter describes persistent pressure from aggregate demand exceeding supply, alongside shocks that affect households unevenly. Higher rates aim to slow demand sufficiently for capacity and spending to come into balance. She explains why restraining inflation can be necessary even when mortgages, household expenses and weaker activity are already straining spending. The interview gives a communication account of the trade-off and stresses that the aim is sustained disinflation while limiting a severe downturn.

Hunter declines to say what the Board will decide next. Her signal is therefore a description of the staff’s problem and transmission channel, with no personal vote or policy commitment. The RBA’s publication archive states that the interview was recorded before the broadcast. Event work needs an independently verified first public time and should account for a possible weekend broadcast and thin trading around publication.
