questions.evidence: Compare consumption indicators by leverage and rolling fixed-rate expiry cohorts.

questions.question: Could the release add anything beyond earlier RBA communications?
questions.evidence: Compare interview remarks with the October minutes and check dated Australian market opening prices.

questions.question: How are external cost shocks interacting with local demand?
questions.evidence: Compare fuel-sensitive components with domestic prices and business liaison reports.

title: Physical shocks and economic resilience: a central bank perspective — James Talbot
locator: Full speech and footnotes, especially the transmission, monetary policy response, resilience and insurance sections.
summary:
James Talbot argues that insurance and adaptation affect how long physical climate shocks disrupt the economy and how readily monetary policy can see through the initial price rise. He sets out a method for diagnosing a shock. He does not announce an MPC decision or give a near-term rate forecast. A temporary shock with anchored expectations can call for patience because rates act with a lag. The case for a response strengthens if the effect spreads into wages, expectations and prices across sectors. The economy’s position when the shock arrives matters. Weak demand and spare capacity make pass-through less likely, while elevated inflation and fragile expectations increase the risk of persistence.

The initial effect depends on the hazard and the sectors exposed. A drought can reduce agricultural supply and raise food prices. Floods can destroy assets and reduce spending, yet damage to transport or essential infrastructure can raise input prices. In the examples Talbot cites, Rhine water levels constrained freight capacity, while the Valencia floods damaged output and triggered claims under Spain’s insurance system. Exposure is international. Imported commodities can transmit foreign production losses into UK headline inflation. The UK food-price channel matters partly because households form inflation perceptions from frequently purchased items. Talbot points to model-based Bank analysis as evidence of the channel. The estimates depend on how the model identifies global weather disruption.

His framework distinguishes the first change in relative prices, wider costs along supply chains and eventual changes in wages or expectations. A sequence of isolated disturbances may keep aggregate inflation pressure elevated even when each disturbance is temporary. Settled evidence on magnitude and transmission can enter a central forecast. Where the balance between demand and supply effects is uncertain, Talbot favours a scenario analysis that makes those channels explicit. Monitoring also needs to cover credit and collateral, since the shock can impair the transmission of the eventual rate response.

The long-run concern is a loss of the buffers that initially helped economies recover. Insurance and fiscal capacity can finance recovery, but frequent losses can make coverage more expensive or scarce and leave governments with larger contingent liabilities. The historical output-loss estimates cited in the speech are larger in poorer countries, where financing and insurance capacity are typically more limited. For UK mortgages, the Bank’s scenario moves the uninsured share from roughly 5% towards 7–10% by 2050, with a severe flood scenario reaching up to 16%. These figures are conditional model estimates. Talbot describes relatively small aggregate banking effects against the scale of Bank stress tests and potentially material concentrations of losses for individual borrowers, lenders and regions.

The distinction between aggregate resilience and local exposure is important for credit as well as rates. Paying claims quickly can shorten disruption and support recovery. Risk transfers among insurers, reinsurers, banks and governments affect who finances that recovery. Physical adaptation can improve the insurability of the assets in the first place. The speech points to collaboration on risk measurement and protection gaps through multilateral groups, including the NGFS, as a way to improve comparisons across countries.

questions.question: When do imported food-price shocks produce persistent UK inflation pressure?
questions.evidence: Talbot identifies a link between global weather and UK prices. Use the Bank’s cited model, commodity-level import costs and household expectation surveys to compare pass-through across initial inflation states. This matters for a rates scenario that distinguishes a brief CPI impulse from a change in the expected policy path.

questions.question: When does household demand weakness outweigh the supply loss?
questions.evidence: Flood damage can raise some prices while tightening credit and reducing spending. Use the NGFS case studies, regional retail spending, business borrowing and reconstruction outlays to assess the relative timing. That timing determines whether nominal rates and credit spreads should be expected to move together in a given scenario.

questions.question: Which lenders and borrowers carry concentrated uninsured mortgage exposure?
questions.evidence: The aggregate stress effect is small in the cited Bank simulation, while regional exposures may be material. Use the Bank’s mortgage modelling, lender disclosures, local hazard maps and effective insurance terms to assess where lower collateral values and cash-flow shocks could coincide.

questions.question: What determines whether insurance and adaptation shorten the recovery period?
questions.evidence: Cross-country examples show different degrees of protection without identifying insurance’s standalone causal contribution. Compare claims paid and payout lags with infrastructure recovery and pre-event balance sheets in the cited disaster studies. The answer determines how long to carry output and credit stress in a macro scenario.

title: Laporan Kebijakan Moneter Triwulan III 2026
locator: Indonesian original: Executive Summary, Chapters 1–3, charts on CPI components and the 2026 outlook. Selected exhibits read with the narrative; small chart labels omitted.
summary:
Bank Indonesia’s third-quarter report ranges 2026 real GDP growth between 4.9% and 5.7% and projects a current-account deficit of 1.6–2.4% of GDP. It cites government support and improving confidence as domestic growth drivers and expects inflation to remain in the 2.5% ± 1 percentage point corridor in both 2026 and 2027. The report describes external pressure from higher global energy costs, fairly high US yields and limited demand for emerging-market assets. As of 20 October it records the rupiah at IDR 17,985 per dollar, down 0.61% from end-September.

The inflation chapter reports September CPI rising to 3.28% year on year from 3.19%, even as core inflation fell to 2.84%. The chart of CPI and its components shows why the mix matters: regulated prices and volatile food can move differently from core. The discussion of food coordination and exchange-rate measures ties each instrument to a distinct channel into the inflation forecast. These report forecasts are conditional on the policy and external assumptions discussed in the outlook.

The report records September bank credit expanding 13.26% year on year and deposits growing 8.22%. It also notes unused approved credit, which is a stock of available limits rather than drawn lending. The October policy mix combines the BI-Rate hold, a higher deposit facility rate, staged reserve changes, spot and forward FX operations and targeted liquidity incentives. The announced steps are intended to support market functioning and lending alongside rupiah stability. Their combined effect on borrowing costs depends on how banks use the facilities and on funding conditions.

questions.question: Could a larger current-account deficit make the growth forecast harder to sustain?
questions.evidence: Reconstruct the oil and non-oil trade components and stress-test portfolio financing assumptions.

questions.question: How much of the gap between loan and deposit growth can banks finance sustainably?
questions.evidence: Compare unused lines, deposit mix, interbank activity and binding reserve requirements before and after each step.

questions.question: Does the inflation outlook rely more on food measures or exchange-rate stability?
questions.evidence: Track CPI group contributions and estimate the sensitivity of import costs to the rupiah under alternative commodity scenarios.

questions.question: Did the corridor and reserve changes transmit to the rates relevant for firms?
questions.evidence: Compare INDONIA, deposit and loan pricing with the scheduled reserve reductions and actual facility use.

title: Jonathan Heath · Mexico’s Inflation and Monetary Policy Outlook
locator: Headline and Core annual inflation charts, neutral and ex ante real short-term rate chart
summary:
Heath’s deck compared headline and core inflation with the 3% target. The annual headline chart shows an increase from the mid-2026 low to 3.45% in September. The core exhibits provide a separate view of underlying prices, with different movements visible from the headline line. Reading the latest headline point alone would miss the composition of the remaining inflation gap.

The real rate figure subtracts survey expectations over the coming 12 months from the overnight policy target. Its shaded band is Banxico’s estimated long-run neutral range, not a directly observed market value. For a policy-path assessment, the exhibit frames how a change in either expected inflation or the policy target can change the real stance.

questions.question: Which components account for the latest change in annual inflation?
questions.evidence: Compare component contributions, seasonally adjusted monthly rates and base effects.

questions.question: How sensitive is the stance to the expectation measure?
questions.evidence: Recalculate using the survey distribution, alternative horizons and the neutral range shown.

questions.question: Did investors reprice the timing of a policy change?
questions.evidence: Check Mexican front-end swaps with verified release timing and earlier communications.

coverageLimitation: Analysis covers the named slides in the official deck. The archive date is the date Banxico lists for the presentation.

title: Financial System Report (October 2026)
locator: Executive summary and stress-test scenarios described on the release page. The linked report provides models and exhibits.
summary:
The Bank judges Japan’s financial system stable overall. Bank intermediation was functioning smoothly with demand for loans and willingness to lend, although the report asks readers to watch asset prices. Its scenario analysis considers a shock of global-financial-crisis proportions and a compound scenario combining higher oil prices, weaker AI profitability expectations and sharply higher rates. Foreign nonbank portfolio adjustment is one transmission channel, reflecting the role of such intermediaries in financing global AI investment.

Banks in aggregate withstand the report’s specified scenarios on capital and funding metrics. That conclusion depends on the shock, exposures and feedbacks modelled. The report also examines the effects of higher inputs and rates on small businesses, households and bank portfolios. For rates and risk analysis, changes in the financial-system buffers and differences across institutions matter independently from the central bank’s policy stance.

questions.question: Which balance sheets carry concentrated losses under the compound shock?
questions.evidence: Compare exposure by bank, security duration, FX funding and credit composition with the stress-test assumptions.

questions.question: When would the nonbank amplification channel transmit to Japan?
questions.evidence: Track counterparties, collateral haircuts, cross-border fund flows and intermediary liquidity in a market correction.

questions.question: How quickly are higher rates transmitted to borrowers and bank earnings?
questions.evidence: Compare repricing dates, bank funding costs and loan performance by firm size and household leverage.

coverageLimitation: Analysis uses the bank’s executive summary. The detailed stress-test calibrations and full exhibits were not independently checked.

title: Consumer Price Developments in September 2026
locator: Linked official release, Charts 1–2 and inflation outlook on PDF pp. 1–5
summary:
The joint MAS publication reports headline CPI inflation of 2.2% year on year in September, down from 2.3% in August. Core inflation, which excludes accommodation and private transport, eased to 2.0% from 2.2%, though core prices still increased 0.1% month on month. Services and retail goods inflation slowed, private transport inflation was lower and food inflation rose. The component chart shows percentage-point contributions to headline inflation, distinct from individual components’ own inflation rates.

The release keeps forecast core inflation at 1.5–2.0% in 2026 and 1.5–2.5% in 2027. It expects more discernible easing from mid-2027 as imported pressures abate and domestic costs remain contained, with risk still tilted upward. A one-month decline led by selected categories must be read with the outlook and cost assumptions. The publication gives a data update under the existing policy stance.

questions.question: Is the decline widespread across underlying core items?
questions.evidence: Reconstruct weighted contributions and examine successive month-on-month observations.

questions.question: Which components are most exposed to a renewed energy or food shock?
questions.evidence: Compare the latest input costs alongside the timing of utility tariff changes and historical pass-through.

questions.question: Could subsidies be masking a persistent service-cost pressure?
questions.evidence: Compare affected service categories with untargeted services and unit labour costs.

title: Responsible wage formation pays off — Per Jansson
summary: Jansson credited balanced wage formation with allowing faster disinflation and easing in Sweden. He noted stronger activity, helped by fiscal policy, alongside higher energy costs and a softer krona. Temporary food VAT relief and transport subsidies reduced measured inflation, while their expiry could mechanically push it up. A more persistent energy shock could also spread into broader price setting. He said his September assessment favoured somewhat faster policy normalisation than anticipated in June.

questions.question: Are pay settlements still consistent with disinflation?
questions.evidence: Compare wage drift, productivity and services prices.

questions.question: How much headline variation reflects fiscal measures?
questions.evidence: Compare tax-adjusted CPIF with expected VAT and transport changes.

questions.question: Could stronger demand broaden pass-through?
questions.evidence: Compare producer costs, price plans and realised consumer prices.

locator: Official presentation summary
coverageLimitation: The bank’s written summary is the basis of this entry.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
title: Press Release on Interest Rates (2026-45)
locator: Decision paragraph and guidance on domestic demand, inflation and policy transmission.
summary:
The Committee reduced the one-week repo rate from 37% to 36%, and cut both overnight rates by one percentage point. It pointed to slowing underlying inflation, weak domestic demand and limited pass-through from recent supply shocks. Elevated energy prices remained an upside risk and the Committee said it would monitor how global developments feed into costs, activity and expectations.

The instrument move eases nominal rates at this decision. The Committee described its overall stance as tight and said the pace and size of later moves would depend on realised and expected inflation and the interim disinflation path. It retained the option to tighten if the outlook deteriorated materially and persistently, and of macroprudential action if credit or deposit markets developed unexpectedly. A market surprise depends on what participants were pricing ahead of the statement.

questions.question: How far did weak demand mitigate energy and FX pass-through?
questions.evidence: Compare seasonally adjusted core and services prices with import costs, FX and demand data.

questions.question: Did retail and business lending rates transmit the cut?
questions.evidence: Review deposit, commercial loan and consumer loan rates and credit growth after the decision.

questions.question: Did local forwards imply a larger or smaller move before release?
questions.evidence: Source pre-announcement TRY swap quotes and compare them with the 100 bp decision and the subsequent rates and FX changes.

title: Perceived Monetary Policy Rules: Evidence From Professional Forecasters in Australia
locator: Abstract, non-technical summary, estimated rules and cash-rate disagreement section
summary:
The authors estimate how professional forecasters believed the RBA would react to economic conditions between 2015 and 2025. They map survey expectations for macro variables into rate forecasts with rules whose parameters vary over time. Before the pandemic, forecasters perceived a relatively modest inflation response, in part because they doubted low inflation would induce easing when policymakers stressed employment and financial stability. After COVID, belief in a stronger inflation response rose once tightening began in 2022.

Differences in projected economic conditions usually explained more rate disagreement than differences in the perceived reaction function, although disagreement about the response to higher inflation mattered in the post-pandemic episode. For a speech-monitoring project, the implication is that textual signals should be evaluated against both new macro evidence and the policy actions that establish credibility. The estimates reflect survey-implied beliefs of the forecaster sample and the paper’s specifications. They do not identify the RBA’s true policy rule or translate directly to live market pricing.

questions.question: Does the result persist beyond professional economists’ surveys?
questions.evidence: Estimate analogous perceived responses from meeting-dated market prices and alternative surveys, with changes in risk compensation considered.

questions.question: How sensitive are the results to rule specification?
questions.evidence: Compare estimates with alternative horizons and macro inputs, including financial conditions and policy lags.

questions.question: When does communication lead followed policy?
questions.evidence: Line up narrative changes, forecast revisions and realised decisions around distinct inflation and activity shocks.

title: Monetary Policy Decision and Opening Remarks to the Press Conference
locator: Monetary Policy Decision and Opening Remarks, inflation and financial stability passages.
summary:
The Monetary Policy Board unanimously held at 3.00% after two previous increases. Growth was stronger than expected on exports and investment, with semiconductors supporting both and recovering consumption expected to contribute more. The Board judged that growth in both years was likely to exceed the August forecasts. September headline and core inflation were 2.9% and 2.8%, respectively. Further cost pass-through and rising domestic demand led the Board to expect inflation above target for some time, with 2027 inflation projected higher than in August.

It held to assess the effects of earlier hikes and uncertainty about the Middle East and policy in major economies. The forward-looking language explicitly called for assessing the timing and pace of further rate increases. The stability concern centres on Seoul-area property prices and housing loans, even as total household loans moved lower in the period discussed. The Bank also describes exchange-rate, bond and equity movements occurring before the release, which it associates with both domestic and global factors. The statement does not quantify the marginal market reaction to the decision.

questions.question: What evidence would pull forward the next hike?
questions.evidence: Compare revised 2027 projections, detailed CPI contributions and housing data with subsequent Board language and market-implied meeting pricing.

questions.question: Is the rise in housing credit being obscured by headline borrower flows?
questions.evidence: Review monthly household lending by secured category and region together with property-price measures.

questions.question: How dependent is growth on the semiconductor upswing?
questions.evidence: Use Korean export volumes, business investment and employment by sector to separate direct strength from spillovers into consumption.

title: 22 October policy-rate decision as recorded by the BSP
summary:
The October Monetary Board raised the target reverse repurchase rate by 50 basis points to 5.50%. In its subsequent Philippine Economic Updates, the BSP links the October action to broadening inflation and upside risks. The briefing describes limiting second-round effects and anchoring expectations as the goals. It identifies domestic fuel prices and transport fares as important contributors to inflation in October.

This entry uses the event date on the BSP’s monetary policy calendar and links to the BSP’s November recap for the October action. The rate change is a realised decision. The 6.1% and 6.0% inflation figures cited on the slide are the Board’s central projections for 2026 and 2027 as of the October meeting. The release time and intraday market response need separate verification.

questions.question: How much of the increase had already been anticipated?
questions.evidence: Check local rates and consensus on the morning of the announcement, then compare the same instrument around the official release.

questions.question: Did fuel and transport costs spread into broader prices and expectations?
questions.evidence: Compare the CPI components and survey measures of expectations available around the meeting.

questions.question: How quickly does the RRP increase transmit into short-term funding and loan pricing?
questions.evidence: Review matched-period overnight fixing, auction and lending rate data.

locator: BSP Philippine Economic Updates, November 2026, slide “Decisive monetary policy”; meeting date verified in the BSP 2026 Calendar of Monetary Policy Meetings.

title: Minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee Meeting, 5–7 October 2026
summary:
The October minutes document a unanimous vote for a 25 basis point repo rate rise to 5.50% and a split over what to signal next. Nagesh Kumar and Ram Singh supported the rate increase but backed keeping a neutral stance. The majority endorsed calibrated tightening, which allows a pause as data evolve and places near-term cuts outside the committee’s stated policy options at the time.

The resolution reproduced in the minutes weighs resilient activity against rising food and energy prices, broader price increases and a risk of spillovers into expectations. It also flags limited evidence of domestic demand pressure and difficulty separating direct and indirect supply effects from changes in firms’ pricing behaviour. The vote split matters because agreement about the current rate action leaves room for disagreement over how much information to give markets about the next meeting. The publication of individual views provides a separate opportunity to test whether market pricing changed.

questions.question: Which data would bring neutral-stance voters and tightening-stance voters closer together?
questions.evidence: Compare the members’ individual statements with incoming CPI components and their assumptions for growth.

questions.question: Did markets reprice the next meeting when the individual views were published?
questions.evidence: Obtain the official publication time and timestamped OIS quotes for the minutes window.

questions.question: Can expectations measures identify broader second-round inflation?
questions.evidence: Compare the household and professional surveys with inflation diffusion and payroll data rather than relying on headline CPI alone.

locator: Opening resolution and table of votes on the repo rate and policy stance.

title: BI-Rate Held at 5.75%: Strengthening Stability, Supporting Economic Growth
summary:
Bank Indonesia held the BI-Rate at 5.75% and Lending Facility at 6.50%, and raised the Deposit Facility to 5.00%. Alongside the corridor change, the bank announced phased cuts in average reserve requirements from 9% to 7% for conventional commercial banks and 7.5% to 5.5% for the specified Sharia institutions, starting in November. An accompanying adjustment reduces the maximum macroprudential liquidity incentive in December.

The bank continued orienting monetary policy towards rupiah stability and its 2.5% ± 1 percentage point inflation target. It paired market intervention across spot and forward instruments with incentives for banks to hedge foreign funding. The combination matters for transmission. The higher deposit rate can influence the overnight floor, while the reserve change and incentive adjustment affect available liquidity and credit conditions. A headline rate hold captures only part of the change in the operating framework.

questions.question: How much did the Deposit Facility increase raise money-market rates given the reserve cuts?
questions.evidence: Track overnight INDONIA, standing facility use and the balance of market liquidity before and after the steps.

questions.question: How much additional liquidity will banks get after the incentive adjustment?
questions.evidence: Check eligible banks’ effective requirements, incentive uptake and reserve balances.

questions.question: Did hedging incentives change rupiah funding costs or foreign inflows?
questions.evidence: Compare forward prices, market turnover and portfolio flows on the eligible tenors.

locator: Opening decision, policy measures 1–3, and exchange-rate measures.

title: Andrew Hauser: Fireside chat at Citi’s Australia & New Zealand Investment Conference
locator: Opening discussion on the deteriorating outlook, supply shocks and domestic demand
summary:
Hauser said the inflation outlook looked materially worse than in August while the staff forecast was still being finalised. He identifies energy prices roughly one-third above the August assumption, inflation in technology-related goods and pressure from data-centre construction, plus persistent constraints on Australian capacity. This sits alongside weak household confidence, a correction in housing and softer labour data. Overseas activity and parts of business investment were still resilient.

The two-sided trade-off is whether to tighten further to contain persistence or wait to protect employment and observe the lagged effect of earlier moves. Hauser outlines when policymakers could look through a supply shock: its effects must be temporary and expectations sufficiently anchored. With an extended shock and signs of higher expectations, the costs of waiting may be greater. The remarks predate the next vote and indicate concern about the inflation outlook while leaving the decision open.

questions.question: Are cost pressures broadening beyond oil-sensitive items?
questions.evidence: Use trimmed-mean CPI and detailed goods and services components with business pricing intentions.

questions.question: How different were live oil assumptions from the August vintage?
questions.evidence: Compare forward oil and refined-products curves at the two dates.

questions.question: Did the transcript shift expected meeting pricing?
questions.evidence: Compare timestamped OIS quotes around the scheduled remarks against preceding domestic data.

title: Pan Gongsheng at the Financial Street Forum: Issues in Focus for Markets
locator: PBOC transcript republished by the Shanghai municipal financial authorities on 20 October. See the opening measures and the first, second and third policy questions.
summary:
Pan’s central monetary proposal was to align the maturity of the PBOC’s main operation with the target already used in practice. He described DR001, the interbank overnight repo rate, as an active gauge of funds supply and demand. The seven-day maturity of the principal operation and its policy rate differed from the maturity of that target. An overnight reverse-repo anchor would narrow that mismatch. He framed it as a future change subject to timing and paired it with a wider choice of loan benchmarks. The LPR could remain useful for small firms and households, while firms able to manage more complex pricing could negotiate a floating benchmark tied to interbank rates.

Proposed safeguards included liquidity against high-quality collateral in a systemic bond fund redemption and selling cycle, an expanded standing facility, links between interbank and exchange-traded bond markets and wider onshore FX access for selected offshore RMB clearing banks. Pan separately emphasised a managed float with two-way flexibility. At the speech date the operating proposal pointed to a change in transmission and market structure. The transcript specifies neither a new rate level nor realised market repricing.

questions.question: Would quoting the operative rate at an overnight tenor tighten control of effective funding costs?
questions.evidence: Compare the distribution of DR001 minus the operation rate at tax and month-end dates using CFETS observations and PBOC tenders.

questions.question: Which borrowers would genuinely reprice faster under alternative loan benchmarks?
questions.evidence: Compare contract pricing, spreads and reset frequency across corporate samples with LPR and money-market references.

questions.question: How would the nonbank facility affect liquidity without encouraging risk taking?
questions.evidence: Check eligibility, collateral haircuts, access through parent institutions and stress-period secondary-market liquidity once operating terms are published.

title: Monetary Council decision, 20 October 2026
locator: Rate table and paragraphs on Hungary’s inflation, risk assessment and rate decision.
summary:
The Monetary Council maintained the base rate at 5.50%, the overnight deposit at 4.50% and the overnight collateralised loan rate at 6.50%. September headline inflation of 1.6% matched its forecast and core inflation was 1.9%. The Council nevertheless expected annual average inflation to rise from 1.8% in 2026 to 3.1% in 2027, primarily owing to fuel and tobacco excise effects, before declining towards the 2.5% target at the end of the policy horizon. The 2.5% target takes effect on 1 January 2028. The weak agricultural harvest weighed on activity, partly offset by industrial exports, and nominal wage growth was slowing.

The Council put weight on currency stability and positive real rates as channels for anchoring expectations. It identified high external yields and energy prices as constraints, and said the fiscal path and expectations around euro adoption would influence Hungary’s risk premium. The announcement therefore describes a cautious hold despite low current inflation. These are the Council’s own assessments. Its references to global rate pricing concern other central banks and do not establish the surprise in Hungarian assets.

questions.question: Which domestic price categories account for the forecast 2027 rise?
questions.evidence: Compare the MNB’s component projections with realised fuel, tobacco and core services prices.

questions.question: How much policy space depends on the forint’s exchange-rate channel?
questions.evidence: Track HUF exchange rates, domestic yields relative to peers, and importer and household expectations alongside fiscal announcements.

questions.question: What did local markets expect before the hold?
questions.evidence: Compare timestamped BUBOR-based forwards and EUR/HUF before and after the official publication.

title: Loan Prime Rates for 20 October 2026
locator: Authorised National Interbank Funding Center release, benchmark values and validity paragraph.
summary: The PBOC-authorised release lists the one-year and five-year-plus loan prime rates at 3.00% and 3.50%, respectively, effective until the next publication. These two different loan pricing references are quoted at the same release time. The one-paragraph notice gives the fixes and validity period but supplies no motive, committee forecast, individual bank submissions or transaction rates. The observed fixings therefore answer a question about published bank loan references; their pass-through to household or business borrowing requires other data.

questions.question: Did banks’ realised loan prices move while these benchmark levels applied?
questions.evidence: Compare new mortgage and corporate lending rates with the published fixings and separate changes in borrower mix from changes in margins.

questions.question: Which part of the credit curve moves most around the two publications?
questions.evidence: Collect same-clock quotes on funding rates and onshore swaps around the scheduled LPR publication, with separate adjustment for higher-frequency news.

questions.question: How much cross-bank dispersion sits behind the aggregates?
questions.evidence: Review any disclosed benchmark methodology, quote contributions and evidence on contract usage by borrower segment.

title: Learning about earnings: Can we rely on labour market slack to mitigate the latest supply shock? — Megan Greene
summary:
Greene’s concern was that UK labour market slack would provide less protection against persistent energy shock effects than the headline indicators suggested. Private sector regular average weekly earnings and tax payroll measures pointed to stalled wage disinflation. Her reading of the Decision Maker Panel, reported settlements and posted wages was that wage growth could settle nearer 3.5% than 3% over the coming year. Elevated headline inflation would coincide with a substantial share of the next round of pay bargaining.

She favoured leaning proactively against the risk. The staff scenarios she cited suggest that tightening against stronger second-round effects, then adjusting if they fail to materialise, can be less costly than discovering persistence after a weaker response. Her argument depends on the amount of slack, the timing of pay resets and the risk of recent shocks influencing expectations, and reflects her individual view.

questions.question: Is underlying wage growth plateauing across employers?
questions.evidence: Compare realised settlements with Decision Maker Panel expectations, private sector tax payroll and AWE data, adjusting for bonuses and worker composition.

questions.question: How tightly are 2027 pay settlements linked to headline inflation?
questions.evidence: Look for firm and sector survey evidence on pay setting, negotiation dates and margins ahead of the main settlement period.

questions.question: How much weaker could output become under the preventive strategy?
questions.evidence: Compare the output and inflation paths of the Bank staff scenarios under different estimates of policy lags.

locator: Conclusion and discussion of pay indicators, labour market slack and staff simulations.

title: Governor’s Special Address at the 21st Kuala Lumpur Islamic Finance Forum
summary:
Governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour uses Islamic finance to discuss Malaysia’s capital allocation and access to finance. He argues that sustainable economic participation depends on protection, skills and market access alongside loans. The iTEKAD programme is offered as an example that combines financing and training. Its reported reach across entrepreneurship, employment and protection programmes is nearly 16,000 people. The speech supplies a participant example, without estimating the programme’s aggregate impact.

The governor highlights risk sharing for areas such as food security and climate resilience and describes a review of the Shariah Contract Framework. He expects a strategy paper and exposure draft during the year. For macro research, the agenda matters to the composition of credit and capital formation over time. The speech does not update the OPR outlook.

questions.question: Which constraints prevent credit from becoming productive investment among small firms?
questions.evidence: Compare programme outcomes for financing-only and financing-plus-training cohorts, checking selection into the programmes.

questions.question: Which risk-sharing tools could change funding for productive capacity?
questions.evidence: Review the promised strategy paper and compare actual transaction terms and take-up.

questions.question: Can additional participation improve persistence of firm growth?
questions.evidence: Track survival, formal credit histories and onward employment in matched cohorts.

locator: “Finance that empowers” and “Collective stewardship, greater impact”; footnotes 2–3.

title: Ellis Connolly: Fireside chat at the AFIA Conference
locator: Payments priorities, financial market infrastructure and settlement discussion
summary:
Connolly outlines the RBA’s priorities for reliable payments, competition and the future of money. He says providers’ growing reliance on common third parties can cause an outage to affect multiple institutions. He links the payments work to the broader financial stability assessment, including oversight of clearing and settlement systems and the domestic real-time gross settlement system.

The discussion also covers work on account-to-account payments and consultation on how settlement infrastructure might evolve if tokenised markets expand. Access to cash remains a parallel priority in the RBA’s programme. The market relevance lies in settlement reliability, potential changes to the demand for settlement assets and continuity of core functions. The transcript describes priorities and consultation.

questions.question: How concentrated is the provision of essential settlement services?
questions.evidence: Compare provider dependencies and fallback arrangements across clearing, settlement and payments venues.

questions.question: How could tokenised settlement affect liquidity requirements?
questions.evidence: Review design choices for settlement timing and settlement assets, and test end-of-day and intraday funding use cases.

questions.question: Which initiatives have defined implementation commitments?
questions.evidence: Check the consultation and industry project updates for dates, scope and decision rights.

title: Edward S. Robinson: Some Observations on the AI Economy & Monetary Policy
locator: Paragraphs 1, 10–18 and Conclusion
summary:
Robinson contrasts the immediate demand effects of AI investment and higher asset values with possible future supply gains that have yet to be demonstrated at scale. He uses the example of AI diffusing into local services to show how productivity could spread beyond tradables, reduce costs and increase the ability of workers to perform technically demanding tasks. The policy questions hinge on observed diffusion and whether investment is translating into productive capacity.

He cites MAS’s calibrated April and July tightening in the context of stronger activity and a projected wider output gap. For the future, his prescriptions are state contingent: demand pressure may warrant restraint early in the investment boom, while stronger verified productive capacity can change the balance later. The direction of the neutral rate is uncertain because better expected investment returns and precautionary saving could work in opposite directions. He argues that macroprudential policy has a role in addressing leverage built around uncertain future revenues. This speech provides an analytical framework without a dated change in the exchange-rate band.

questions.question: Which indicators distinguish an investment boom from durable supply gains?
questions.evidence: Compare hardware and construction expenditure with measured services productivity and business adoption.

questions.question: How big is the leverage channel if expected AI earnings disappoint?
questions.evidence: Track project financing, issuer debt maturities and valuation sensitivity to revised revenues.

questions.question: What evidence would alter the estimated neutral exchange-rate path?
questions.evidence: Test productivity diffusion and domestic saving scenarios against the MAS macroeconomic assessment.

title: Focus market survey: 16 October 2026 reference date
summary:
The Focus release captures respondents’ forecasts as of 16 October. The median 2026 IPCA forecast was 5.22% and the 2027 median rose to 4.32%. The 2027 GDP growth median fell to 1.32% from 1.40% one week earlier. The median year-end Selic forecast held at 13.25% for 2026 and 12.00% for 2027. The table shows heterogeneous response counts and separately lists the forecasts submitted over the five most recent working days.

The forecast combination suggests markets surveyed saw weaker growth alongside elevated inflation. The figures belong to survey respondents. They cannot establish either Copom's forecast or how the market was pricing specific meeting outcomes at a given time.
locator: Aggregate medians table and weekly comparison notes

questions.question: Is the change in the median broad-based across respondents?
questions.evidence: Use subsequent Focus distribution releases and compare survey counts over time.

questions.question: How does the survey relate to actual meeting pricing?
questions.evidence: Compare the survey’s year-end forecasts with dated DI futures and count remaining policy meetings.

questions.question: Do higher price expectations reflect current inflation or more persistent pressures?
questions.evidence: Compare future Focus horizons with IPCA components and regulated-price expectations.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Explanation of the Recent Depreciation of the New Taiwan Dollar
locator: Chinese original release, observations of the exchange rate and foreign investors’ transactions.
summary:
The CBC attributed the 12–16 October weakening of the New Taiwan dollar against the US dollar mainly to global equity volatility, foreign net equity selling and remittance of dividends. The report gives a move from NT$31.895 to NT$32.338 per USD and a reported depreciation of 1.37%. In its account, this coincided with net foreign equity sales of US$19.402 billion and net outward remittance of US$17.961 billion. Those refer to different transaction measures and should not be added. The central bank said it would remain attentive to international conditions and flows and adjust as supply and demand evolve to maintain orderly currency movements.

The release gives the CBC’s explanation of a preceding multi-day move. It contains no scheduled change to the discount rate and does not establish whether flows dominated every part of the adjustment or caused subsequent trading.

questions.question: Was the release itself followed by a distinct FX move?
questions.evidence: Check timestamped TWD spot and offshore forward quotes separately around publication, using a basket of contemporaneous currencies to compare dollar effects.

questions.question: What portion of equity sales was reflected in foreign exchange transactions?
questions.evidence: Compare investor flows, currency conversions and dividend settlement dates without presuming one-for-one pass-through.

questions.question: Did the front end move alongside the currency?
questions.evidence: Compare overnight and bill observations with the currency move to assess whether it coincided with tighter domestic funding.

title: Christopher Kent: Fireside chat at the Commonwealth Bank’s Global Markets Conference
locator: Transcript on global bond yields, neutral rates, the Australian dollar and capacity pressures
summary:
Kent links recent global bond moves to overlapping shocks instead of a single change in policy expectations. The discussion points to energy disruption and resilience in demand, high sovereign issuance, geopolitical risk and recurring uncertainty about neutral interest rates. He notes that rising short-term inflation expectations could threaten longer-run anchoring even while longer-horizon market measures looked comparatively stable. A structural rise in global neutral rates would change how one reads a given cash rate, but productivity and demographic effects remain hard to assess.

He describes the Australian dollar as still sensitive to global risk and cautions that estimates of a long-run equilibrium exchange rate are uncertain. For domestic activity he notes slowing in households despite stronger pockets of spending and identifies low productivity as relevant for unit labour costs. The market implications depend on whether higher yields reflect domestic rates, imported conditions or compensation for risks. The transcript reports Kent’s interpretation and also contains questions and claims from the interviewer.

questions.question: What share of the long-yield move was common across markets?
questions.evidence: Compare curve moves, oil, sovereign supply and cross-market inflation compensation at matched times.

questions.question: Is the AUD reacting to relative short rates or broader risk?
questions.evidence: Compare major crosses, commodity proxies and rate differentials over several episodes.

questions.question: Do labour costs imply a domestic persistence problem?
questions.evidence: Track nominal wage measures, productivity and the breadth of domestically generated inflation.

title: Christopher Kent: Interview on News 24 with Ross Greenwood
locator: Interview passages on negative rates, the Bond Purchase Program, and its effects
summary:
Kent looks back at bond purchases during the pandemic. He says negative rates were viewed as poorly suited to a banking-based system, and purchases aimed to reach maturities beyond the short end already addressed by a near-zero cash rate. He identifies an exchange-rate channel as central banks abroad were also easing and an appreciation would have made it harder to lift inflation.

His estimate of the overall purchase programme’s effect was a reduction in yields across the curve of about 30 basis points. He qualifies the estimate as imprecise and argues that other tools, including the Term Funding Facility, were more effective. He also explains why higher cash rates could tighten conditions without the RBA having to sell those bonds. These are retrospective remarks about policy tools and estimated transmission, not a forecast of current purchases or of the cash-rate path.

questions.question: Which purchases moved yields once peer-country policy is accounted for?
questions.evidence: Compare announcements with intraday relative yields and FX, then check purchase-flow and announcement effects separately.

questions.question: How did funding relief translate to lending?
questions.evidence: Compare bank funding costs and loan pricing by reliance on the facility.

questions.question: When would balance-sheet runoff add restraint beyond the rate path?
questions.evidence: Link maturity schedules and net sovereign supply to estimated term premia and market liquidity.

title: MNB account of Mihály Varga’s IMF annual meeting remarks
locator: Official press account, first three paragraphs. Full conversation unavailable in this record.
summary:
Governor Mihály Varga told the IMF annual meeting audience in Bangkok that Hungary’s outlook had improved but that global uncertainty and high energy prices continued to justify caution. He said inflation could remain below the then-current 3% target in 2026 while growth could strengthen. He discussed the September decision to lower the future target to 2.5% and connected durable low inflation to the case for economic convergence.

On the euro, Varga framed adoption as a comparison of costs and benefits and did not propose a firm timetable. The remarks therefore give context on the governor’s policy priorities rather than a decision or a measured market response.

questions.question: Which domestic components are driving the improved outlook?
questions.evidence: Examine the national accounts, exports and household demand in the latest MNB forecast.

questions.question: Would an additional energy shock change the domestic reaction?
questions.evidence: Review the MNB’s alternative inflation scenarios and data on expectations and import prices.

title: Anthony Brassil and Michele Bullock: Overview of the RBA Annual Conference on Monetary Policy Trade-offs
locator: Overview pp. 1–3. Conference 8–9 October, overview released 16 October.
summary:
Brassil and Bullock argue that the policy cost of returning inflation to target depends on the shock, the economy and the credibility of policy. A persistent adverse supply shock pushes prices up while weakening output and real income. Tightening can limit persistence but adds to near-term demand weakness. A slower return can lessen the immediate employment effects while increasing the chance that higher inflation becomes embedded.

The overview cautions that inflation costs are widespread and partly difficult to observe, such as the time spent seeking lower prices or renegotiating wages. Unemployment costs are concentrated and more visible and can have long-lived effects on workers’ skills and matches. The paper summarises contributions on measuring these costs and how anchored expectations change the trade-off. The macro use is in assessing the reaction to a particular shock and the distribution of adjustment costs. It is a conference overview.

questions.question: What distinguishes a supply shock from a broad excess-demand episode in real time?
questions.evidence: Compare the joint behaviour of prices, output and employment by sector and use the conference papers’ identification approaches.

questions.question: Which indicators measure costly loss of inflation anchoring early enough to matter?
questions.evidence: Compare expectation horizons, firm price plans and wage contracts after previous cost shocks.

questions.question: Who bears the labour-market adjustment?
questions.evidence: Use household and labour microdata to examine job loss, duration, wage scars and consumption rather than relying on aggregate employment alone.

title: Junko Koeda in Kumamoto: Economic Activity, Prices, and Monetary Policy in Japan
locator: Speech §§I–II, notably charts 1–2 and 12–15, and the final section on policy conduct.
summary:
Koeda saw scope for further accommodation withdrawal if the outlook materialised, while focusing on the cumulative impact of earlier rate increases and changes in risk. She set out three lenses: AI demand and prospective supply gains, geopolitical shocks and natural disaster resilience. In her account of the recent shock, oil prices and yen depreciation both raised import costs. Less evident safe-haven appreciation makes it important to assess the FX response alongside the direct oil shock.

The immediate effects of AI exports and labour-saving investment can add to demand and inflation, while the longer-run productivity effect remains uncertain. She regarded conditions as accommodative after the September move to about 1.25%, pointing to generally favourable corporate funding and resilient plans. She distinguished variable-rate mortgages from households’ interest-bearing assets and stronger pay, with the distribution and cumulative effect relevant for consumption. That makes the current policy rate and nominal yields incomplete measures of the burden across sectors.

questions.question: How much imported inflation came through oil prices versus the yen?
questions.evidence: Use the two currency denominations of the import-price series and compare their pass-through to producer and consumer categories.

questions.evidence: Compare floating mortgage reset schedules, debt service and deposit income by household age and leverage.

title: Current economic developments and the SNB’s monetary policy — Petra Tschudin
summary: Tschudin described a global economy facing weaker activity and rising inflation from higher energy and input costs. Inflation in Switzerland remained comparatively low. The international rate charts separate market pricing from the SNB’s own assessment. Wider rate differentials had contributed to a weaker franc, while manufacturing had begun to show signs of recovery. The SNB expected moderate growth and referred to the September decision to maintain the policy rate at 0%. The conditional Swiss inflation outlook was slightly higher than in June and remained within the price stability range.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Post-Meeting Press Conference Presentation (2026 Q3)
locator: Attached slides, sections I–IV and accompanying forecast and credit charts.
summary:
The slides associated with the September meeting explain why strong GDP growth and inflation near 2% did not lead the Board to raise the discount rate. They report a revised 11.48% growth forecast for 2026, with a high base effect contributing to a slower 2027 projection. Forecasts for headline and core CPI rose to 2.03% and 2.16% in 2026. The easing next year, to 1.83% and 1.89%, depends partly on a lower oil price profile and contained demand pressure. The slides distinguish CBC forecasts from outside consensus and realised statistical observations.

The Bank also presents M2 as a monitored reference and argues that slower money growth than the sum of real growth and inflation is consistent with restraint. Its estimates of stance and much milder cumulative inflation compared with peers depend on the reported measures and chosen comparisons. Housing indicators show that credit concentration and the growth of real estate lending had moderated by the meeting. This is the September presentation released in October.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: Michelle Bowman · Supervisory Modernization After Silicon Valley Bank
locator: Independent review findings, revised operating principles and Financial Stability Board discussion
summary: Bowman used the 2023 banking stress review to make a case for clearer escalation and a focus on risks capable of causing material harm. The revised operating principles emphasise supervisory judgement, early identification and timely intervention. She tied those lessons to the FSB’s work on aligning supervisory intensity with size, complexity and interconnectedness. Her policy proposal concerns supervision. The implications for funding resilience depend on how quickly examiners identify exposures and how institutions respond.

title: Macroeconomic Review, October 2026
locator: Key Messages, Global Economy, Singapore Economy and Labour Market and Inflation. Summary focuses on the published overview.
summary:
The MAS review presents an above-trend, technology-led expansion supported by strong global demand for AI inputs and domestic capacity expansions. It expects this source of growth to ease in 2027 as the technology cycle moderates and global financial conditions tighten. The picture outside technology is more varied, so the investment read-through depends on whether additional income and spending spread to domestic sectors.

The inflation outlook is for the core rate slightly above 2% to persist around recent levels through the first half of 2027 before easing more clearly in the second half. The near-term pressure reflects earlier external cost increases. The projected easing assumes those costs fade and domestic labour and other costs remain contained. The review places the October decision to maintain the appreciating band in that context. Its forecast is tied to the October release and does not measure surprise relative to market expectations. The questions below target its central assumptions.

questions.evidence: Use sector-level industrial production, orders and value-added data to measure breadth.

questions.question: Is the assumption of subdued domestic costs robust?
questions.evidence: Compare unit labour costs with services prices and price effects of temporary subsidies.

questions.question: Which transmission channel matters if global financial conditions tighten?

title: MAS Monetary Policy Statement, October 2026
locator: Paragraphs 1–11 and Chart 1
summary:
MAS kept the appreciation rate of the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange-rate policy band, its width and its centre unchanged. It had increased the slope very slightly in July, so the existing band continued to appreciate. Chart 1 and the accompanying text describe a modest strengthening within the upper half of the band. The instrument is the trade-weighted exchange-rate band. A single bilateral exchange rate is only one of the prices relevant to an event study.

The statement describes strong technology-led growth and a positive output gap expected to narrow in 2027. It cites advance GDP growth of 5.4% year on year in Q3 and a rise in MAS core inflation to 2.1% in July–August from 1.5% in Q2. The statement projects 2027 core and headline inflation to average 1.5–2.5%, with clearer easing from midyear as import costs fade and domestic costs remain contained. Upside risks include another energy or food shock and stronger spillovers from AI demand. Counterweights include tighter global financial conditions, weaker technology investment or a faster energy supply recovery.

title: Minutes of the September 2026 Monetary Policy Board meeting
locator: Meeting held 29 September, minutes released 13 October. Considerations for monetary policy and The decision
summary:
The September policy decision, described in these October minutes, was a unanimous 25 basis point increase from 4.35% to 4.60%. Members judged domestic excess demand larger than previously assessed. Unit labour costs were elevated despite limited nominal wage pressure, pointing to weaker productivity, while energy and AI-related price pressures made the inflation path less favourable. The Board saw a risk that prolonged above-target inflation would feed into medium-term expectations and judged the economy sufficiently resilient to tighten at that point.

The minutes also discuss waiting because delayed effects of earlier tightening or falling house prices could weaken activity more than anticipated. Higher global neutral rates, if the signal from markets was correct, would make a given cash rate less restrictive. The minutes matter as a description of the Board’s risk weighting after the September action. A same-day event study belongs on 13 October, independently of the price reaction to the September decision.

questions.question: Did markets learn anything from the minutes beyond the September decision?
questions.evidence: Compare the decision-day materials with the minutes and measure the 13 October OIS reaction in a narrow release window.

questions.question: How much does slower productivity explain inflation persistence?
questions.evidence: Compare unit labour costs, individual wage growth and productivity across industries.

questions.question: Would weaker housing alter the demand outlook enough to change policy?
questions.evidence: Compare consumption and mortgage cash-flow measures with the Board’s housing sensitivity analysis.

title: MNB account of Mihály Varga’s remarks on euro adoption
locator: Official press account of the event, including benefits, risks and preconditions.
summary:
Governor Mihály Varga discussed the possibility of euro adoption as a question of economic readiness. He argued that removing exchange-rate and conversion costs could help firms and that lower rates could reduce financing costs. The reported HUF 130 billion annual saving concerns currency conversion fees and is a claim made in the remarks.

He said that adopting a shared currency would also remove a domestic monetary policy tailored to Hungarian conditions and could make it harder to respond to asymmetric shocks. He emphasised fiscal balance, sustained low inflation, productivity and competitiveness alongside formal convergence requirements. September inflation of 1.6% was cited as current evidence, while external inflation risks still warranted caution.

questions.question: What explains the quoted conversion-cost estimate?
questions.evidence: Request the underlying measurement and the distinction between business and consumer conversion fees.

questions.question: How large are Hungary’s asymmetric shocks?
questions.evidence: Compare sector exposure, demand and inflation cycles with those in the euro area.

questions.question: Does the euro adoption discussion change domestic term premia?
questions.evidence: Review forward rates and sovereign spreads around separately timed fiscal and policy announcements.

title: When the policy mix meets supply shocks — Agnès Bénassy-Quéré
summary:
Bénassy-Quéré argued that supply shocks complicate coordination because inflation rises as output weakens. Temporary energy support can cushion incomes and reduce the measured CPI peak, while broad fiscal support can sustain demand and increase financing pressure. Higher nominal growth does not guarantee improved fiscal space when spending is indexed and debt service rises. Support that eases a bottleneck can affect inflation differently from general demand support.

France’s energy shield is the main case study. The Banque de France research cited in the speech estimates that the shield reduced inflation by around 2.6 percentage points in 2022. Part of that effect reversed in subsequent years. The evidence leaves open whether a lower peak also moderated wage and expectation persistence. Comparisons between French and aggregate euro area prices are descriptive and cannot identify the shield’s full long-run impact on their own.

questions.question: How much of the lower measured inflation reflected postponed price increases?
questions.evidence: Review the shield study’s counterfactual, regulated tariff schedules and pass-through after support was wound back.

questions.question: Did a lower inflation peak change bargained wages and expectations?
questions.evidence: Compare sector wage deals, household expectations and cross-country evidence controlling for other shocks.

questions.question: What is the cost of financing renewed support?
questions.evidence: Assess the programme’s primary balance effect, debt maturity and sensitivity to long yields.

locator: Slides 5–8 and the France case study.

title: Macroeconomic projections and quarterly report on the Spanish economy — Q3 2026
summary:
The Banco de España lifted its GDP growth projection to 2.6% for 2026 from 2.3% in June and to 2.2% for 2027 from 1.7%. Stronger second-quarter activity and a better view of the second half explained much of the revision. The report projected some deceleration in household consumption and pointed to a high saving rate as a buffer against higher rates and energy costs. In the first half, equipment and intangible investment both supported productive investment.

The external environment remained uncertain. Between the report assumptions’ cutoffs, oil rose 4% and gas 52%, with substantial variation. The report’s comparison across ten-year sovereigns showed Spain’s yield up 55 basis points, and discussed issuance, shifts in expected policy rates, inflation compensation and credit risk as possible contributors. The figures refer to the intervals and assumptions used by the report. The association between the projection revision and higher yields does not by itself identify the amount of tightening reaching households or firms.

questions.question: Is the 2026 growth upgrade mainly a carry-over or a change in forward momentum?
questions.evidence: Compare GDP vintages and the quarterly profile in the June and October forecasts.

questions.question: How much can household savings cushion higher energy and funding costs?
questions.evidence: Check savings and debt servicing by income and mortgage type rather than aggregate balances alone.

questions.question: What explains Spain’s share of the global long-end sell-off?
questions.evidence: Separate Bund and swap moves from Spanish spread dynamics, issuance and flow data.

locator: Global context, Chart 1 and GDP, consumption and investment projection discussion.
coverageLimitation: Summary focuses on the macro projections and financial context. The report’s separate survey boxes are not all covered here.

title: Belanjawan 2027
summary:
BNM’s response to Malaysia’s 2027 budget details measures involving finance and household access to credit. It highlights another RM5 billion for the SME Stabilisation Relief Facility, expected to reach about 9,000 more businesses, including microenterprises. As of 30 September, BNM reports RM3.8 billion of financing approvals from the initial RM5 billion allocation across more than 6,800 SME accounts. The release distinguishes the announced capacity from financing approved.

The facility addresses temporary working-capital pressure. The release also describes a basic credit-card option with a maximum annual rate of 14% and a simpler product structure. For research on policy transmission, the measures matter to borrowing terms and access for selected households and firms. The aggregate budget impulse requires the full fiscal numbers and the pace of implementation.

questions.question: Do facility approvals lead to additional working capital for firms facing constraints?
questions.evidence: Compare disbursement, utilisation and eligibility against the initial facility and ordinary lending.

questions.question: How much of the fiscal support reaches demand quickly?
questions.evidence: Read the budget’s cash-flow schedule and the timing of financing approvals and disbursements.

questions.question: Does basic credit improve affordability for new borrowers?
questions.evidence: Compare effective annual costs, fees, approval rates and repayment outcomes for comparable borrowers.

locator: SME Stabilisation Relief Facility and basic credit card bullets.

title: The Governor’s autumn lecture: Why is the last mile of disinflation taking so long? — Ida Wolden Bache
summary:
Bache asked why Norwegian inflation was still above target after the initial rise had subsided. She considered different speeds of price adjustment, wage and price formation in an open economy, and inflation expectations. A sequence of higher import prices can feed through gradually. Higher export prices can also improve exporters’ capacity to pay, allowing wage deals in the traded sector to support cost increases elsewhere. Coordinated bargaining therefore has different effects depending on whether the original shock mainly raises costs or strengthens the income of firms setting the wage norm.

A stylised model illustrates how higher foreign real rates can weaken the exchange-rate channel and how domestic real appreciation can damp imported price pressure. The calibrations are illustrations, with no estimated historical contribution for the individual mechanisms. Bache also observed that the decline in expectations had stalled and discussed the difficulty of separating the causal influence of expectations from other simultaneous developments.

questions.question: How much of domestic services inflation is coming from wage-setting spillovers?
questions.evidence: Compare manufacturing wage settlements, exporter margins and service-sector unit labour costs across periods with different terms-of-trade shocks.

questions.question: How strong is krone transmission when policy rates rise abroad as well?
questions.evidence: Use Norges Bank model comparisons, exchange-rate data and the import price response to test the mechanism rather than treating the simulation as an estimate.

questions.question: Are firms’ inflation expectations changing actual price decisions?
questions.evidence: Follow the cited Norges Bank staff work on firm expectations and compare surveys with observed repricing.

locator: Illustrative model charts and notes 13–22.

title: Strong growth and inflation risk — Erik Thedéen sees grounds for an interest rate increase
summary:
Thedéen argued that stronger-than-expected Swedish growth and rising inflation risks made a near-term increase plausible. The official presentation note points to second-quarter strength across consumption, exports and investment. Higher commodity costs, supply disruptions and a weaker krona could raise costs further. The governor was concerned that strong demand could make it easier for firms to pass these costs through to a broader part of the consumption basket.

Thedéen said this was consistent with his September meeting position. He had already considered a November increase possible and an upward adjustment of the rate forecast appropriate. He stressed uncertainty about further increases in the following year and said September inflation would be assessed with other incoming data. He separately noted that rising global long yields could damp activity and increase borrowing costs.

questions.evidence: Examine September and subsequent CPIF components, services prices and firm pricing plans.

questions.evidence: Compare effective exchange rates, credit costs and the Riksbank’s policy scenarios.

institution: Banco Central de Reserva del Perú
title: Programa Monetario de Octubre 2026: reference rate held at 4.25%
summary:
The BCRP's official announcement and video describe a hold at 4.25%. The video attributes much of the inflation overshoot to fuel, electricity and transport costs. It gives annual inflation excluding food and energy at 4.5%, while that measure excluding transport was 1.8%. The bank cites a 3.1% twelve-month inflation expectation and 2.5% at twenty-four months. This horizon difference matters for assessing how persistent the shock is expected to be.

Activity indicators continued to perform well. The bank expected inflation to return towards 2% as adverse supply shocks faded and flagged risks from El Niño and Middle East tensions. It remained alert to inflation, expectations, activity and shock duration when assessing whether to adjust the stance. The published rate series shows 4.25% on the surrounding business days.

questions.evidence: Compare activity and credit indicators highlighted by the bank with sector-level prices.

coverageNote: The central bank’s official video transcript was available. The policy-note PDF could not be opened, so the rate series was used to corroborate the rate level.

title: Policy Position on the Renminbi Exchange Rate
locator: PBOC original on the Shanghai municipal financial authority’s website. The 8 October original release date is corroborated by the Wuhan municipal financial authority’s 9 October publication.
summary:
The PBOC presents the renminbi as a managed float, based on market supply and demand with reference to a currency basket. It argues that the exchange rate responds to growth, monetary policy, markets and shocks, and that a current-account surplus by itself cannot identify a misaligned exchange rate. Its account points to multiple episodes of appreciation and depreciation as evidence of growing two-way flexibility. The bank attributes export competitiveness to structural factors and rejects competitive devaluation as a policy objective.

The paper is the issuing central bank’s position in a debate about exchange rate valuation. Its critique of using a single estimated equilibrium level is relevant for scenario analysis, because model assumptions can change a misalignment estimate. The publication does not supply a numerical exchange rate target or an observed price reaction to the statement.

questions.question: Which observable measure would distinguish two-way flexibility from smoothing in stress?
questions.evidence: Compare daily fixing deviations, spot and offshore gaps with contemporaneously published net FX trading and cross-border flow measures.

questions.question: How sensitive is a currency valuation estimate to its model assumptions?
questions.evidence: Compare real effective exchange rates, external balances and several externally estimated equilibrium models under the same data vintage.

questions.question: Where do changes in the exchange rate affect exports and margin most?
questions.evidence: Compare invoice currency, hedging and pass-through for exporters across industries and trading partners.

title: Minutes of the policy decision announced on 24 September 2026
summary:
The board unanimously left its overnight interbank target at 6.50% in September. The published minutes present the September hold as a decision to evaluate how ongoing disinflation, spare capacity and the existing degree of monetary restraint interact. Currency pass-through and inflation expectations were central to the next decision. The board stressed that Mexican conditions could justify a different response from the Federal Reserve.

The relevant distinction for a rates event study is between the September decision and information about the reaction function disclosed when the minutes came out in October. Rate or FX moves around those releases would answer different questions.
locator: Sections 3–4, policy decision and vote

questions.question: What would make an easing decision compatible with still-elevated inflation expectations?
questions.evidence: Compare core price composition and survey expectations with the board’s disinflation criteria.

questions.question: How strong is MXN pass-through under spare capacity?
questions.evidence: Test regional import-price and CPI categories against MXN changes and measures of domestic slack.

questions.question: What fresh information did investors get in October?
questions.evidence: Compare the September statement to the minutes and check short-dated swaps around the minutes release.

coverageNote: Focuses on the policy decision and vote. The statistical annex and all figures have not been independently reviewed.

title: MNB account of Mihály Varga’s Istanbul Economic Forum remarks
locator: Official press account of the governor’s panel remarks. Scope excludes a full panel transcript.
summary:
Governor Mihály Varga linked the MNB’s new 2.5% inflation target, effective in 2028, to its recent record of cautious monetary policy. He argued that a stable price environment makes long-horizon business planning and financing easier and said central banks need flexibility to assess alternative scenarios in the face of energy and geopolitical risks. The release attributes to him a continued focus on inflation, global developments and Hungarian risk premia in individual rate decisions.

The account offers an explanation of the framework and reasons for maintaining caution. It gives no new policy-rate setting or release-window evidence.

questions.question: Have firms’ plans become less sensitive to inflation shocks?
questions.evidence: Compare surveys of planned investment and price setting with evidence on inflation expectations.

questions.question: Which risks would cause the Council to change pace?
questions.evidence: Review the Council’s later scenario analysis and measure changes in energy and domestic risk premia.

questions.question: What was new to the audience relative to the target decision?
questions.evidence: Compare the Istanbul release and any available panel recording with the earlier target-review statement.

title: Financial resilience in an age of repeated shocks — Andrew Bailey
summary:
Bailey argued that the resilience of banks, borrowers and core markets gives policymakers room to respond to repeated supply shocks. Higher energy costs weaken real activity while persistence can threaten inflation expectations. A policy response can raise financing costs as incomes and earnings come under pressure, making collateral values and credit availability material for the outlook.

He also described a shift in government bond ownership towards more leveraged, price-sensitive buyers. This may have helped markets absorb issuance. During stress, margin calls and forced sales could amplify moves and transmit losses across jurisdictions where the same investors hold positions. He advocated explaining the conditions that would trigger policy action and discussed central clearing, haircuts and risk management as ways to strengthen core markets. The speech offers a financial stability mechanism without a specific rate path or quantitative market reaction.

questions.question: Where is leveraged sovereign duration risk concentrated?
questions.evidence: Consult funding and margin data, positioning reports and regulatory evidence on repo and futures trades across gilt, Treasury and euro sovereign markets.

questions.question: Which movements in long yields reflect supply and intermediation pressures?
questions.evidence: Compare auction results, collateral and repo conditions, maturity-matched swaps and term premium estimates.

questions.question: Could weak borrower cash flows amplify a renewed energy shock?
questions.evidence: Examine refinancing schedules, debt servicing ratios and collateral buffers by sector.

locator: The interaction with financial stability, A changing market structure, and policy response.

title: Enjeux actuels de la politique monétaire — Antoine Martin
summary: Martin presented the September decision in the context of the SNB’s price stability range and a slightly firmer medium-term inflation outlook than in June. The presentation’s conditional CPI chart shows the forecast revision while both projections maintain a 0% policy rate assumption. The SNB kept its rate at that level in September. The slides set the decision in the context of Switzerland’s realised inflation components and describe how the central bank evaluates the inflation outlook.

questions.question: What explains the higher inflation path?
questions.evidence: Compare domestic and imported CPI contributions across projections.

questions.question: How much does the exchange rate drive the forecast?
questions.evidence: Examine the assumptions and the import price data.

questions.question: What did markets anticipate?
questions.evidence: Compare rates pricing at the September decision and before these remarks.

locator: French slides on CPI and the September conditional forecast
coverageLimitation: Official French slide deck reviewed. No separate transcript was available.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: Christopher Waller · The Signaling Value of the Summary of Economic Projections
locator: Economic update, communication examples, September SEP and market-pricing discussion, footnote 1
summary:
Waller attributed his support for September’s quarter-point increase to a shift in risks over several months. Labour conditions had stabilised and inflation remained above target. He cited August core PCE inflation of 3% year over year and judged that returning inflation to target required further hikes if incoming data followed his baseline.

He argued that the Fed can signal the likely extent of tightening and leave its timing contingent on the data. His three-hike example illustrates the communication mechanism. September’s projections put at least one more 2026 hike in 16 of 18 participants’ submissions, while his account of the previous day’s fed funds futures shows the market attaching a range of probabilities to the timing and number of moves. The market pricing he cites was available before the speech.

questions.question: What did the speech add to the path already priced?
