questions.evidence: Check meeting-dated futures around the verified first public release and compare with the prior day's curve.

questions.question: Which inflation data would change the pace of tightening?
questions.evidence: Compare incoming core PCE components and employment data with Waller’s stated baseline.

questions.question: What does dispersion among the dots hide?
questions.evidence: Compare the September SEP’s end-year points with futures pricing at individual meetings.

title: Assessing Household Debt Risks Using the Korean Household-Level Consumer Credit Panel
locator: Bank of Korea Issue Note 2026-23, public summary items 1–5 and linked report.
summary:
The study groups credit records by household using address information. Its panel includes about 2.06 million households, allowing it to track other household members’ credit alongside that of a primary borrower. The authors argue that individual records alone can miss exposure across people who share financial decisions. Their stress exercise estimates a broadly steady delinquency rate among borrowing households overall after a rate shock but a larger response for a defined set of highly leveraged homebuyers. For that subgroup, a 1 percentage point rise in rates was estimated to increase delinquency probability by 0.81 percentage points. The group is identified by the increase in debt service relative to income at purchase.

These are conditional estimates from a staff study. An aggregate result can conceal distributional tail risk and contagion among household members. The source does not imply that policy is committed to reining in credit solely through the policy rate.

questions.question: How robust are the results to alternative ways of linking co-residents?
questions.evidence: Check the note’s validation samples and test sensitivity to address changes, family structure and co-borrowing.

questions.question: Which households have near-term cash-flow repricing?
questions.evidence: Match debt-service burdens with reset dates and fixed versus floating rates.

questions.question: Can targeted lending rules contain the tail without strong aggregate effects?
questions.evidence: Use borrower-level approval and loan performance around earlier prudential changes and compare similar groups.

coverageLimitation: Analysis uses the official web summary. Appendix and robustness tables in the linked full note were not verified.

title: Account of the monetary policy meeting of 9–10 September 2026
summary: The October account records a September decision supported by every member to raise the three ECB policy rates by 25 basis points. Members saw a risk that persistent energy costs would leave medium-term inflation above target. They judged the move robust to milder, adverse and severe staff scenarios. The Council retained discretion about the future path and planned to watch energy prices, expectation measures and price and wage setting. September is the policy decision date. October is when the discussion was published.

questions.question: What was priced before the account was released?
questions.evidence: Compare dated euro short-term-rate OIS around the release.

questions.question: Why did all staff scenarios support a hike?
questions.evidence: Compare assumptions about energy and second-round effects.

questions.question: Which inflation indicators show broader pressure?
questions.evidence: Compare core prices, wages and expectations.

locator: Monetary policy discussion and decisions

title: Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee, 5–7 October 2026
summary:
The MPC unanimously raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%. The overnight standing deposit facility moved to 5.25%, while the marginal standing facility and Bank Rate moved to 5.75%. A majority adopted calibrated tightening. Nagesh Kumar and Ram Singh backed the hike but preferred a neutral stance. The resolution describes the new guidance as a choice between another hike and a pause, conditional on the data.

The case for tightening rested on inflation risks against resilient domestic activity. The MPC projected FY 2026–27 growth at 7.1% and CPI inflation at 5.2%, with inflation reaching 6.0% in the third fiscal quarter. Food and fuel drove much of the recent inflation rise, but the weighted share of CPI items above 4% had also increased. The committee saw limited evidence that demand was already driving inflation, while strong money and credit growth gave it a reason to monitor that risk. It also acknowledged that the available indicators cannot cleanly distinguish input-cost pass-through from more durable changes in price setting. Charts 1 and 2 present the MPC’s conditional forecasts rather than market expectations.

questions.question: How broad is the rise in prices beyond food, fuel and precious metals?
questions.evidence: Compare CPI component diffusion and the core measures reported with survey and firm price-setting data available around the decision.

questions.question: How long would expensive energy have to persist before another rate increase became likely?
questions.evidence: Compare the RBI’s oil assumptions and transmission estimates with the maturity profile of crude prices and administered fuel prices.

questions.question: Did the change in guidance alter front-end expectations?
questions.evidence: Check pre-announcement overnight indexed swaps and match the release time against subsequent quotes and other news.

locator: Resolution paragraphs 2, 7–15 and Charts 1–2. The figures here come from the resolution text.

title: NBP Monetary Policy Council communiqué, 6–7 October 2026
locator: Source checked against the original communiqué reproduced by the NBP in its November Inflation Report, chapter 3, pp. 29–30. The direct release page returned HTTP 403 during review.
summary: The Council held the reference rate at 3.75%. Statistics Poland’s September flash CPI estimate had risen to 4.0% year on year, largely because of transport fuel. The Council estimated that core inflation had edged down. Retail, industry and construction had grown in August, while corporate employment was falling. It identified global energy, domestic energy regulation, fiscal policy and wages as risks for future decisions.

questions.question: How much of the higher headline print was imported or fuel-related?
questions.evidence: Use the revised CPI breakdown, core measures and transport fuel prices.

questions.question: Did falling corporate employment signal broader weakening?
questions.evidence: Compare business-sector payrolls with labour force data, vacancies and the next wage releases.

questions.question: Did the announcement change the expected rate path?
questions.evidence: Compare timestamped PLN forwards and EUR/PLN around the first publication, accounting for other releases.

title: Monetary Policy Report – October 2026
locator: Focused read of the Executive Summary, Chapter II.3 and Table II.7, and Chapter V including Table V.2, Table V.3, Chart V.7 and Box V.1. Numbers taken from the accompanying report text and tables.
summary:
The RBI’s October report projects 7.1% real GDP growth and 5.2% CPI inflation for fiscal 2026–27. It identifies private consumption, fixed investment and external demand as supports for first-quarter GDP growth of 7.8%. Activity remained resilient in high-frequency readings after that quarter, with some moderation. The report records a deterioration in rural households’ current confidence and softer year-ahead expectations for urban and rural households. The growth forecast depends in part on sustained consumption helping to broaden private investment.

The projected inflation path peaks at 6.0% in fiscal Q3 before easing to 5.7% in Q4. The baseline raises the assumed oil price to US$95 per barrel in the second half of 2026–27 and allows for a weaker monsoon. It distinguishes conditional model estimates from survey expectations and presents a range of inflation outcomes. The oil scenario attributes the initial inflation increase mainly to direct effects, with indirect cost pass-through mattering later. Higher energy costs also reduce spending power and squeeze margins. The model allows monetary policy to dampen medium-term inflation at a cost to activity.

In the funding chapter, RBI reports a rise in surplus liquidity in September driven mainly by swap facilities. Despite the unchanged policy rate during the period covered, lending rates on new rupee loans had risen while new term deposit rates had declined through August. New and outstanding loan rates can move at different speeds. That makes financing terms, input costs and inflation expectations relevant to testing the baseline rather than relying on the repo rate alone.

questions.question: What changes if oil exceeds the revised baseline or stays high for longer?
questions.evidence: Replicate Box V.1 across alternative oil, fuel-price and exchange-rate paths. Check which effects are assumed immediate and which accumulate.

questions.question: How durable is the consumption support for capital expenditure?
questions.evidence: Compare RBI consumer surveys with consumption volumes, company investment intentions and credit by borrower sector.

questions.question: Is the divergence between new loan and deposit rates broad based?
questions.evidence: Check Table II.7 across bank categories and compare with maturity and product mix on new originations.

questions.question: Which indicators could distinguish persistent inflation from indirect energy effects?
questions.evidence: Compare CPI diffusion, survey expectations and wage or selling-price data with the report’s alternative scenarios.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: FOMC minutes · September 15–16 meeting
locator: Participants’ views, committee policy actions, domestic policy directive
summary: The minutes document September’s unanimous quarter-point increase to 3.75–4.00%, released to the public on October 7. The statement recorded resilient spending, strong capital investment and limited change in unemployment alongside above-target inflation. The domestic directive maintained the ample-reserves framework, allowing purchases of Treasury bills and, as needed, short-dated Treasuries. For market work, the time of the September rate announcement and the October minutes release are distinct events.

questions.question: How much of the rationale was already public?
questions.evidence: Compare the September statement, press conference and projections with the detail first published in the minutes.

questions.question: Did the minutes affect the expected pace of tightening?
questions.evidence: Use meeting-dated futures around 2 p.m. ET on October 7 and check other scheduled releases.

questions.question: How do reserves purchases differ from shifts in policy stance?
questions.evidence: Check Desk purchase schedules and reserve measures alongside the directive and policy-rate expectations.

title: Abridged minutes of the Monetary Council meeting on 22 September 2026
locator: Publication date on cover. Scope covers section 1, the Council’s assessment and decisions.
summary:
The minutes set the prospective 2.5% inflation target from 1 January 2028 and retain a symmetric one percentage point tolerance band. The meeting discussion illustrates the conditions under which members viewed the change as viable. Domestic inflation had been close to or below the bottom of the previous tolerance band for much of the year and some members reported that household and business expectations had fallen. Members also highlighted higher external inflation, oil and European gas prices, and signs that major central banks might tighten further. Some singled out upcoming wage negotiations as relevant for the domestic inflation path.

The publication contains a framework change and the Council’s assessment of policy conditions. Shifting the inflation anchor changes the horizon over which the Council evaluates price stability and is distinct from the rate choice at one meeting.

questions.question: Is the new anchor reflected in medium-term expectations?
questions.evidence: Compare expectation horizons before and after the announcement, and account for contemporaneous energy and wage developments.

questions.question: Do year-end pay deals support the new target?
questions.evidence: Compare wage settlements and productivity with the assumptions in the September report.

questions.question: Does tighter external policy alter local room for manoeuvre?
questions.evidence: Track relative HUF yields, FX and energy import prices alongside overseas decisions.

title: The Impact of the IMF’s EBA Model Revision on the Assessment of Korea’s Current Account
locator: Official summary paragraphs 1–3, and linked BOK Issue Note 2026-26.
summary: The staff note distinguishes the IMF’s observed current account from its model-based benchmark. Korea’s surplus increased from 5.3% to 6.6% of GDP and the IMF External Balance Assessment norm fell from 4.7% to 3.3%; both widened the measured gap. The note estimates that the revision to the model, especially demographics, lowered Korea’s norm by 1.10 percentage points in a held-constant comparison. Most of that change showed up as an unexplained residual in the model. The authors question whether the revised specification captures Korea’s demographic structure. The implied current-account gap is therefore sensitive to model choice as well as to measured flows. The note describes a technical assessment rather than a monetary-policy commitment.

questions.question: Can the model account for demographic effects without putting them into the residual?
questions.evidence: Compare estimates using old and revised specifications on the same observed inputs and use alternative demographic variables.

questions.question: Which parts of the current account increase are durable?
questions.evidence: Separate goods, services and primary income against sector-level savings and investment measures.

questions.question: Does the gap remain large after accounting for cohort and institutional differences?
questions.evidence: Compare Korea with similar economies under alternative saving, pension and household-portfolio assumptions.

coverageLimitation: Analysis uses the official web summary. The underlying model appendix was not verified.

institution: Banco Central de la República Argentina
title: Relevamiento de Expectativas de Mercado – September 2026
summary:
The survey published on 6 October pools 44 respondents who submitted forecasts on 28–30 September. Participants estimated September monthly inflation at 1.9% and core inflation at 1.8%. Their estimate for seasonally adjusted GDP growth in the third quarter was revised down to −1.0% quarter on quarter, while their fourth-quarter estimate was raised to 1.8%. The two GDP estimates capture a weaker current quarter and an expected rebound, with 2026 annual growth of 1.5% across respondents.

These figures are market survey estimates and projections. The central bank publishes them as a way to observe expectations and does not adopt them as its own forecast.
locator: Official summary, publication date, coverage and expectations paragraphs

questions.question: Did the rebound forecast depend on a few respondents?
questions.evidence: Compare the median and ranges with the top-ten forecast group and subsequent realised data.

questions.question: What drove the upward core inflation revision?
questions.evidence: Compare the next CPI release’s item breakdown with the September forecast.

questions.question: Do market prices imply a similar distribution of outcomes?
questions.evidence: Compare breakevens and FX instruments with surveyed expectations after checking for instrument and liquidity differences.

coverageNote: Analysis covers the public survey summary. Survey microdata and underlying distributions were not fully reviewed.

title: Monetary policy implementation in an environment with abundant reserves — Antoine Martin
summary: Martin described tiering of interest on SNB sight deposits as a way to sustain trading in secured money markets while aligning SARON with the policy rate. The different rates on either side of a bank’s reserve threshold can give banks reasons to trade. Under negative rates the upper tier earned zero. With non-negative policy rates, the upper tier earns the policy rate, and the SNB absorbs reserves to keep deposits scarce relative to thresholds. The volume of operations adjusts to what is needed to maintain control of short rates.

questions.question: How far could balances rise before the trading incentive weakens?
questions.evidence: Compare the distribution of reserves against thresholds and repo volumes.

questions.question: Which operations most effectively limit SARON deviations?
questions.evidence: Compare repo and SNB Bill auctions.

questions.question: What makes a low-volume benchmark fragile?
questions.evidence: Test sensitivity to transaction sizes and counterparty concentration.

locator: Presentation slides 10–15
coverageLimitation: Official slide deck reviewed. No separate transcript was available.

title: Monetary Policy Review – October 2026
locator: Scope: official landing-page overview of headline inflation, GDP and cumulative policy changes. Full PDF, slides and data require separate review.
summary:
The SARB’s overview describes the Middle East energy disruption as spilling into core inflation through refinery, transport and production costs, with additional food risk from weather and fertiliser constraints. It reports Q2 South African headline inflation rising to 4.5% from 3.2% in Q1 and projects it above 5% into the second quarter of 2027, with a return to target from the fourth quarter. The MPC had raised the policy rate by a cumulative 50 basis points to 7.25% across the review period. The bank lowered its 2026 GDP growth projection from 1.4% in April to 1.2%, with growth projected to improve as structural reforms advance.

The central concern is whether fuel, food and administered prices become embedded in wage and price setting. The SARB’s growth and inflation projections are its baseline as of this review. The release does not, by itself, identify any particular market pricing or post-publication reaction.

questions.question: How much of the inflation overshoot comes from second-round effects?
questions.evidence: Read the report’s inflation decomposition and compare it with wages and longer-term expectations.

questions.question: How dependent is the growth recovery on structural assumptions?
questions.evidence: Check the report’s path for electricity and logistics and compare it against implementation data.

questions.question: Did the release affect the expected policy path?
questions.evidence: Verify the release timestamp and compare ZAR interest-rate swaps and the rand within a predeclared window.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: Michelle Bowman · Modernizing the Regulatory and Supervisory Landscape
locator: Regulatory thresholds and Refocusing Supervision on the Risk of Material Financial Harm
summary: Bowman proposed using risk and complexity, alongside asset size, to determine supervisory intensity. The speech describes how fixed thresholds can move a conventional lender into standards intended for more complex firms. She linked threshold modernisation, proportionality and faster identification of material risks. The speech discusses changes already made to supervisory principles alongside future reforms under consideration. The latter should be tracked through rulemaking before assessing their effect on credit availability or bank capital.

questions.question: Which firms face the largest threshold effects?
questions.evidence: Map public bank sizes and activities to the proposed categories as proposals become available.

questions.question: Would lighter reporting increase lending capacity?
questions.evidence: Compare costs and lending decisions around relevant thresholds and implementation dates.

questions.question: Can earlier supervisory action preserve resilience?
questions.evidence: Assess escalation timing and material findings across comparable supervisory cases.

title: Jan Frait on the Czech koruna and fifty years of the post-Bretton Woods system
locator: Opening remarks on the Jamaica Accords, interest-rate cycles, credit expansion and the closing discussion of fiscal dominance.
summary:
Deputy Governor Jan Frait used the anniversary of the Jamaica Accords and the founding of Czechoslovakia’s central bank to discuss how floating exchange rates, global capital flows and financial feedback complicate policymaking. He argued that market participants, central bankers and academics can reinforce prevailing views, helping to explain abrupt reversals in rates. He questioned confident narratives about persistently high long rates and fiscal dominance, citing the limited number of financial cycles observed under the modern system.

His concern was that prolonged credit and fiscal expansion may initially support activity while raising debt and vulnerability, with eventual risks in either direction for inflation. He also cautioned against relaxing bank regulation in ways that weaken attention to liquidity and sovereign risk. This speech addresses the policy framework and financial cycles. It supplies no explicit decision or short-term rate path.

questions.question: Does the change in Czech long yields reflect expected rates or term premia?
questions.evidence: Use maturity-specific swaps, government yields and an explicit term-premium model.

questions.question: Does a long upswing in credit lead to greater funding and sovereign risk in the Czech data?
questions.evidence: Compare sector balance sheets, bank funding maturities and sovereign exposures over several cycles.

questions.question: How much do major-central-bank surprises pass through under the floating koruna?
questions.evidence: Compare matched Czech rates and FX around externally identified ECB and Fed surprises.

title: Shinichi Uchida: AI, Big Data, and Monetary Policy
locator: Sections II and III on nontraditional data and economic effects.
summary:
Uchida presented AI and nontraditional data as a way to expand what central banks can measure. Models can process large datasets and convert text to structured inputs, while examples such as mobility data and vessel tracking can inform assessments before conventional evidence arrives. He emphasised that usefulness depends on the data and state of the economy. This distinction is relevant for speech scoring too, since measured patterns still need validation against real-time information and policy outcomes.

His second question concerned the economy. AI could raise productivity by taking over routine cognitive tasks or assisting innovation, but the speed and distribution of adoption are uncertain. Bottlenecks in complementary human work and disruption to job transitions could shape the overall result. The remarks set a research agenda on methods and economic effects, rather than conveying a new short-term policy stance.

questions.question: Do alternative data improve monitoring out of sample?
questions.evidence: Compare models on real-time vintages and forecast errors in distinct conditions, especially during breaks in reporting.

questions.question: Where would wider AI adoption raise productivity fastest?
questions.evidence: Measure adoption and observed output by task and firm, controlling for pre-existing business performance.

questions.question: What keeps estimated exposure from becoming actual displacement?
questions.evidence: Compare changes in hiring, redeployment and pay with task-level measures of human complementarity.

title: Shifting Ground: How Geopolitics Is Reshaping Growth, Monetary Policy and the Role of Gold as a Reserve Asset — Joachim Nagel
summary:
Nagel saw the euro area economy as more resilient than expected after the energy shock, with exports, consumption and recovering industry supporting activity. He distinguished the September ECB staff projections from his own account of the risks. He cited projected euro area inflation of 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028, while warning that gas storage, refining and food supply could increase the upside. At the time he saw limited evidence of broader wage and price effects and cited longer-term expectations near target. He characterised the June and September increases as a response to persistence risks and stressed that the outlook depended on geopolitical developments.

The speech also explains the place of gold in reserve diversification amid geopolitical fragmentation. This is a discussion of the investment role of a reserve asset, with no trading allocation or short-term return forecast.

questions.question: What would indicate that energy inflation is becoming self-sustaining?
questions.evidence: Track wages, producer price pass-through and longer-term expectations alongside oil, gas and refinery margins.

questions.question: How resilient would demand be under another disruption?
questions.evidence: Compare household cash flow and order data with alternative scenarios in the ECB projections.

questions.question: How much gold demand reflects official reserve diversification?
questions.evidence: Use central-bank reserve disclosures and distinguish purchased quantities from valuation changes.

locator: Sections 2–4, especially the monetary policy discussion.

title: September policy meeting minutes: increase of 25 basis points to 12.25%
summary:
The October release records a divided September rate increase. Four directors chose a 25 basis point increase to 12.25%, two preferred a hold and one wanted a 50 basis point increase. The majority cited broad price pressure, with annual headline inflation at 6.2% in August and inflation excluding food and regulated prices at 6.1%. It worried that El Niño and international energy or input costs could prolong inflation and affect expectations.

The hold voters argued that policy was already markedly restrictive and that past increases were still feeding through. They also noted that another hike would have a limited short-run effect on administered, food and indexed prices while increasing costs to credit, activity and post-earthquake reconstruction. July activity indicators already pointed to a slowdown, yet retail sales were still growing in annual terms.
locator: Vote counts, policy arguments and updated activity indicators

questions.question: Is disinflation held back by indexation or excess demand?
questions.evidence: Compare rents and regulated-price adjustments with cyclical and non-cyclical services prices.

questions.question: How fast is cumulative tightening reaching households and firms?
questions.evidence: Track the evolution of new loan rates and issuance by type alongside the rate path and reconstruction activity.

questions.question: Can survey and market measures corroborate de-anchoring?
questions.evidence: Compare survey forecasts with nominal and inflation-linked TES pricing after adjusting for liquidity.

coverageNote: Main minutes text reviewed. Statistical appendix and separate capital-markets attachment are outside this card.

title: Diagnostic Challenges for ECB Monetary Policy — Philip R. Lane
summary:
Lane set out three tests for a policy response to the energy shock: the inflation outlook and its risks, underlying inflation, and the strength of transmission. September headline inflation was 3.8% and the energy component was up 18.8% year on year, while non-energy inflation was 2.3%. The underlying mix had nevertheless changed since late 2025, with non-energy goods inflation higher and food and services inflation lower. Lane saw little evidence at that point of the unusually fast repricing mechanisms observed in 2022.

The September staff projections anticipated lagged pass-through lifting non-energy inflation to 2.6% in 2027 before it returned to 2.3% in 2028. He argued that financial conditions matter twice: tighter conditions directly depress demand, and they change how strongly a given monetary stance affects the economy. The decision therefore depends on whether energy costs broaden and on whether other financial conditions strengthen or offset policy restraint.

questions.question: Is repricing becoming faster or broader in response to energy?
questions.evidence: Check item-level HICP price adjustment frequencies, services inflation and the underlying inflation measures cited in the speech.

questions.question: Is lagged energy pass-through consistent with the staff path?
questions.evidence: Compare the September projection assumptions with wholesale energy, producer prices and reported pricing intentions.

questions.question: How much of tighter financial conditions is delivering restraint independently of the policy rate?
questions.evidence: Track the ECB’s cited conditions indices and decompose changes in credit costs and market rates.

locator: Three diagnostic criteria and the September inflation data discussion.

title: Summary of Opinions at the Monetary Policy Meeting on September 17 and 18
locator: § II, views for and against a September increase and on the future conduct of policy. Published 1 October.
summary:
The published opinions for the September meeting show why a rate increase could coexist with unease about immediate tightening. Views supporting an increase pointed to resilient activity and accommodative conditions. Some saw the faster interval than before as a response to this resilience and argued that a policy rate closer to neutral would leave room to react in either direction. Views favouring a hold stressed recent inflation below 2% and the absence of clear acceleration in activity and prices. These arguments reflect different weights on recent outcomes and forward-looking underlying inflation.

The summary also points to a possible change in the policy problem: underlying inflation had moved closer to 2%, leading some to distinguish sustaining it near target from continuing to push it upward. An overshoot scenario could justify a faster pace, while others saw little evidence of an imminent overshoot and preferred to move in a measured way. This condensed record gives individual views without named attributions.

questions.question: Which arguments were associated with votes in the eventual minutes?
questions.evidence: Compare the opinions with the named vote and dissent explanations after the longer minutes are released.

questions.question: Is the underlying rate close to 2% across measures?
questions.evidence: Compare trend inflation estimates, service prices, annual wage settlements and tax- or subsidy-adjusted CPI.

questions.question: Are the next meeting and the endpoint of the rate path priced differently?
questions.evidence: Compare separately the near meetings and longer expectations in matched yen OIS forward rates.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: Philip Jefferson · The U.S. Economy and Monetary Policy
locator: Economic Activity and the Labor Market, Inflation, Monetary Policy, figures 1–8 and accessible chart tables
summary:
Jefferson saw continued resilience in activity and employment but judged the inflation risk to be skewed upward. Figure 1 puts first-half GDP growth at a 2.4% annual pace. He noted robust AI investment and resilient spending, with price sensitivity among consumers and uncertainty from energy, tariffs and the scope of the AI buildout. Figure 3 shows unemployment had moved roughly sideways in 2026 and fell to 4.1% in August, a level he regarded as close to maximum employment.

The PCE charts distinguish total inflation from core inflation and split core goods from services. Jefferson considered several shocks jointly and thought it premature to specify the policy path after September’s increase. He noted yields had risen since the meeting, but the speech does not measure a move attributable to the remarks. The views are his own.

questions.question: Which components explain the acceleration in core prices?
questions.evidence: Check the next PCE release against figures 6 and 7 and separate goods and service contributions.

questions.question: How concentrated is growth in AI capital expenditure?
questions.evidence: Use GDP expenditure details and capital-spending disclosures to test the resilience of demand.

questions.question: How much tightening did markets already expect?
questions.evidence: Compare the pre-speech fed funds futures curve with the September policy path and verified event-time changes.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: Michelle Bowman · Modernizing Financial Regulation: Initial Observations from eSLR
locator: Binding leverage requirements, supervisory data, market outreach and footnotes
summary:
Bowman argued that the supplementary leverage requirement had become a binding constraint for some large bank dealers and that recalibration could support balance-sheet-intensive Treasury intermediation. She cited supervisory data showing dealer Treasury holdings rose from about $600 billion to over $700 billion by the end of April, with more growth among banks that had smaller buffers under the prior rule.

She also cited market outreach and indicators such as narrower spreads and lower volatility around auctions. These are preliminary observations, and the reported change in holdings has a different evidentiary status from statements by individual market contacts. The suggested mechanism is more capacity for dealers to absorb Treasury supply, with implications for liquidity and cash–futures positioning.

questions.question: Can holdings growth be attributed to the calibration?
questions.evidence: Compare affected and less constrained dealers, conditioning on issuance and market volatility.

questions.question: Does capacity remain available in stress?
questions.evidence: Compare quote depth, repo terms and dealer holdings on the busiest auction or volatility days.

questions.question: How has exposure moved between dealers and leveraged funds?
questions.evidence: Cross-check Treasury positions, repo funding and futures exposures over the same period.

title: Financial conditions: what’s priced in? — Catherine L. Mann
summary:
Mann judged UK real financial conditions insufficiently restrictive once the rise in inflation compensation was taken into account. Her comparison of nominal and real indices shows why higher quoted yields can give a misleading impression of restraint after an inflationary supply shock. Nominal conditions tightened somewhat after the conflict escalated, but the real measure initially eased and had only partly retraced by its latest observation in August. She had supported a 25 basis point increase at each of the previous two meetings.

Chart 11 attributes nearly all the increase in three-year nominal yields in its comparison to inflation compensation. That compensation incorporates both expected inflation and an estimated risk premium, each of which rose. Mann also considers compensation for uncertainty about the policy path. Her conclusion is that clearly explaining the policy response and following through with a sufficiently restrictive Bank Rate can help contain these premia. These decompositions depend on models and are the policymaker’s assessment at the time.

questions.question: How much of the upward SONIA curve represented expected Bank Rate?
questions.evidence: Compare matched-horizon SONIA forwards and the Bank’s Market Participants Survey to see whether term premia materially change the inferred policy path.

questions.question: Which parts of the transmission mechanism had actually tightened?
questions.evidence: Check inflation-adjusted gilt yields, new mortgage rates and corporate credit spreads alongside the financial conditions indices.

questions.question: Would clearer guidance lower policy uncertainty while preserving restriction?
questions.evidence: Compare SONIA option distributions around releases of decisions and individual speeches and control for other news in those windows.

locator: Financial conditions, Charts 1 and 11, and Monetary policy strategy.

title: Financial Stability Review, October 2026: financial stability assessment
locator: Overall assessment and international stability risk sections
summary:
The RBA assesses Australian banks and most household and business borrowers as resilient despite weakening activity and housing prices. Prudent underwriting and strong bank capital provide scope to absorb losses. The consequences of higher rates still vary by borrower, and the assessment identifies possible blind spots as non-bank lending expands and international risks rise.

The assessment connects rising global sovereign yields to policy repricing and competition for debt financing, including AI-related corporate issuance. It highlights how leverage among price-sensitive investors could amplify a disorderly sovereign bond sell-off and notes that compressed risk premia leave credit and equity markets vulnerable to an abrupt change in expectations. AI-related borrowing carries multiple transmission paths through concentrated valuations, opaque funding structures and operational exposure. The source describes vulnerabilities and scenarios. It does not establish their likelihood or give a policy-rate decision.

questions.question: Could sovereign market stress transmit through a leveraged unwind?
questions.evidence: Review repo and basis metrics, dealer balance sheets and changes in liquidity around a large yield move.

questions.question: What exposures are missing from bank balance-sheet measures?
questions.evidence: Compare non-bank lender portfolios and off-balance-sheet commitments with bank disclosures and supervisory estimates.

questions.question: How much borrower stress is masked by aggregate buffers?
questions.evidence: Examine arrears and cash-flow gaps by income bucket, loan age and rate-reset timing.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: Christopher Waller · The Data Version of Godzilla versus Kong: FRED Takes on AI
locator: FRED history, data provenance and AI discussion
summary: Waller described FRED’s role in standardising access to data from producing agencies and announced that users seeking some Board data would be directed to its tools. He saw AI as a way to expand access and speed search, summaries and visualisation, while stressing the value of a trusted data conduit. For macro research, these benefits depend on preserving the link to the producing agency, the series definition and the version used. This talk concerns economic data infrastructure.

questions.question: How can AI outputs retain series provenance?
questions.evidence: Audit generated charts against original series IDs, release dates and metadata.

questions.question: How frequently do revisions change an apparent turning point?
questions.evidence: Compare the values available on each release date with later vintages.

questions.question: What would a consistent data interface improve for cross-country work?
questions.evidence: Test identical variable definitions, release timing and missing-value behaviour across providers.

institution: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
title: The low-hire, low-fire labour market is calm but fragile
locator: Economic Bulletin, Charts 1–4, underlying worker transitions and counterfactual notes.
summary: The bulletin argues that low job loss was doing more to hold down unemployment than robust hiring. The authors estimate a job-finding rate of 34%, below 39% in 2019, and show longer spells out of work. Employer hiring and separation data point to a similar slowdown in flows. The scenario exercise applies changes in job loss and finding from past downturns to different starting labour markets. A 2001-type shock produces unemployment near 8% from current conditions versus around 6% from the 1999 comparison. This counterfactual illustrates sensitivity to a downturn. It carries no probability or recession date.

questions.question: Which workers face the largest decline in job finding?
questions.evidence: Break the CPS transitions down by age, industry and unemployment duration.

questions.question: How much labour deterioration would be visible before unemployment moves sharply?
questions.evidence: Compare claims, hiring conversions and hours as possible leading indicators.

questions.question: How sensitive is the stress scenario to the steady-state approximation?
questions.evidence: Run the same flow shocks through a transition model with lags and test different participation responses.

title: Quarterly Bulletin 3/2026 — Monetary policy report and business cycle signals
locator: Published key points for the Monetary policy report and Business cycle signals. Review limited to the official online summary.
summary:
The SNB’s bulletin says unusually strong chemicals and pharmaceuticals output raised second-quarter headline GDP above underlying momentum, while activity outside that effect remained solid and broad-based. The SNB forecasts 1.5–2% GDP growth in 2026 and around 1.5% in 2027. Swiss inflation rose from 0.6% in May to 0.8% in August on imported inflation, especially oil products, while longer-term expectations were broadly steady.

Companies in the SNB’s third-quarter interviews described strong business activity across manufacturing, services and construction. Hiring intentions improved and wage increases were expected to slow from 1.5% in 2026 to 1.3% in 2027. The bulletin reports an upward shift in the Confederation yield curve and a franc depreciation since mid-June, a comparison across months.

questions.question: How much of second-quarter GDP strength is likely to persist?
questions.evidence: The bulletin highlights unusually strong chemicals and pharmaceuticals output and cites broad underlying growth and resilient third-quarter business reports.

questions.question: What would indicate imported energy inflation is spreading to domestic prices?
questions.evidence: The bulletin attributes the observed inflation rise to imported oil-related costs and reports broadly unchanged longer-term expectations.

questions.question: How do firms’ strong demand and improving hiring plans fit with slower expected wage growth?
questions.evidence: The company talks anticipate stronger hiring, easier recruitment and an average wage rise of 1.3% in 2027 after 1.5% in 2026.

title: PBOC Adjusts Targeted Monetary Policy Tools
locator: Original PBOC announcement on an official Guangdong mirror, four numbered changes. Associated facilities notices dated 28 September.
summary:
The PBOC lowered its one-year pledged supplementary lending rate from 1.75% to 1.50% and extended eligibility to infrastructure networks including power, water, computing and logistics. The technology and equipment relending quota rose from ¥1.2 trillion to ¥1.4 trillion and the supported proportion increased from 60% to 100%. The combined quota for agriculture, small business and rediscounting went from ¥4.35 trillion to ¥4.85 trillion, of which ¥300 billion was an increase in the private-enterprise quota.

The combination reduces funding costs for one tool and increases the capacity and coverage of other tools. These are prices and limits of particular facilities, while the notice does not measure utilisation or state a new general policy rate. The stated mechanism is to encourage intermediaries to extend credit to eligible projects and borrowers. The strength of that channel depends on banks’ willingness to lend and firms’ investment responses.

questions.question: Do facility drawdowns rise following higher ceilings and support ratios?
questions.evidence: Compare reported drawings, applicant approvals and bank funding use with the revised limits.

questions.question: Which projects gain new credit or lower effective loan costs?
questions.evidence: Compare funded projects, maturities and loan margins before and after revised infrastructure eligibility.

questions.question: Is subsidised funding replacing other loans or supporting additional capital expenditure?
questions.evidence: Match financing records and borrower investments using comparable firms that did not receive support.

title: Economic and Monetary Conditions for August 2026
summary:
The Bank of Thailand saw August activity as broadly stable from July. Technology demand kept merchandise exports excluding gold at a high level, although technology shipments moderated from their earlier pace. Machinery and equipment investment strengthened, while production and service activity softened. Foreign tourist numbers rose, supported by Chinese arrivals in the bank’s account, but shorter stays held tourism receipts broadly steady.

The bank attributes higher headline inflation to fresh food affected by weather and input costs and more expensive retail fuel. It also reports a rise in core inflation, particularly as prepared-food prices reflected cost pass-through. A trade surplus supported the current-account surplus. The bank saw a broadly stable labour market and flagged the increase in unemployment-benefit claimants. A monthly trade and investment improvement can coexist with weak labour indicators or uneven production.

questions.question: How much do data-centre imports explain the difference between spending and domestic production?
questions.evidence: Trace capital equipment volumes, inventories and local construction activity to the corresponding investment measures.

questions.question: Which firms are raising prepared-food prices and which absorb higher input costs?
questions.evidence: Compare producer inputs, restaurant price surveys and household inflation by category.

questions.question: Is the rise in unemployment claims specific to certain sectors?
questions.evidence: Look at claims, employment and wage changes by sector, firm size and region.

locator: Release 37/2026, summary and August detail. Note focuses on the release text and omits the separate statistical tables.

title: Board raises the monetary policy interest rate to 12.25%
summary:
Four directors voted to raise the policy rate by 25 basis points to 12.25%, two voted to hold and one preferred a 50-basis-point increase. August headline inflation was 6.2%, services inflation 7.2%, and inflation excluding food and regulated prices 6.1%. Analyst expectations for year-end 2026 increased to 6.8%, while the two-year measure eased to 4%.

Second-quarter GDP was 3.4% above a year earlier, while the July activity indicator grew 1.1%. The Board cited risks from El Niño, earthquake effects and fiscal measures, and noted that government-bond-implied inflation expectations exceeded the 3% target.
locator: Official release, vote paragraph, inflation and activity points, and outlook.

questions.question: What explains the gap between near-term and two-year expectations?
questions.evidence: Year-end analyst expectations rose, while the two-year measure fell. Compare survey distributions with government-bond inflation compensation after allowing for liquidity to assess which part of the curve reflects persistent inflation risk.

questions.question: How should services inflation be weighted relative to slowing activity?
questions.evidence: Services inflation was 7.2% and the July activity indicator grew more slowly than second-quarter GDP. Use disaggregated CPI and the activity indicators available at release to test whether service pressure or wider demand weakness better predicts core momentum.

questions.question: Which inflation or demand outcomes would shift members on either side of the 25-basis-point majority?
questions.evidence: The published vote shows hold and larger-increase alternatives. Study subsequent officially published minutes as they become available and track the inflation or demand measures each group cites in explaining its vote.

institution: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
title: Unwavering dedication — John Williams on the outlook
locator: The Economy and Labour Market, Inflation, Monetary Policy and the Economic Outlook, Conclusion and footnotes.
summary: Williams saw enough resilience in spending and employment to put more weight on inflation. Refining bottlenecks had increased refined-product prices relative to crude, and scarce inputs for AI investment were beginning to lift prices of other goods. He saw less pressure from earlier tariffs, declining housing-services inflation and anchored expectations. In his forecast real GDP grew about 2.25% this year and next, overall inflation was about 3.5% in 2026 and reached 2% in 2028. Weak labour-force growth and imported equipment limited the domestic GDP boost from AI spending. The September hike gave him time to collect evidence. If the economy followed his forecast, he saw scope for one further increase late in 2026.

questions.question: How much energy pressure comes from refining capacity?
questions.evidence: Compare crude, gasoline and diesel spreads, refinery utilisation and inventories to gauge how persistence differs by input.

questions.question: Will imported AI inputs limit the near-term contribution to US growth?
questions.evidence: Examine equipment imports, domestic construction and power investment alongside national accounts and industry-level producer prices.

questions.question: Did the conditional reference to another increase change pricing?
questions.evidence: Separate September 29’s speech time from other releases and compare immediately adjacent fed funds futures and two-year yields.

title: Quarterly Bulletin – September 2026
locator: Scope: SARB’s official bulletin overview on expenditure, labour, prices and external trade. The complete PDF and individual statistical tables require separate review.
summary:
The SARB bulletin describes weak Q2 production and stronger expenditure. Household consumption rose 0.4% quarter on quarter and inventories added 0.6 percentage points to GDP growth, while net exports subtracted 1.1 points as imports rose faster than exports. Job losses and expansion of the labour force took unemployment to 33.6%. The bulletin cautions that stronger measured productivity partly reflected weaker labour absorption.

Fuel and fertiliser costs raised domestic prices in the first half of 2026. August headline inflation eased to 4.4% after a 5.0% June reading, while several underlying measures ran above the new 3.0% target. It is a dated summary of activity and price data with a lag on quarterly outcomes.

questions.question: Were inventories accumulated voluntarily or through weaker sales?
questions.evidence: Compare stock-to-sales ratios, orders and firm-sector inventory contributions.

questions.question: How durable was the rise in measured labour productivity?
questions.evidence: Cross-check hours worked, sector output and employment from successive releases.

questions.question: Has the shock broadened beyond fuel, fertiliser and related services?
questions.evidence: Track the disaggregated producer and consumer inflation series alongside transport and import costs.

title: Monetary Policy Board decision: cash rate raised to 4.60%
locator: Opening assessment and unanimous Decision
summary:
The Board unanimously raised the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.60%. Upside risks highlighted in August had started to materialise. The Board cites a widening Middle East conflict and energy prices well above assumptions, faster global inflation in technology goods associated with AI demand, and continuing domestic capacity constraints. It also reports stronger-than-expected local inflation and liaison evidence of firms raising prices or planning to. The release says the earlier increases had tightened conditions and slowed the economy.

The decision reflects a judgment that more restraint was needed to return inflation to target in a reasonable period, even as housing weakened and weak growth scenarios remained possible. Trading-partner growth had held up, partly through AI expenditure, while weak productivity constrained domestic supply. Further tightening remains conditional on the outlook. The relevant comparison for an event study is the hike and statement relative to expectations immediately before release.

questions.question: Which part of the move surprised the curve?
questions.evidence: Compare meeting-specific OIS pricing around the statement and again around the Governor’s press conference.

questions.question: Would falling oil prices change the projected need for restraint?
questions.evidence: Compare updated energy prices with August assumptions and monitor underlying domestic inflation separately.

questions.question: Could housing weakness amplify the effect of tightening?
questions.evidence: Track borrowing, prices, construction and spending among interest-sensitive households.

title: Michele Bullock: September monetary policy media conference
locator: Opening statement and Q&A on productivity, capacity and policy transmission
summary:
Bullock explains why the Board raised the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60%. She describes pressure from renewed increases in global energy prices and inflation in technology-related goods, alongside concern about domestic capacity and weak productivity. In the Q&A she explains that weaker supply growth affects how far demand can expand without generating price pressure. The deterioration in the inflation outlook shifts how the Board weighs the trade-off with employment, while it continues to pursue both objectives.

The Governor says rates could rise again if needed. The remarks clarify the motives behind the decision and the conditional nature of further action. To estimate any market information attributable to the press conference, use the conference’s separate scheduled window after the policy statement rather than attributing the entire day’s price move to her Q&A.

questions.question: What did the press conference add about future rate moves?
questions.evidence: Compare market pricing immediately after the written decision with pricing during and after the press conference.

questions.question: How much of the inflation revision could reflect slower potential growth?
questions.evidence: Compare productivity data, underlying prices and activity against previous staff assumptions.

questions.question: Does weaker demand make the stated trade-off easier in later quarters?
questions.evidence: Track spending and hiring responses at different policy lags and look for persistent wage and price pressure.

institution: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
title: How and why — Alberto Musalem on policy communication
locator: Prepared remarks on forecasts, rate-path guidance and the framework for reacting to data.
summary: Musalem argues that explaining how policy decisions are made helps market participants interpret news and improves accountability. He distinguishes publishing an outlook, promising a path and explaining the factors that change the policy decision. A framework allows private forecasts to differ while giving investors a way to form expectations about the response. He argues that repeating a projected rate path can crowd out the independent information the central bank seeks in markets. A clear framework might also change term premia by reducing uncertainty about how policy responds. The remarks do not quantify that effect or express a particular next-rate preference.

questions.question: Do clearer reaction-function explanations improve market forecasts?
questions.evidence: Compare errors in meeting-dated rates after statements with different amounts of conditional guidance.

questions.question: Does communication alter expected short rates or term premia?
questions.evidence: Use yield-curve decomposition and options around comparable news and communication events.

questions.question: Can outside forecasters recover the same conditional rule?
questions.evidence: Compare their responses to inflation and employment surprises, allowing for changes in their economic outlook.

coverageNote: This analysis covers the prepared remarks. The subsequent discussion is outside the reviewed text.

title: Chee Hong Tat: Connecting Capital and Opportunity
locator: Growth-capital ecosystem discussion and paragraphs on the Equity Market Development Programme
summary:
Chee describes Singapore’s approach to connecting institutional funding with firms that need growth capital and developing a more liquid listed market. He reports that allocations under the Equity Market Development Programme reached S$5.4 billion after the third batch, compared with S$3.95 billion in the earlier two batches. The speech discusses building a broader capital ecosystem and states the aim of improving trading liquidity and reducing execution costs for the relevant stocks.

The speech contains amounts allocated and stated objectives. Assessing the impact on firms’ financing requires evidence on deployment, turnover and spreads over time. A mandate allocation could change ownership, market depth or active coverage without necessarily causing a comparable change in new financing. The effects on listed and private firms should be examined using distinct measures.

questions.question: Do stocks targeted by the programme show improved execution quality?
questions.evidence: Compare spreads, depth and turnover with comparable firms before and after allocation and deployment.

questions.question: Is additional capital reaching new issuance or mostly secondary markets?
questions.evidence: Review manager mandates, deployment and offerings by growth firms.

questions.question: Does the third allocation batch change concentration across managers or sectors?
questions.evidence: Use disclosures on the new mandates and compare portfolio holdings where available.

title: Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey — September 2026
locator: Current report, results table and collection notes for output, hiring, prices and forward balances.
summary: The September production index rose to 29.5 and new orders to 30.7 in the Texas manufacturing survey. Capacity use and shipments also rose. The employment balance improved while hours were broadly steady. Raw-material and finished-goods prices and the wage balance increased. At the same time the company outlook balance dropped from 19.2 to 8.7 and respondents reported more uncertainty. This combination indicates stronger current activity with less widespread improvement in expectations. The release is a regional business diffusion survey, based on 63 responses.

questions.question: What accounts for stronger output and a softer outlook?
questions.evidence: Distinguish backlogs and current orders from responses on future demand, financing and costs.

questions.question: Are higher materials prices reaching downstream buyers?
questions.evidence: Compare finished goods price balances by subsector and realised shipment prices.

questions.question: How much should the results shift the national growth outlook?
questions.evidence: Combine the survey with non-Texas manufacturing releases and control for industrial and energy exposure.

title: Minutes of the July 30–31 Monetary Policy Meeting
locator: Sections II–III and policy vote records near the end; release 28 September for the July meeting.
summary:
The minutes record an 8–1 July vote to maintain the overnight guideline around 1%. Takata proposed 1.25% because he believed underlying inflation had reached the target and saw value in getting closer to neutral faster. Other members backed leaving the guideline at its earlier level. Approval of the statement text and approval of the Outlook’s Bank’s View are different decisions, with their own results. The release makes visible the difference between the policy rate vote, the personal proposal and the text voted on.

The meeting considered simultaneous pressures from expensive energy and a more robust technology cycle. Staff reports also describe ongoing reductions in Japanese government bond purchases under the June plan. These are historical minutes published in September after the later decision. Their July description of rates should not be read as a fresh September setting.

questions.question: Which details add information beyond the August summary of opinions?
questions.evidence: Compare the policy-vote details and draft proposals with the earlier condensed version and statement.

questions.question: How do differences in the outlook relate to the hold vote?
questions.evidence: Compare the separate outlook and operating-guideline votes and subsequent public rationales by named members.

questions.question: How did the purchase schedule affect the long end?
questions.evidence: Combine actual JGB operations and issuance with maturity-specific term premia and liquidity indicators.

coverageLimitation: The voting record and key policy discussion were checked. Detailed staff exhibits and every subsection were not independently verified.

title: State of the Economy, September 2026
summary:
The Bulletin authors describe resilient Indian demand alongside a more challenging external environment. They cite 7.8% year-on-year GDP growth in Q1 of fiscal 2026–27, driven by consumption and investment, and strengthening food, fuel and core price pressures in August. August headline CPI reached 4.8% in their account. Near-term demand indicators and the monthly inflation readings capture different aspects of the cycle. Net services income and remittances helped contain the first-quarter current-account deficit, while foreign portfolio flows shifted from inflows in August to outflows in September to the authors’ cutoff.

The financial-conditions section shows why short-term funding and sovereign yields can diverge. System liquidity rose after use of the RBI’s swap facility linked to foreign currency non-resident bank deposits, then moderated with tax-related outflows. Commercial paper and certificate-of-deposit yields softened during the liquidity surge before firming. Government yields had already moved higher amid rising US yields, oil volatility and geopolitical risk. The authors’ discussion links those developments with funding conditions, and the charts present market levels with dates and tenors rather than identifying event reactions.

questions.question: How persistent is the liquidity created by the deposit swap facility?
questions.evidence: Reconcile swap tenors, tax outflows, government balances and durable liquidity over subsequent maintenance periods.

questions.question: Why did government yields rise when private money-market yields initially softened?
questions.evidence: Compare maturity-matched price changes and the effects of liquidity, duration supply and global yields.

questions.question: Which inflation pressures are domestic demand effects?
questions.evidence: Decompose food, fuel and core changes and check against measures of selling prices and demand.

locator: Introduction and Sections III–IV, including chart references IV.1–IV.3 and footnotes on liquidity and market observations. Focused read of the domestic and financial-conditions sections.

title: Monetary Policy Guidelines for 2027
locator: Official gazette, 25 September, cover and chapters 1–2. The Council adopted the resolution on 8 September. The guidelines apply from 1 January 2027.
summary:
The Monetary Policy Council retained the medium-term CPI target of 2.5% with a symmetric tolerance range of ±1 percentage point. Policy rates remain the principal instrument under a floating exchange rate. The Council retained the option of FX intervention and said the return-to-target horizon would depend on shocks and the costs of adjustment.

The operating goal for 2027 is to keep POLONIA close to the reference rate, subject to movements within the standing-facility corridor. The NBP expects excess banking-system liquidity to persist, with weekly operations normally issuing seven-day NBP bills. The resolution sets the policy framework and operating instructions and gives no forward path for the reference rate.

questions.question: How has the tolerance band functioned across demand and supply shocks?
questions.evidence: Match de-identified episodes of target deviations with Council decisions, inflation contributions and revisions to inflation forecasts.

questions.question: Does surplus liquidity affect how closely POLONIA tracks the reference rate?
questions.evidence: Use daily POLONIA, auction allotments, settlement flows and standing facility balances to compare end-month with normal days.

questions.question: How does a floating exchange rate affect the return-to-target horizon?
questions.evidence: Compare real-time NBP assessments of identified currency shocks with import prices, pass-through estimates and forecast vintages.

title: Minutes of the 17 September Bank Board meeting
locator: Bank Board minutes, discussion of core inflation, financial conditions and the policy choice; see CNB calendar for the publication date.
summary:
The Bank Board judged its current stance appropriate as tighter longer-dated market rates, the June rate rise and a strong koruna gave it time to assess further data. Members described risks of persistent core inflation and second-round commodity effects, and several distinguished August headline inflation of 1.9% from still elevated services prices. They noted that food and administrative energy measures helped contain the headline measure and could fade.

The discussion identified a conditional case for additional restriction if domestic demand and credit remained strong while the external cost shock persisted. Members also highlighted softer growth and the possible restraint already delivered by long yields and client rates.

questions.question: What part of the transmission is coming from the long end?
questions.evidence: Compare maturity-matched market rates, mortgage offers and corporate borrowing costs.

questions.question: Which services prices show signs of durable inflation?
questions.evidence: Track the breadth, monthly momentum and wage sensitivity of services components.

questions.question: Would core inflation remain elevated after energy prices ease?
questions.evidence: Examine alternative shock scenarios, input-cost pass-through and firm pricing expectations.

title: L’economia svizzera nel contesto globale — Martin Schlegel
summary:
Schlegel linked the Swiss economy’s resilience to exports and discussed how the exchange rate affects sectors and export markets differently. The slides show a relatively stable real effective franc since 2020, while the bilateral and sector exposures behind that average can vary. Business conversations showed improved confidence. Swiss GDP had been especially strong in the second quarter and was expected to grow more moderately ahead.

Oil products explained much of the rise in domestic inflation. The slides referred to the September hold at 0% with somewhat firmer inflation pressure than in June. The combination of better recent activity and a contained medium-term forecast anchored the presentation.
locator: Official Italian slides 3–11 and 13–16

questions.question: How broad was export growth outside pharmaceuticals?
questions.evidence: Check official export volume and sector contributions.

questions.question: Which real exchange rates most affect the different exporters?
questions.evidence: Compare sector destination weights and costs.

questions.question: Is the energy shock reaching domestically set prices?
questions.evidence: Review the CPI composition and business pricing evidence.

coverageLimitation: Official Italian slide deck reviewed. No separate transcript was available.

title: Rate decision September 2026
summary:
Norges Bank raised the rate to 4.5%. August CPI was 3.3%, lifted by energy, and CPI-ATE was 3.0%, below the June forecast. Imported goods inflation slowed and the krone was stronger than projected, while domestic price pressure remained elevated, supported by earlier business costs and labour costs. Employment had held up somewhat better than expected. Measures of spare capacity did not all give the same signal.

The committee judged that keeping rates restrictive remained necessary. The deliberations explicitly report that markets already priced a further Norwegian rate increase during 2026 and that rate expectations abroad had risen. The committee weighed domestic price persistence and uncertain external inflation pressures against the milder underlying near-term readings.
locator: Monetary Policy Report summary and committee deliberations on international conditions, inflation and stance

questions.question: How persistent are domestic price components?
questions.evidence: Compare rent, wages and services measures with prior forecasts.

questions.question: What explains the difference between the central-bank path and market pricing?
questions.evidence: Compare dated NOK rates with the report’s risk and baseline paths.

questions.question: How far does a stronger krone offset foreign input costs?
questions.evidence: Compare import prices with the I-44 index and external price pressures.

title: Policy rate unchanged at 1.75 per cent — September decision
summary:
The Riksbank held at 1.75% but projected more tightening than in June. Spare capacity and inflation measures excluding the direct effects of temporary fiscal measures near 2% supported waiting. Stronger activity and persistent foreign supply pressures provided a case for later increases. The Board expected the increases to start during 2026 if the outlook remained in line, with faster tightening possible if inflation proved more persistent.

The published forecast raised 2027 average CPIF inflation to 2.1% from 1.7%. The forecast path now put the policy rate at 2.24% in the second quarter of 2027, compared with 1.93% in June. These are averages conditional on the forecast. They do not specify the rate at any particular meeting.
locator: Decision and the inflation, GDP and policy rate forecast tables

questions.question: How does the updated path compare with market pricing?
questions.evidence: Line up Swedish OIS dates with the quarter-average forecast.

questions.question: How much of measured inflation is attributable to fiscal relief?
questions.evidence: Compare tax-adjusted and headline CPIF with measure expiry dates.

questions.question: What would warrant a faster path?
questions.evidence: Track demand, energy pass-through, wages and core prices against the forecast.

title: Notice on Overnight Reverse Repos Around the End of September
locator: Open-market business notice no. 9 of 2026, dated 23 September and posted on the official Heilongjiang mirror on 24 September.
summary:
The PBOC announced that it would conduct overnight reverse repos from 28 September to 8 October to match banks’ short-term liquidity needs. These operations were set up as quantity tenders at a fixed rate and subject to a daily maximum of ¥1 trillion. The notice specifies the operating period and ceiling but gives neither a transaction amount nor a new rate level. The timing makes it relevant to how overnight funding needs change across the quarter-end and adjoining dates.

A tender adds available liquidity at the tenor offered. On a net basis the effect also depends on maturities and other operations. The announcement does not establish whether later traded repo rates moved because of the schedule. Daily tender results and funding quotes would help distinguish the availability of support from actual take-up and realised rates.

questions.question: Did the scheduled operations offset an unusual short-term funding demand?
questions.evidence: Compare calendar-matched repo rates, turnover and dispersion around quarter-end using official operation dates.

questions.question: How far below the headline ceiling did actual usage fall?
questions.evidence: Compare daily allocations and maturities, incorporating other injections and drains.

questions.question: Did funding relief extend beyond deposit-taking institutions?
questions.evidence: Compare DR001 with broader repo rates and volumes over the same dates.

title: Monetary policy assessment of 24 September 2026
summary:
The SNB held its rate at 0% and retained the option to intervene in exchange markets. The discount above banks’ sight-deposit thresholds stayed 0.25 percentage points. Swiss inflation rose to 0.8% in August from 0.6% in May, primarily because of petroleum-related goods prices. The conditional forecast, assuming the rate remained at 0%, was 0.7% in 2026 and 0.8% in both 2027 and 2028. Prices for oil products raised the near-term outlook and franc depreciation contributed to a small medium-term revision.

Swiss growth was unusually strong in the second quarter. Chemicals and pharmaceuticals overstated the aggregate momentum, while activity outside those sectors was also broadly positive. The SNB expected 1.5–2.0% growth for the year and around 1.5% in 2027. International developments remained the main risk.
locator: Policy decision, conditional inflation forecast and Swiss outlook

questions.question: How far is higher inflation concentrated in energy?
questions.evidence: Compare CPI contributions with the new forecast and domestic price trends.

questions.question: Which industries explain the stronger growth baseline?
questions.evidence: Check national accounts contributions and manufacturing utilisation.

questions.question: What would make intervention more likely?
questions.evidence: Compare import prices and effective CHF with the scenarios in the assessment.

title: Monetary policy announcement – September 24, 2026
summary:
The Governing Board unanimously kept the overnight interbank target at 6.50%. From the first half of July to the first half of September, annual headline inflation rose from 3.10% to 3.42%, driven by non-core inflation, while core fell from 3.95% to 3.79%. The Bank lowered its near-term headline forecast, modestly lifted its third- and fourth-quarter 2026 core forecasts, and retained fourth-quarter 2027 convergence to 3%.

The Board reported slowing activity and slack. The announcement noted a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve increase and described differences in domestic transmission relevant to Mexico's policy decision.
locator: Official statement pp. 1–2, activity, inflation forecast table and final paragraphs.

questions.question: Which price components explain the different revisions to headline and core forecasts?
questions.evidence: The Bank lowered the near-term headline path while lifting two near-term core forecasts. Compare the statement's vintage tables with INEGI CPI contributions to identify which assumptions could alter the expected pace of easing.

questions.question: How might domestic slack mediate pass-through from external rates?
questions.evidence: The Board reported slack and emphasized differences in monetary transmission. Compare local lending rates, the peso and measures of credit and utilization after external moves to see whether changes in US rates reach domestic inflation.

questions.question: How does the decision compare with the market's pre-release probability of a rate change?
questions.evidence: The Board voted unanimously for an unchanged rate after discussing external tightening. Compare TIIE pricing just before the published time with like-for-like rates afterward and identify other releases within the same window.

title: Monetary Policy Report – September 2026
summary:
The Bank lowered its 2026 GDP growth forecast from 2.0% to 1.8% and projected 1.4% in 2027. Second-quarter GDP rose 0.5% from the previous quarter after 1.1% in the first quarter. Household consumption fell and cyclical sectors slowed, while the labour market remained strong.

Annual headline inflation fell from 4.72% in May to 4.22% in August. The report said services inflation remained elevated. The reference projection for the first quarter of 2028 remained 3.2%, with a generally higher inflation path and a projected 5.2% at the end of 2026.
locator: Report executive summary, pp. 5–6, output, inflation and reference scenario. BCB publication date September 24.

questions.question: What portion of the GDP downgrade stems from household spending versus other cyclical components?
questions.evidence: The Bank cites Q2 composition and weak early Q3 indicators. Compare the Bank's sector forecasts with national accounts and early Q3 consumption to estimate the weight of rate-sensitive domestic demand.

questions.question: Which services components remain elevated despite slowing overall prices?
questions.evidence: The report contrasts easing headline inflation with services persistence. Compare CPI subindexes with wages and service activity to test which components could slow the return toward the target.

questions.question: What offset higher expected inflation and a larger output gap at the forecast horizon?
questions.evidence: The report identifies recent inflation surprises and a near-term reversal in oil prices as downward offsets. Use the report's forecast decomposition and alternative scenarios to estimate which offsets would still hold if oil prices and expectations moved together.

coverageNote: Review covers the official executive summary.

title: Monetary Policy Report 3/2026
locator: Monetary Policy Statement; sections 1 and 3; Annex, Table 3. Publication date from the September meeting’s release page.
summary:
Norges Bank raised its forecasts for headline CPI inflation to 3.3% in 2026 and 2.6% in 2027. It lowered its CPI-ATE forecasts for the same years to 3.0% and 2.7%, respectively. Underlying inflation had softened faster than projected in June even as energy and other commodities raised the headline measure. The report estimates a negative mainland output gap, projected to widen from −0.3% in 2026 to −1.1% in 2028.

The September path keeps the policy rate elevated for somewhat longer than the June forecast. The annual CPI and CPI-ATE rates both reach 2.1% in 2029 in the baseline. The Committee says stronger external price pressures could require higher rates while quicker disinflation or labour-market weakness could result in a lower path.

questions.question: Which prices explain the opposing revisions in 2026 headline CPI and CPI-ATE?
questions.evidence: The forecasts move 0.1 percentage point up for headline CPI and 0.2 point down for CPI-ATE. The report identifies energy and commodity pressures alongside lower underlying inflation.

questions.question: How does the policy path balance persistence risks with a widening negative output gap?
questions.evidence: The rate path stays elevated longer than in June and the projected mainland output gap widens through 2028.

questions.question: What would distinguish faster underlying disinflation from a temporary move in CPI-ATE?
questions.evidence: The Committee names faster disinflation as a possible reason for lower rates while the report finds near-term underlying inflation upside risk above its historical average.

title: Monetary Policy Committee Q3 Meeting Readout
locator: Committee readout on 19 September meeting, issued by PBOC on 24 September and republished by the Shanghai municipal authorities on 28 September. Policy stance, operating framework and market stability paragraphs.
summary:
The Monetary Policy Committee called for continued moderately loose policy, stronger countercyclical adjustment and coordination with fiscal policy. Its diagnosis combines a generally stable economy with stronger supply than demand and uneven sector outcomes.
