It encourages using broad and targeted tools to maintain liquidity, support demand and help prices recover. It says credit-market practices and loan fees should support low all-in financing costs. The readout is a statement of policy direction and gives no new operating rate or fixed timetable.

The committee also says it will watch long yields from a macroprudential perspective and wants markets to determine the exchange rate while guarding against self-reinforcing moves. That supports separate analysis of credit easing, bond-market risks and exchange rate management. The release's reference to earlier low financing costs describes the committee’s assessment at the time, with no data on the market reaction to publication.

questions.question: Which sectors explain the gap between capacity and demand?
questions.evidence: Compare sales, inventories and utilisation by industry, and look at whether financing is associated with changes in those gaps.

questions.question: How do fiscal and monetary actions interact at the short end?
questions.evidence: Match issuer and Treasury cash flows with tenders, repo rates and liquidity around major settlements.

questions.question: Which part of the bond curve reflects term premia rather than near-term rate expectations?
questions.evidence: Compare maturity-specific CGB yields, swaps, issuance and balance-sheet constraints before interpreting changes in the long end.

title: Inflation Report – September 2026
locator: Assessment of the Monetary Council and baseline projection. The official MNB calendar gives 24 September at 10 a.m. The forecast is conditional on assumptions available at publication.
summary:
The MNB projected average inflation of 1.8% in 2026 and 3.1% in 2027. It expected inflation to reach the level of the new 2.5% target in the second half of 2028. It projected real GDP growth of 1.8% in 2026, 2.9% in 2027 and 2.8% in 2028. The Bank expected household consumption to support activity and investment to remain weak in 2026.

Bank lending strengthened in the second quarter. Outstanding corporate loans were 10.5% higher in the year to June and household loans increased 18%. Banks reported increasing demand for short-term business loans, with no increase in demand for longer-term investment financing. The report identifies the Home Start programme as a contributor to household lending growth.

questions.question: What accounted for higher average inflation in 2027 despite the 2026 undershoot?
questions.evidence: Compare the baseline path by component and identify base effects, regulatory measures and underlying price changes.

questions.question: Which parts of the growth forecast depend on an investment recovery?
questions.evidence: Compare the expenditure decomposition across baseline and risk scenarios, then track construction and capital goods data.

questions.question: How much of household credit growth is attributable to the Home Start programme?
questions.evidence: Compare eligible and comparable ineligible originations, loan sizes and bank underwriting before and after the programme.

institution: Banco Central de Reserva del Perú
title: August 2026 liquidity and credit statistics – Private-sector credit in soles
summary:
The Bank reported that the outstanding stock of private-sector credit denominated in soles rose 9.1% from a year earlier and 1.6% from July. The Bank's release describes a currency-specific aggregate for August.

The Bank's other highlights for the August edition include the same 1.6% monthly increase for total private-sector credit and a 10.3% annual increase in that broader measure. The different coverage matters when comparing the annual rates.
locator: Bank’s chart release for sol-denominated credit and the adjacent official total-credit highlight in the August liquidity and credit release.

questions.question: What explains the gap between local-currency and total annual credit growth?
questions.evidence: The official highlights report 9.1% in soles and 10.3% overall. Compare the original-currency balance sheets and methodology to separate actual dollar credit expansion from valuation.

questions.question: How widespread was growth in sol credit across borrower types?
questions.evidence: The chart is a private-sector aggregate. Check BCRP loan balances by recipient and purpose, plus supervisory delinquency figures if assessing bank credit risk.

questions.question: Are household and corporate borrowing costs consistent with the rise in balances?
questions.evidence: The chart reports balances over time. Compare rates on new loans and sector-level loan flows for evidence of pass-through from the policy rate.

coverageNote: Review covers BCRP's published highlights on local-currency and total lending. The underlying research-note link was inaccessible.

title: The Indian Economy in an Ever More Volatile and Complex World
summary:
Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta argues that India has absorbed several external shocks at once, including energy disruption, trade uncertainty and El Niño risk. She describes policy as initially aimed at securing essential supplies, then allowing some energy costs to reach consumers as the shock persisted. She links resilience to domestic consumption and investment, export diversification and fiscal discipline. The IMF public-debt projection she cites is an external forecast.

Gupta sees a divergence across markets. In her assessment, government bonds benefited from fiscal credibility and sustained growth prospects, while equities had a weaker relative run following earlier gains. She distinguishes the current account’s structural services and remittance support from commodity-import costs and shifts in capital flows. She cites a 13.0% point-to-point rupee depreciation from 31 March 2025 to 17 September 2026. Her prospective adjustment in the balance of payments depends on expectations about future trade and asset flows. The historical currency move predates the speech.

questions.question: How much of the external gap reflects oil and gold prices versus underlying volumes?
questions.evidence: Separate import valuation and real volumes, with services receipts and remittances on the same basis.

questions.question: What would induce a durable recovery in foreign portfolio flows?
questions.evidence: Compare valuation and earnings revisions with FX-hedged returns and allocation flows across peers.

questions.question: How sensitive is fiscal room to higher borrowing costs?
questions.evidence: Test debt dynamics under alternative effective interest costs and nominal-growth paths, distinguishing those scenarios from the quoted IMF projection.

locator: Section II and the discussion of bond, equity and foreign-exchange markets, including footnotes 2–5.

title: Testing for contemporaneous exogeneity in linear time-series models
locator: Working Paper 2026-14, abstract, Phillips-curve applications and Section 8.
summary: Dovonon and Gospodinov develop a specification test for whether a time-series regressor is contemporaneously exogenous. They construct an expanding collection of moments from the regressors themselves. The method can test a single subset of regressors under its assumptions without requiring external instruments. They apply it to measures of labour tightness and slack in alternative Phillips-curve specifications. This matters for macro research because slack can move in response to the same forces that move inflation. A regression coefficient alone cannot identify policy transmission under such simultaneity. The paper supplies a model diagnostic. Its assumptions about sample size, moments and regressor dynamics matter for interpreting the test.

questions.question: Are the candidate slack proxies equally exposed to feedback?
questions.evidence: Use the paper’s empirical specifications to compare results for labour tightness and the unemployment gap over the same vintage.

questions.question: Is the test informative in short post-pandemic samples?
questions.evidence: Use the documented simulations as a starting point and vary sample size, persistence and shocks.

questions.question: Does choosing a better-specified measure change the inflation forecast?
questions.evidence: Compare rolling out-of-sample errors and policy-scenario responses for models using the tested proxies.

coverageNote: The note focuses on the test, the application and the conclusion. It does not assess every proof or simulation.

title: Statement of the Monetary Policy Committee, 23 September 2026
locator: Official statement and footnotes on the oil assumption, inflation peak, survey expectations and QPM path.
summary:
The MPC unanimously raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 7.25%, effective 25 September. It raised its near-term inflation outlook as the renewed fuel shock lifted the Brent assumption, with headline inflation expected to exceed 5% late in 2026 and to return to around 3% toward the end of 2027. Longer-run survey expectations remained around 4%. The bank distinguished that pre-fuel-increase survey from market measures that had picked up more recently.

The central forecast put 2026 GDP growth at 1.2% rather than 1.4%. Even with weak activity, the bank saw a risk of fuels feeding persistent services inflation and expectations. The Quarterly Projection Model implied a broadly stable policy rate near term and lower rates as inflation receded, while the committee retained a meeting-by-meeting approach.

questions.question: Are inflation expectations moving in response to fuel or broader prices?
questions.evidence: Compare later business and household survey vintages and inflation compensation by tenor.

questions.question: How much of the rate decision was anticipated?
questions.evidence: Check dated front-end ZAR pricing and comparable assets around the statement and Q&A windows.

questions.question: What if global rates or oil stay higher than assumed?
questions.evidence: Use the MPC’s alternative scenarios and track transport costs, exchange rates and service prices.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Financial Conditions (August 2026)
locator: Monetary aggregates and loans and investments paragraphs; August observations published 23 September.
summary:
The August financial conditions release reports that M1B and M2 grew from July on a daily-average basis, by 0.72% and 0.65%. Their annual rates declined to 6.65% and 6.79%, respectively. The CBC links the slower growth in broad money mainly to slower growth in foreign-currency and passbook savings deposits. Loans and investments of monetary financial institutions grew 9.43% from a year earlier, compared with the revised prior rate of 9.08%, with stronger growth in claims on private borrowers and government enterprises. Including insurance company lending and adjustments for reclassification and write-offs gives a lower annual growth rate of 7.69%.

The divergence between deposit growth and asset growth suggests checking composition and financing separately. These data do not themselves establish whether lending standards loosened or demand accelerated.

questions.question: Which deposits drove the change in broad money growth?
questions.evidence: Examine the component tables with consistent assumptions on exchange rates and deposit definitions.

questions.question: Does the higher growth of claims reflect new credit or changes in stock treatment?
questions.evidence: Compare new originations and sector claims with the broader adjusted measure.

questions.question: Did stronger private claims show up in business investment or household borrowing?
questions.evidence: Follow separate consumer, mortgage and corporate accounts and actual capital expenditure.

coverageLimitation: The analysis uses the official release text. Detailed supporting spreadsheet entries were not checked.

title: Consumer Price Developments in August 2026
locator: Joint MAS report, Charts 1–2 and Outlook. PDF verified via the co-publisher's release.
summary:
MAS and its co-publisher report core inflation at 2.2% year on year in August versus 2.0% in July, with monthly core prices rising 0.3%. Higher inflation in services, retail goods and food accounted for the core increase. Headline inflation edged up to 2.3% from 2.2% as the rise in core outweighed the effect of lower private transport inflation. Headline prices increased 0.6% on the month. The contribution charts relate components to the headline rate, while MAS core omits accommodation and private transport.

The report expects elevated energy costs to keep feeding into tariffs and transport charges, with global weather and supply conditions also affecting food. It anticipates more limited local pressure from services unit labour costs and subsidies. The overall 2026 forecast remains 1.5–2.5% for both measures, with core inflation expected to cool more clearly around mid-2027. An extended external cost shock or stronger investment spillovers could make inflation more persistent.

questions.question: Is this rise broader than the July rise?
questions.evidence: Compare inflation contributions in services, goods and food, with special attention to narrowing or expanding breadth.

questions.question: What part of domestic inflation depends on administered prices or subsidies?
questions.evidence: Check changes in sector tariffs, healthcare subsidies and other managed prices before comparing core trends.

questions.question: Does the data change expectations for the next MAS review?
questions.evidence: Compare analyst forecasts and dated SGD basket and market observations, allowing for broader USD moves.

title: BI-Rate Held at 5.75%: Strengthening Stability, Supporting Economic Growth
summary:
Bank Indonesia held its policy rate and standing facilities at 5.75%, 4.75% and 6.50%. The bank maintained its emphasis on rupiah stabilisation with external headwinds and a 2.5% ± 1 percentage point inflation target. It described using offshore non-deliverable forwards, domestic forwards and spot transactions, and expanded reductions to premiums on eligible hedging swaps. The revised discounts were 15%, 20% and 25% on three-, six- and twelve-month tenors, respectively. The tenor schedule changes the relative incentive to hedge longer funding exposures.

The bank reported the rupiah at IDR 17,855 per US dollar on 22 September, 0.78% weaker than at end-August, and noted that end-August reserves covered 5.4 months of imports by its measure. These are pre-decision observations. The maintained policy rate coexisted with changes to implementation and continued macroprudential credit support.

questions.question: How did take-up vary by tenor after the premium schedule changed?
questions.evidence: Compare eligible hedge volumes, maturities and all-in costs with the pre-change schedule.

questions.question: Which USD/IDR exposures were driving the need for stabilisation?
questions.evidence: Compare trade and portfolio flows alongside information on market liquidity and forward curves.

questions.question: How much policymaking space does reserve adequacy provide under stress?
questions.evidence: Compare short-term external obligations, potential capital outflows and alternative import-cover paths.

locator: Press release 28/193/DKom, opening policy decision, policy measures 1–3 and balance of payments and FX assessment. The signed English dateline and Indonesian publication both show 23 September.

title: Why hike? — Tom Barkin
locator: Prepared remarks explaining the price-stability rationale, resilient demand, and firm pricing.
summary: After the September increase, Tom Barkin explained why he gave more weight to inflation risk than to the employment side of the mandate. July headline and core PCE inflation in the speech were 3.7% and 3.3%, and price increases had spread beyond directly affected supply categories. August hiring recovered and unemployment was 4.1%. Barkin observed that higher-income households held up spending and that some other households protected spending volumes by switching to cheaper products. Firms he spoke with sounded more able to pass through costs than before the pandemic. Low hiring remained a weakness, with slower labour-force growth limiting its effect on the unemployment rate. The case for the increase was based on persistence and breadth, as described in the remarks.

questions.question: How should inflation breadth be measured across different PCE weights?
questions.evidence: Reproduce the distribution used in the remarks and compare it with alternative trim and frequency measures.

questions.question: Are firms’ pass-through accounts visible in actual pricing?
questions.evidence: Match regional firm contacts’ industry exposure to product-level producer and consumer prices.

questions.question: When could labour-market risks overtake the inflation concern?
questions.evidence: Monitor job openings, hiring and separations alongside changes in labour-force growth and real spending.

title: Monetary Council review of the inflation target
locator: Framework announcement, paragraphs on the target, adjustment horizon and policy calendar.
summary:
The Council set a 2.5% medium-term CPI target with the existing symmetric tolerance band of one percentage point on either side, starting 1 January 2028. It saw low inflation, declining risk premia and a stable currency as conditions that would help anchor expectations lower. The Council argued that the remaining half-point gap to the euro-area target allows some price-level convergence while reducing the short-term adjustment burden. It also announced a move to eight scheduled policy meetings per year from 2027.

The release describes a change in the framework and its intended long-run effects on predictability and financing costs. It gives a transition period for households and firms to adapt.

questions.question: Did longer-term inflation expectations shift toward 2.5%?
questions.evidence: Compare survey vintages and inflation-linked pricing where liquid, allowing for changing risk premia.

questions.question: How much of Hungary’s price convergence is explained by service prices?
questions.evidence: Compare price levels, productivity and wage trends with the euro area and regional peers.

questions.question: How will a less frequent meeting cycle alter policy communication?
questions.evidence: Track the new calendar, unscheduled communications and dispersion of market pricing between decisions.

title: Monetary Council decision, 22 September 2026
locator: Rate table and statement sections on the domestic outlook, risk scenarios and policy guidance.
summary:
The Council kept the base rate at 5.50% and the overnight deposit and lending rates at 4.50% and 6.50%. August CPI was 1.3%, below the June forecast and analysts’ expectations, while core inflation was 2.0%. Nonetheless, the September forecast left 2026 annual inflation at 1.8% and raised the 2027 projection to 3.1%, citing energy and a change to tobacco excise duty. This year’s offsetting forces were quicker pass-through from earlier forint appreciation and higher fuel prices.

The Council cited elevated energy prices and external uncertainty as reasons to maintain settings despite low spot inflation. It said the new 2.5% target would take effect in January 2028. Strong real wages and industrial activity supported domestic momentum, while drought depressed agriculture. The Council viewed growth and inflation risks as broadly balanced around the new baseline.

questions.question: How much did the exchange rate offset the fuel shock in the projection?
questions.evidence: Review the forecast decomposition and track import prices and domestic fuel and tradables inflation.

questions.question: Do services and wages point to higher underlying inflation?
questions.evidence: Compare pay settlements and services price momentum with the report’s persistence scenario.

questions.question: Did the hold or the target news drive any repricing?
questions.evidence: Identify the respective release times and use local rates, the forint and expectations with suitable controls.

title: Michele Bullock: Fireside chat at CEDA
locator: Governor’s transcript, supply-shock, inflation-expectations and productivity passages
summary:
Bullock describes the policy trade-off when adverse supply shocks raise inflation and simultaneously weaken activity. Repeated shocks matter because a sequence of price increases can change the inflation expectations of households and firms. She says monetary policy can limit the propagation of those shocks through demand, price setting and expectations. That is different from offsetting the first-round change in a relative price.

She also discusses the pressure of mortgage costs on household budgets and the difficulty of explaining the distinction between those costs and consumer-price inflation. For productivity, she sees possible benefits from AI over time alongside risks during a transition, including changes in labour-market matching. Her comments concern the policy objective and medium-term trade-off. The market question is whether her emphasis on expectations and supply implied a materially different response from what investors had priced.

questions.question: Are repeated shocks changing price-setting behaviour?
questions.evidence: Compare price plans and wage settlements over successive episodes, controlling for import-cost exposure.

questions.question: Would lower household confidence magnify transmission?
questions.evidence: Compare spending in indebted and less indebted households and track home loan repricing.

questions.question: Does the speech materially change the policy message since the testimony?
questions.evidence: Compare wording on second-round effects with the 18 September testimony and check price changes around the event.

title: Financial Stability Review 2026
locator: Report Foreword, Overview pp. 1–2 and stress test discussion. Selected sections reviewed.
summary:
The MAS review, using information available through 17 September unless stated otherwise, sees higher global sovereign yields, fiscal pressure and persistent input costs as sources of financial risk. AI investment and exports can support earnings and activity in the economies most exposed to the technology cycle. The same exposure makes those economies vulnerable if projects or valuations disappoint. The review distinguishes the effects of higher refinancing costs on sovereigns and private borrowers from the potential risk of a more abrupt change in asset prices.

MAS finds generally sound Singapore corporate, household and bank balance sheets. Borrowing costs had eased domestically and credit spreads had narrowed. Stress tests suggest most borrowers and financial institutions have buffers, while highly leveraged firms and a subset of lower-liquidity borrowers remain vulnerable. The resident credit-to-GDP ratio was 133% in Q2, down slightly from 134% in Q4 2025 and below trend. MAS says the countercyclical capital buffer will stay at 0% in 2027. This is a banking resilience assessment and a macroprudential setting. Its stress-test findings are conditional on scenario design.

questions.question: How would an AI valuation shock reach Singapore credit?
questions.evidence: Trace export, market funding and revenue exposure to the technology cycle across sectors and identify the most leveraged borrowers.

questions.question: Do aggregate buffers conceal concentration in vulnerable firms or households?
questions.evidence: Compare debt-service ratios and liquidity distributions against the report’s stress assumptions.

questions.question: What would justify reassessing the countercyclical capital buffer?
questions.evidence: Track the credit gap alongside credit allocation, property exposure and bank underwriting trends.

title: Copom minutes – 281st meeting
summary:
The September minutes describe accumulating evidence of restrictive policy reaching economic activity. Copom distinguished the initial effect of supply shocks from possible second-round effects and considered inflation risks tilted up. The members present listed in the minutes all supported reducing the Selic target to 13.75%.

Copom's reference projections were 5.2% for 2026, 3.9% for 2027 and 3.2% in the first quarter of 2028. The minutes present these projections separately from private expectations.
locator: Minutes, sections B–D, paragraphs 14–20 and Table 1. September 15–16 meeting, release dated September 22.

questions.question: Which data best capture the lagged response to restrictive policy?
questions.evidence: The minutes say evidence of transmission to activity was accumulating. Compare consumer-credit originations and rate-sensitive investment across several preceding quarters to assess when policy may affect underlying inflation.

questions.question: Where could energy or commodity prices spread into persistent underlying inflation?
questions.evidence: Copom distinguishes direct supply effects from possible second-round effects. Use official price microdata and the bank's oil pass-through work to measure dissemination into services and wages that matter for the policy horizon.

questions.question: What moved the near-term forecast higher while the policy-horizon estimate held?
questions.evidence: The September forecast table can be compared with the August minutes. Read the September Monetary Policy Report's forecast decomposition to identify offsets that could reverse with a change in oil, expectations or slack.

title: Chicago Fed Survey of Economic Conditions — September 2026
locator: September release PDF, overall and sector activity charts, hiring and capital-spending expectations.
summary: The activity index fell to −5 from +5. The release PDF characterised growth as near trend. Manufacturing rose to +25 from a revised +19, while nonmanufacturing declined from −2 to −20. Current and anticipated hiring picked up, though their indexes stayed negative. The balance for expected capital spending turned positive. Labour and nonlabour cost pressures increased from weak readings. Together the survey suggests a divergence between manufacturing and services, alongside spending plans that were stronger than current hiring on these measures.

questions.question: Was the nonmanufacturing decline a temporary regional shock?
questions.evidence: Compare sector respondents, the next survey and realised service-sector activity indicators.

questions.question: Do firmer investment plans increase demand for labour or equipment first?
questions.evidence: Track spending, orders, hours and hiring by industry to separate these responses.

questions.question: How large is the uncertainty from survey revisions?
questions.evidence: Compare the August and September vintages with later releases and examine the sensitivity of the signals to response composition.

title: Trends in manufacturing in the United States
locator: Manufacturing output and employment, Figures 1–4, wage premia, automation and conclusion.
summary: The commentary distinguishes the large absolute size of US manufacturing from its declining shares of output and employment. The workforce shift reflects fewer workers entering manufacturing early in their careers. Workers remaining in the sector have become more educated. The positive wage premium over similarly situated workers in other sectors turned negative in the overall estimates around the early 1990s, with different outcomes by education. Automation can lift output per worker at the same time as local demand for employees falls. The evidence includes long-run descriptive comparisons and results from external studies cited in the piece. It does not establish a current aggregate employment effect from any one factory investment.

questions.question: Which cohorts account for fewer entrants?
questions.evidence: Compare education, location and first-job sector across cohorts using the microdata behind the study.

questions.question: Where do automation gains appear in wages and output?
questions.evidence: Link robot adoption, worker mobility and productivity across plants and local labour markets.

questions.question: Could manufacturing investment raise output without restoring employment share?
questions.evidence: Compare capital intensity, training constraints, domestic input sourcing and production capacity across new projects.

title: Tiff Macklem – Navigating uncertainty and adapting to change
summary:
Governor Tiff Macklem described new US tariffs and elevated energy prices as distinct risks to growth and inflation. He expected relatively contained direct aggregate effects from the latest tariffs because the affected products made up about 5% of Canadian goods exports to the United States, but said broader uncertainty could delay hiring and investment.

He said the Bank would track the persistence of energy costs, their pass-through to goods and services, and whether slack weakened inflation pressure. Macklem said the Bank planned to use its new forecasting model, Prima, as the primary model for the October Monetary Policy Report.
locator: Prepared speech, New challenges ahead and How the Bank is thinking about it.

questions.question: How are investment and hiring responding outside the sectors directly affected by tariffs?
questions.evidence: Macklem distinguishes limited direct tariff exposure from broader effects of uncertainty. Match trade exposure to Canadian investment intentions and job postings to assess whether second-round demand effects exceed the direct export exposure.

questions.question: What would indicate second-round effects of higher energy costs?
questions.evidence: He discusses businesses passing costs on and households changing longer-term expectations. Compare sector selling prices, firm pricing intentions and long-term expectations to distinguish cost recovery from a broad inflation process.

questions.question: How does Prima handle temporary and persistent inflation scenarios?
questions.evidence: Macklem says distinguishing those forces is one purpose of the model. Use the Bank's model documentation and published alternative scenarios to assess how persistence assumptions change the forecast that guides decisions.

coverageNote: Review covers the published prepared speech.

title: The regional effects of monetary policy in Colombia
summary:
Using Colombian city and department observations from 2008 to 2025, Cristian David González-Téllez and Juan Camilo Laborde-Vera report that a rate increase reduces inflation, activity and employment by different amounts across regions. Jointly larger responses in prices and output point to differences in local demand sensitivity in the authors’ interpretation.

The paper identifies surprises using dealer forecasts, narrative evidence and market moves around decisions. It reports larger activity declines in mining regions and greater contractions across the studied outcomes in regions with above-trend bank credit, higher trade integration or more informal employment.
locator: Working-paper landing page, approach, contribution and results. Direct page date is September 21.

questions.question: Which regional results are strongest across the three monetary shock measures?
questions.evidence: The authors use survey, narrative and high-frequency market identification. Read the paper's regional impulse responses and confidence intervals for each measure to assess how much precision regional forecasts can claim.

questions.question: Can credit depth and sector composition separately explain regional transmission?
questions.evidence: The study reports response differences associated with regional credit and industrial mix. Check controls and alternative model specifications before using the estimates to rank regional credit risk.

questions.question: How might a region's trade integration change the relevance of its exchange-rate channel?
questions.evidence: Greater trade integration is associated with larger estimated responses. Use sector trade shares and regional price responses to test whether openness proxies for currency sensitivity or another part of the transmission.

coverageNote: Review covers the official research summary. The findings are the authors’ provisional research, with no policy decision implied.

title: The challenge of innovation — Fabio Panetta
summary:
Panetta argued that AI can improve analysis and change the economy the central bank is trying to forecast. Near-term investment can boost demand for scarce compute, energy and skills before supply is ready. The longer-term supply effect depends on adoption and the productivity gains that follow. The timing of demand and supply shifts therefore determines the inflation consequences.

How gains are distributed also matters. New tasks that strengthen labour incomes can reinforce consumption and investment. Automation that increases insecurity may raise precautionary saving and offset some investment demand. Panetta discussed national differences in diffusion and the potential for larger firms to capture gains sooner. The speech presents mechanisms and cites research estimates. It makes no commitment about the next rate setting.
locator: Section 3 and its subsections on aggregate demand and international divergence

questions.question: Which input constraints could bind before productivity gains arrive?
questions.evidence: Compare energy, compute and specialist wages with adoption estimates.

questions.question: Are household responses affecting consumption yet?
questions.evidence: Track savings and jobs by exposure to automation and new tasks.

questions.question: Which national or sector differences matter for policy?
questions.evidence: Compare firm adoption, output and wage distribution across countries.

title: Monetary policy transmission in the euro area: Sectoral differences between industry, services and construction
summary:
The Bundesbank reports that manufacturing responded more quickly to monetary easing than services or construction in its model estimates. Chart 4.1 shows distributions of differences in real gross value added following a simulated 25 basis point cut. The median initially favours a stronger manufacturing response, with uncertainty around the estimates and timing.

Survey evidence suggests demand plays a larger role in transmitting policy to services. For manufacturing and construction, financing and demand channels both matter in the short term and financing is more important over the medium term. A changing mix of sectors may therefore change the strength and timing of aggregate transmission across economies.
locator: Sections 1–2, Chart 4.1 and interpretation note

questions.question: Does the sector ranking hold for rate increases?
questions.evidence: Compare response estimates for tightening and easing at different starting rates.

questions.question: Which financing exposures best explain the sector gaps?
questions.evidence: Compare maturity structure and debt burdens in firms across sectors.

questions.question: What happens when sector shares change?
questions.evidence: Reweight estimates by national industrial and services structures.

coverageLimitation: Main model and channel results reviewed. Full specifications and survey appendices are outside this note.

title: Michele Bullock: Opening Statement to the House Standing Committee on Economics
locator: Opening statement on inflation and activity, and discussion of payments
summary:
Bullock tells the Committee that the RBA has raised the cash rate by 75 basis points in 2026. She describes renewed oil price pressure and business reports of input cost pass-through as vulnerabilities relative to the August forecast. Inflation at the time remained too high for comfort. Labour conditions had eased gradually, while remaining capacity pressure could still encourage cost increases to reach consumer prices.

The Governor frames the upcoming meeting around whether cumulative tightening will reduce inflation within a reasonable time. She notes the need to balance inflation and employment, and gives no commitment to a particular vote. Payments and card-cost reforms discussed later involve a different policy area and have separate implications for merchants and consumers. The rate-relevant news in the testimony should be judged against what the market already knew from the August decision and subsequent data.

questions.question: Did the testimony add policy information beyond the August upside risks?
questions.evidence: Compare wording, recent releases and short-rate expectations at the hearing time.

questions.question: Which business costs are being passed through most broadly?
questions.evidence: Look at price-setting intentions, inventories and margins alongside energy and transport costs.

questions.question: How much has employment softened without reducing capacity pressure?
questions.evidence: Compare vacancies, hours and industry labour supply to productivity and the output mix.

title: Change in the Guideline for Money Market Operations
locator: Decision §§1–3, implementation footnotes and named dissent.
summary:
Japan’s Policy Board voted 7–2 to set its uncollateralised overnight call-rate guideline at around 1.25%. The new rate became effective 24 September. The deposit facility moved to 1.25% and the basic loan rate to 1.50% on the same date. The Board also voted unanimously to set a floating rate and a quantity limit for funding to support private sector climate efforts. The operational adjustments apply to different types of central-bank funding and should be tracked separately.

The statement relates the increase to the central bank’s assessment of underlying inflation approaching the 2% target and financing conditions remaining accommodative. The two dissenters favoured the previous setting, with reservations about current inflation and strength of activity. That difference makes the subsequent policy path conditional even after a second hike of the year. The document identifies the policy change, vote and effective date. A repricing analysis would require announcement-time rather than implementation-time prices.

questions.question: Did short rates move mainly on the decision or on subsequent guidance?
questions.evidence: Compare yen overnight swaps at separately verified release times for the decision and press conference.

questions.question: How closely did traded call rates track the new guideline after implementation?
questions.evidence: Compare traded overnight rates, facility use and passage to term funding before and after 24 September.

questions.question: Which data could bring the dissenters closer to the majority?
questions.evidence: Compare subsequent speaker views and meeting votes with incoming consumption and measures of underlying inflation.

title: The Future of Banking Study: scenarios for New Zealand in 2035
locator: Publication overview, key findings and methods. Analysis focuses on the published summary.
summary:
The RBNZ study explores how banking in New Zealand could look under three scenarios through 2035. Its scenarios span continued incumbent dominance, a larger role for digital challengers and greater use of platforms that distribute or combine banking services. The horizon and scenarios are inputs for supervisory planning. They do not give probabilities or a central forecast for industry shares.

Competitive entry and new technology could improve efficiency and access, while fragmentation of banking services could create dependencies on concentrated providers and activities outside existing supervisory coverage. The study draws on research, scenario development and engagement. An investor could use the scenarios to identify which parts of the banking value chain are exposed to changes in customer access, funding and distribution, then look for adoption evidence separately.

questions.question: Where is entry most likely to change banks’ competitive positions?
questions.evidence: Track switching rates and changes in retail deposits, payments and lending shares by provider.

questions.question: Can new distribution channels change the pricing of deposits or loans?
questions.evidence: Compare customer acquisition costs, funding composition and lending margins across models.

questions.question: What operational risks would become more concentrated under a platform model?
questions.evidence: Review provider dependencies and how continuity requirements and service arrangements are structured.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
title: Summary of the 10 September Monetary Policy Committee meeting
locator: Committee minutes, sections on inflation, domestic conditions, financial conditions and monetary policy. The note is dated 17 September and covers the 10 September meeting.
summary:
The minutes record a 1.84% monthly CPI rise and 31.51% annual inflation in August. Annual inflation eased by 0.24 percentage points. The committee noted that the placement of private-school tuition and Hajj fees had added around 0.25 percentage points to August inflation and distorted month-to-month readings of the underlying trend. It highlighted energy and freight costs as persistent risks. Household, firm and professional expectations continued to differ materially.

The committee reported that second-quarter GDP expanded by 2.3% from a year earlier and 1.1% from the previous quarter, with private consumption contracting on the quarter and net exports supporting growth. It also recorded lower lira deposit and commercial loan rates between 24 July and 4 September. Those changes describe the financial backdrop to the meeting.

questions.question: How much of August inflation was a shift in timing across months?
questions.evidence: Reallocate tuition and Hajj charges using their collection dates and compare three-month measures of core inflation.

questions.question: Which group’s inflation expectations best predict service repricing?
questions.evidence: Compare survey vintages by respondent group with later service-price changes and wage agreements.

questions.question: What drove the divergence between commercial and housing loan pricing?
questions.evidence: Link product-level rates with funding costs, lending restrictions and changes in borrower or maturity mix.

title: September Manufacturing Business Outlook Survey
locator: Current Activity, Price Indexes, Special Questions, Charts 1–2 and final diffusion-index table.
summary: Third District manufacturers reported continued expansion in September, with new orders and shipments still elevated. Employment growth was less widespread. The employment diffusion index dropped to 11.8, while the shares reporting increases in input and output prices rose. Prices paid reached 48.6 and prices received 31.3. The supplemental questions indicated that 68% of respondents expected third-quarter output to exceed the second quarter and that median capacity utilisation stayed in the 70–80% bracket. More firms cited labour supply as a constraint. Expectations for six-month activity stayed positive even as the corresponding diffusion index eased. These seasonally adjusted balances show the breadth of reported change across respondents.

questions.question: Do higher prices received signal durable pass-through?
questions.evidence: Compare later survey responses with invoices and producer-price data, accounting for industry mix and input costs.

questions.question: Why did employment breadth soften as orders remained strong?
questions.evidence: Use hours, utilisation and regional payrolls to distinguish productivity gains from staffing constraints.

questions.question: How representative is this improvement nationally?
questions.evidence: Cross-check other regional manufacturing surveys and national orders while allowing for sampling and industry differences.

title: Regional Network Report 3/2026 — Minor changes in growth prospects
summary:
Norges Bank’s contacts expected quarterly output growth of 0.3% in the third and fourth quarters, broadly similar to the previous survey for the third quarter. They cited household purchasing power, defence demand and data centre construction as supports. Residential and other construction remained weak and respondents in oil services were relatively cautious.

Reported capacity shortages and difficulties hiring had declined and were below historical averages. Contacts estimated wage growth at 4.5% for 2026 and 4.0% for 2027. The survey provides forward-looking regional evidence. Its estimates are respondents’ views, distinct from national accounts or an official policy forecast.
locator: Overview, Charts 1–2 and discussions of sector activity and employment

questions.question: Is weaker capacity utilisation translating into softer wages?
questions.evidence: Compare contacts’ estimates with settlements and official hourly wage data.

questions.question: How dependent is output growth on data centre and defence projects?
questions.evidence: Compare order books and project delivery dates by supplier.

questions.question: Is a residential construction recovery delayed or cancelled?
questions.evidence: Check new-home sales, permits and developer funding.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Monetary Policy Decision of the Board Meeting (2026 Q3)
locator: Sections II–V: forecast, policy-rate hold, selective credit controls, and FX framework.
summary:
The CBC kept its discount rate at 2.00%, secured refinancing at 2.375%, and temporary accommodations at 4.25%. It saw contained inflation despite a substantial upward adjustment to its growth outlook. Technology exports and investment supported an 11.48% growth forecast for 2026, with the Bank projecting 5.82% for 2027 against a high base. Core and headline forecasts remained just above 2% for 2026 and were expected to ease below 2% in 2027. Its assessment of the external energy shock and inflation outlook supported a hold while monitoring global conditions, capital flows and domestic prices.

The board separately eased a targeted constraint: the second-home mortgage loan-to-value ceiling rose from 60% to 70%, and a construction-timing affidavit for land loans was removed. The changes took effect 18 September. The CBC linked the adjustment to a decline in banks’ real estate lending concentration and improvements in internal controls. The mortgage decision could affect particular borrowers independently of the policy rate. The statement also retained scope for FX intervention during disorderly conditions.

questions.question: How much does the growth forecast depend on a few AI-related industries?
questions.evidence: Compare exports, output, investment and household demand by industry using the same release vintage.

questions.question: Does loosening second-home LTV ceilings alter financing availability?
questions.evidence: Check new mortgage LTV, approval rates, pricing and credit concentration around implementation.

questions.question: What would unsettle the below-2% inflation forecasts for 2027?
questions.evidence: Compare the assumed oil path, energy relief and service-price persistence with incoming component data.

coverageLimitation: The full statement was reviewed. The separately linked comparative forecast tables and regulatory appendix were not independently checked.

title: CNB Bank Board holds the two-week repo rate at 3.75%
locator: Board decision and linked press-conference slides, pp. 2–3 and 10–13. Seven Board members voted for the decision.
summary:
The Board held the two-week repo rate at 3.75%, the discount rate at 2.75% and the Lombard rate at 4.75%. The briefing reported year-on-year GDP growth slowing to 1.9% in the second quarter from 2.2%, with domestic demand still driving growth and services inflation and property prices elevated.

The Board judged the overall risks to the inflation outlook to be tilted upwards. It cited persistent core inflation, strong wage growth and the potential for credit to increase money growth. Weak activity in some euro-area economies and a possible global asset-price correction represented downside risks. The August forecast, on which the decision drew, had envisaged broadly stable short-term market rates.

questions.question: Is the slowdown in GDP compatible with continuing pressure from domestic demand?
questions.evidence: Decompose real GDP and private domestic demand and compare both with labour costs and service-price growth.

questions.question: How concentrated is loan growth across household and government borrowers?
questions.evidence: Compare maturity-adjusted loan growth and money aggregates with mortgage flows and the timing of fiscal financing.

questions.question: Did the risk assessment carry information beyond the widely observed policy rate?
questions.evidence: Separate the decision and briefing timestamps, then compare changes in Czech rate expectations, the koruna and global controls.

title: Bank Rate maintained at 3.75% — September 2026 Monetary Policy Summary and Minutes
summary:
The Monetary Policy Committee voted 6–3 to hold Bank Rate at 3.75%, with three members preferring an increase of 25 basis points. The committee saw greater upside risks to inflation than in July after renewed energy price increases and slightly stronger activity. August CPI was 3.1%. So far the evidence of broader wage and price effects was limited, and the weaker labour market and higher private borrowing costs were expected to restrain inflation over time.

The committee unanimously agreed to wind down gilt holdings financed by reserves to zero by the end of 2034. The announced plan averaged £46 billion of annual reduction, with £20 billion of annual sales alongside maturities. Rate guidance and changes in gilt supply may differ in their effects on the front end and on longer maturities.
locator: Monetary Policy Summary and minutes on rate vote and gilt holdings

questions.question: How much did the vote distribution matter for rate expectations?
questions.evidence: Compare SONIA before and after the summary and around later communication.

questions.question: Which firms and workers are increasingly passing costs through?
questions.evidence: Compare Agents’ reports, earnings and pricing surveys.

questions.question: How does the agreed gilt run-off affect duration supply?
questions.evidence: Match the maturity and sales calendar with auction results and gilt–swap spreads.

title: Summary of Governing Council deliberations – September 2, 2026
summary:
Governing Council held the policy rate at 2.25%, judging growth and inflation broadly in line with the July forecast. Members discussed whether weakness linked to new US tariffs would absorb the impact of higher energy prices. Excess supply and a soft labour market could keep price pressures contained.

Members agreed that spillovers from higher energy prices to other CPI components could warrant a policy response. They said the durability of the recovery and the extent of pass-through would inform the inflation forecast and its associated risks.
locator: Bank’s deliberations, discussion of the balance of risks and Policy decision. September 2 decision, minutes published September 16.

questions.question: What indicators would establish broader energy-price pass-through?
questions.evidence: Members said material spillover to other prices could warrant a response. Use CPI microdata and supplier-cost surveys to establish whether pass-through has spread enough to affect the near-term rate path.

questions.question: How is tariff-induced uncertainty affecting the durability of the recovery?
questions.evidence: Members linked tariffs and confidence to uncertainty about the recovery. Compare industrial order books and business expectations in more and less exposed sectors before revising the likely duration of slack.

questions.question: Which measures of excess supply explain differences in inflation risk assessments?
questions.evidence: The minutes discuss spare capacity and a soft labour market as possible offsets to energy pressure. Compare the Bank's slack measures with capacity utilization and job vacancies to test whether alternative estimates change the projected inflation response.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: FOMC raises the federal funds target range to 3.75–4.00%
locator: Statement released at 14:00 EDT, decision, vote and accompanying implementation link.
summary: The FOMC raised the federal funds target range 25 basis points to 3.75–4.00% on a 12–0 vote, citing a timelier return to its 2% inflation goal. The statement kept the ample-reserves approach. It described solid activity, resilient domestic spending, robust capital investment and little change in unemployment. Job growth had kept pace with workforce growth in the Committee’s assessment. Geopolitical developments remained a source of uncertainty. The published language places the inflation problem at the centre of the action while describing employment as broadly steady. The statement gives neither a future rate path nor a threshold for the next move.

questions.question: How much of the increase was already priced before 14:00 EDT?
questions.evidence: Use options and futures on the policy rate and timestamped two-year Treasury data. Separate the target-range surprise from the simultaneous forecasts and later press conference.

questions.question: Which underlying inflation measures would support another increase?
questions.evidence: Track the breadth and short-run momentum of PCE inflation and survey expectations alongside revisions. The statement supplies no numerical trigger.

questions.question: How does a higher administered rate transmit under ample reserves?
questions.evidence: Use the implementation note, daily effective fed funds and reserve and repo rates to distinguish an executed corridor adjustment from pressure in money markets.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: FOMC Summary of Economic Projections — September 2026
locator: Table 1, Figures 1–2 and the accessible distributions and uncertainty tables.
summary:
FOMC participants’ September projections paired stronger growth and lower unemployment with a higher median path for the policy rate than in June. Median real GDP growth for 2026 rose from 2.2% to 2.3%. The 2026 unemployment median fell to 4.1% from 4.3%. Median headline PCE inflation was 3.7% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027. Core PCE was 3.4% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027. The growth and inflation projections compare fourth quarters, whereas unemployment is the fourth-quarter average.

The median funds-rate projection was 4.1% at end-2026 and end-2027, following June medians of 3.8% and 3.6%. The September individual 2027 projections spanned roughly 3.1–4.4% in Table 1, so the median conceals substantial variation. The dots apply each participant’s view of appropriate policy to their individual outlook. A dotted path cannot be read as a collective commitment or as a direct measure of what rates markets priced.

questions.question: How did the distribution of 2027 dots move beyond its median?
questions.evidence: Compare all available dots and central tendencies across June and September, accounting for changes in participation, to see whether the shift was broad or concentrated.

questions.question: How much was a change in inflation tolerance versus stronger demand?
questions.evidence: Use the detailed projection distributions and published explanations by participants to test whether the rate revision covaries with inflation, growth or unemployment assumptions.

questions.question: What was the gap to expectations in forward markets?
questions.evidence: Use contemporaneous meeting-dated rates and the Treasury curve, with a risk-premium adjustment, to distinguish a change in median policy assumptions from a market surprise.

title: Copom reduces the Selic rate to 13.75%
summary:
The Copom reduced the Selic target by 25 basis points to 13.75%. It described a gradual moderation concentrated in more cyclical activities, with a resilient economy and a tight labour market. Focus survey inflation expectations were 4.9% for 2026 and 4.3% for 2027.

The communication emphasized uncertainty in the external environment and the interaction of domestic fiscal conditions with inflation and monetary conditions.
locator: Committee statement, economic backdrop, Focus expectations and decision. Official comunicado 45.963 records the meeting decision.

questions.question: How uneven is the slowdown across cyclical and less rate-sensitive industries?
questions.evidence: The committee described moderation concentrated in cyclical sectors. Compare output and hiring data in rate-sensitive sectors and slower-moving services to assess the breadth of policy transmission.

questions.question: How far above target were private inflation expectations at comparable horizons?
questions.evidence: The decision identifies the 2026 and 2027 Focus survey expectations. Compare the Focus distribution and inflation compensation at the same horizons to determine whether the survey path represents wider market pricing.

questions.question: How can local funding conditions distinguish external rate pressure from domestic fiscal effects?
questions.evidence: The committee discusses external and domestic fiscal influences on financial conditions. Use time-stamped BRL rates and sovereign spreads around independent fiscal and external news to test their relative contribution to domestic duration risk.

coverageNote: The official statement was reviewed from its published text as indexed. The linked site requires JavaScript to display the article in some environments.

title: Minutes of the Monetary Policy Board Meeting (August 2026)
locator: Official publication abstract, 27 August policy meeting majority decision and named dissent.
summary:
The official minutes release records the majority’s preference to raise the Base Rate from 2.75% to 3.00% for the interval before the next meeting. Kunil Hwang preferred keeping the rate at 2.75%. The release attributes the majority’s decision to the combined domestic and global economic and financial circumstances. The publication date of 15 September is distinct from the 27 August decision date.

The vote by itself identifies a disagreement about current timing. The abstract does not provide the member-by-member reasoning or say how the dissenting member would respond to different inflation or housing outcomes. Any attempt to track future preference should use the full stated arguments and subsequent votes.

questions.question: Which arguments differ between the vote summary and full minutes?
questions.evidence: Compare the attached member contributions with the decision statement and the policy press conference.

questions.question: Does the identified dissent reflect a different outlook or a different preference for waiting?
questions.evidence: Read the individual argument against later statements and incoming data known as of each meeting.

questions.question: Was the content newly available on 15 September important for prices?
questions.evidence: Compare the release with disclosures already public on 27 August and measure the announcement-time move separately.

coverageLimitation: The official English abstract was readable. The individual discussion in the linked PDF was not verified.

title: Macroeconomic interim projections — September 2026
summary:
The Banque de France lowered its 2026 GDP growth forecast by 0.1 percentage point to 0.4%. Activity was weak in the first half and the forecast incorporated a lower first-quarter GDP vintage. The central path anticipated growth recovering to 0.9% in 2027 and 1.2% in 2028. Tight financing conditions and fiscal uncertainty limited private investment in the projection.

Headline inflation was projected at 2.3% in 2026, 1.9% in 2027 and 1.6% in 2028. Inflation excluding energy and food was projected to rise from 1.6% in 2026 to 2.3% in 2027, reflecting indirect and second-round effects. The paths are conditioned on the 19 August energy futures assumptions. The unemployment rate was revised higher across the horizon.
locator: Key projections and sections on growth, inflation and projection assumptions

questions.question: How sensitive is French growth to private investment assumptions?
questions.evidence: Compare investment surveys and borrowing costs against June and September projections.

questions.question: Which costs account for higher core but lower headline inflation in 2027?
questions.evidence: Examine energy base effects and the assumptions on sector pass-through.

questions.question: How much of the unemployment revision reflects labour supply?
questions.evidence: Compare employment and participation assumptions with INSEE data.

title: Monetary Policy Report – August 2026
summary:
The BSP’s August-edition report records a 25 basis point increase in the target reverse repurchase rate to 5.0% on 27 August. The Monetary Board saw a case for a measured tightening to protect expectations despite weak recent activity. Current and projected inflation told different stories. July inflation eased from 6.4% to 6.2% owing to fuel and some services, and lower-than-expected midyear readings helped bring the 2026 forecast down to 6.1%. In contrast, the 2027 and 2028 forecasts were revised higher because of the potential agricultural effects of El Niño and higher minimum wage assumptions. Near-term output weakness reflected a smaller-than-expected Q2 GDP reading, with recovery projected for 2027.

The report’s scenarios show how forecasts can change with the persistence of supply shocks, the scope of wage adjustments and domestic demand. Its higher inflation scenario examines oil stress and rice supply, while the lower inflation case includes more localised wage changes and softer spending. Professional forecasters reported lower inflation expectations in August, though the 12-month measure stayed above the upper bound of the target range. The report presents that survey evidence separately from the BSP forecast. The policy decision addresses prospective inflation and expectations, while the report gives conditional paths for growth and prices.

questions.question: How much of the medium-term upward revision comes from the wage assumption?
questions.evidence: Reconcile forecast changes by oil, food and wage assumptions and compare registered wage changes and pass-through.

questions.question: What would make below-target growth the binding policy consideration?
questions.evidence: Compare alternative outputs under different real income, investment and rate paths using the forecast assumptions.

questions.question: Could the survey average mask disagreement on the inflation horizon?
questions.evidence: Examine respondent dispersion, response timing and conditions for the return to target.

locator: Monetary policy summary, Economic Outlook tables and scenarios, and July inflation and forecast survey sections. August edition published 11 September per the BSP release calendar; selected sections and exhibits reviewed.

title: Chia Der Jiun: Building the Financial System of the Future
locator: AI adoption, operational resilience and the UPI–PayNow linkage passages
summary:
Chia describes financial-sector AI use in fraud detection, underwriting, regulatory work and other business processes, and sets out initiatives to validate reusable applications and maintain institutional controls. He emphasises that faster decision-making and delegated transactions could accelerate movements of funds. That increases the relevance of operational resilience and accountable verification alongside potential efficiency gains.

He also recalls the Singapore–India UPI–PayNow retail payments link, which he says had recorded more than a doubling in transaction volumes each year following launch. The speech considers how interoperable payment systems can reduce friction in small cross-border transfers and how usage could expand. The investment issues are whether new payment channels change realised transaction costs and intraday liquidity needs. His claims on adoption and growth describe what was reported to the audience on 11 September.

questions.question: Did the payment linkage lower the total cost of transfers?
questions.evidence: Compare fees, conversion spreads, delays and failures before and after adoption across comparable channels.

questions.question: Could faster transfers change bank funding behaviour?
questions.evidence: Study transaction values and timing alongside deposit rates and intraday settlement balances.

questions.question: Are AI applications improving underwriting or mostly reducing process time?
questions.evidence: Seek actual approval rates, loss outcomes and costs, controlling for participant and borrower mix.

institution: Banco Central de Reserva del Perú
title: September 2026 monetary program – Reference rate maintained at 4.25%
summary:
The Bank announced that it held the reference rate at 4.25%. In the Bank's accompanying video, it reported that August annual inflation rose from 4.1% to 4.4%, influenced by the comparison base, while inflation excluding food and energy declined from 4.6% to 4.5%. The bank reported 12-month inflation expectations of 3.1% and 24-month expectations of 2.5%.

The Bank described energy and transport as important contributors and reported underlying inflation of 1.8% excluding transport. It expected headline and underlying inflation to return to the target range and settle around 2% over its forecast horizon as the supply shocks fade. It cited weather and geopolitical risks and described activity indicators as strong.
locator: Decision-day announcement and official September monetary-program video transcript, especially the inflation and outlook segments.

questions.question: How much of the August rise can be decomposed into base effects and subsequent price momentum?
questions.evidence: The Bank highlighted the comparison base while headline inflation increased. Reconstruct prior-year monthly contributions and the current seasonally adjusted CPI to estimate momentum relevant to the next policy decision.

questions.question: How persistent are the transport pressures embedded in underlying inflation?
questions.evidence: The Bank described energy and transport as key contributors. Use BCRP transport and ex-transport underlying measures with fuel-price series to test how durable the contribution may be.

questions.question: Why were 12-month expectations above two-year expectations?
questions.evidence: The Bank reported 3.1% at 12 months and 2.5% at 24 months. Compare response distributions at matching horizons and other official expectations series to gauge whether the rise reflects temporary shocks or broader concern.

coverageNote: Based on the official decision announcement and accompanying video transcript. The detailed decision PDF was inaccessible during review.

related.label: Official September program video and transcript

title: Monetary policy decisions
summary:
The ECB raised its three policy rates by 25 basis points. From 16 September the deposit facility rate was 2.50%, the main refinancing rate 2.65%, and the marginal lending rate 2.90%. Staff projected headline inflation at 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028. The Governing Council judged that prolonged energy pressures made it appropriate to tighten so that inflation returned to 2% over the medium term.

Council guidance retained a meeting-by-meeting approach. Underlying inflation dynamics and the degree of transmission remained relevant alongside the outlook. Asset purchase programme portfolios continued to run down without reinvestment. The statement provides the policy shift and outlook; market repricing would require dated market data.
locator: Decision, new staff baseline and interest rate and portfolio sections

questions.question: Was the decision anticipated?
questions.evidence: Compare euro OIS just before the release and in a separate press-conference window.

questions.question: How much medium-term inflation depends on persistent energy prices?
questions.evidence: Compare the staff scenarios with dated gas, oil and refining data.

questions.question: Have higher rates reached financing conditions?
questions.evidence: Review financing costs and bank lending standards by country and borrower type.

title: Monetary Policy Report (September 2026)
locator: Official Korean original. Overview and Parts I–II on operating conditions, decisions and forward guidance.
summary:
The Bank of Korea’s September report reviews two consecutive increases in July and August that raised the Base Rate from 2.50% to 3.00%. It places the moves in the context of stronger exports and investment, recovering consumption, above-target inflation and financial stability risks around property and household loans. It says timing and pace of further increases depend on the evolution of those factors. The earlier spring holds allowed a read of developments in the Middle East before the policy rate was adjusted.

Its discussion of financial markets separates global government bond spillovers and local rate expectations from corporate credit spreads and refinancing. It sees pronounced differences in access to finance among some issuers even when market-wide pricing appears stable. This distinction matters when assessing tightening through credit conditions. This is the September assessment, when it was published in Korean. The full English edition was published separately in November.

questions.question: Did the export upswing feed through to broader domestic wages and spending?
questions.evidence: Compare industry hiring and output with consumption and real income through the same report vintage.

questions.question: How much of the rise in long yields reflected global rates as opposed to domestic policy expectations?
questions.evidence: Compare Korean swaps and government yields with overseas benchmark spreads and issuance patterns.

questions.question: Are refinancing constraints concentrated in particular credit segments?
questions.evidence: Review corporate spreads and realised refinancing by rating and collateral, with separate attention to short-term project finance.

coverageLimitation: The Korean text and published explanations were reviewed. The linked source workbook and underlying data for every exhibit were not independently verified.

title: Kazuyuki Masu in Fukui: Economic Activity, Prices, and Monetary Policy in Japan
locator: Price risk sections, the interpretation of charts 7–8 on real and neutral rates, and policy conduct.
summary:
Masu argued that negative short real rates deserved early attention in an economy that had left deflation. At the time the 1% policy setting was below the lower end of his illustrative 1.1–2.5% nominal neutral range. He built that range by adding the 2% objective to a broad set of model estimates of the natural real rate. He cautioned that neutral could not be pinned to a single number. Persistently negative short real rates could support leverage, encourage businesses to bring investment forward and reduce the purchasing power of households’ savings.

Different shocks implied different policy trade-offs. The Middle East shock affected output as well as input prices; a weaker yen amplified imported prices but was not itself the policy target. AI demand offered an offset for activity and raised some prices. Food inflation could persist beyond rice or energy because of distribution and packaging costs. The evidence and rate assessment represent Masu’s views as expressed in September.

questions.question: How sensitive is the rate gap to estimated expectations and methods?
questions.evidence: Compare several measures of expected inflation and trend growth when constructing a range of real and neutral rates.

questions.question: Is rising food inflation spreading after removing narrowly volatile items?
questions.evidence: Track processed-food prices, distribution and packaging costs and selling-price revisions.

questions.question: How exposed is Japan if global investment in AI equipment decelerates?
questions.evidence: Compare semiconductor materials and equipment exports, orders and corresponding profit sensitivity.

coverageLimitation: The official transcript was reviewed. The standalone chart pack was not independently validated.

title: ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area — September 2026
summary:
ECB staff revised 2027 growth up to 1.4% from 1.2% and headline inflation up to 2.5% from 2.3%. The baseline projected annual growth of 0.9%, 1.4% and 1.5% over 2026–28. Staff expected activity to recover, though competitiveness limits the export boost and the euro area’s own production of AI-related goods was relatively small. The projection for 2027 core inflation rose 0.1 percentage point to 2.6%.

Table 1 shows why the risks cannot be reduced to one central path. In the severe energy scenario, 2027 inflation was 5.4% and growth 0.4%, while in the milder case the same projections were 1.9% and 1.5%. These scenarios vary the size and duration of the energy shock and the strength of pass-through. They are conditional comparisons, without assigned market probabilities.
locator: Overview, Table 1 and scenario assumptions

questions.question: Which energy assumptions separate the scenarios?
questions.evidence: Compare gas, oil and shipping assumptions with the futures and physical markets at the cutoff.

questions.question: How much of firmer core inflation depends on wage growth?
questions.evidence: Compare labour cost and services prices with the projection.

questions.question: Do the alternative scenarios imply materially different financing conditions?
questions.evidence: Compare market pricing and credit costs with each scenario’s mechanisms.

coverageLimitation: The baseline, scenario table and main drivers were reviewed. Separate analytical boxes are not all covered.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
title: CBRT holds the policy rate at 37%
locator: Press release 2026-38 and CBRT’s 17 September MPC minutes, paragraphs 27–30, which reproduce the decision and guidance.
summary:
The committee left the one-week repo rate at 37%, overnight lending at 40% and overnight borrowing at 35.5%. It judged that recent data and leading indicators pointed to underlying disinflation despite monthly fluctuations. Indicators and the limited pass-through of supply shocks pointed to weak domestic demand. The committee identified elevated energy prices as an upside risk and was monitoring the geopolitical effects on costs, activity and expectations.

The committee pledged to tighten if the inflation outlook deteriorated significantly and persistently. The policy path remained data dependent, with macroprudential and liquidity tools available to support transmission.

questions.question: Which August components explain the gap between annual CPI and the committee’s underlying reading?
questions.evidence: Use seasonal adjustments, component contributions and statistical core measures, with a check for calendar shifts.

questions.question: How much restrictive pressure remains at a 37% repo rate?
questions.evidence: Compare the forward-looking real policy rate, effective funding and market loan rates against estimates of neutral conditions.

questions.question: How can future easing be distinguished from a liquidity adjustment?
questions.evidence: Compare decision statements, auction policy, the realised funding mix and rate expectations around each release.

title: Monetary Policy Council press release, 8–9 September 2026
locator: Page 29 of the NBP’s November 2026 Inflation Report, September Council discussion and rate decision immediately before the October statement.
coverageNote: The original 9 September press-release page returned HTTP 403. The note uses the NBP’s retrospective account of the September meeting.
summary:
The NBP’s later account of the meeting records that the Council kept its reference rate at 3.75%. The Lombard and deposit rates stayed at 4.25% and 3.25%, with the bill rediscount and discount rates at 3.80% and 3.85%. The account records that a view was expressed that prevailing rates were too low.

Members emphasised that future decisions would depend on incoming information about Poland’s inflation and activity outlook. The discussion singled out global commodity prices and inflation amid changing geopolitical conditions. It also identified fiscal policy, domestic activity and wages as risks to inflation.

questions.question: Were the commodity pressures becoming visible in domestic prices beyond energy?
questions.evidence: Use the price and exchange-rate vintages available by 9 September, then compare later import, producer and core consumer price data.

questions.question: Which domestic data supported concern that rates were too low?
questions.evidence: Compare the discussion with contemporaneous wage, labour cost and activity data and any member positions explicitly attributed in later records.

questions.question: Did the decision change expectations for the next few meetings?
questions.evidence: Check the official release timestamp and compare matched intraday PLN forwards, two-year yields and the zloty around the release with regional controls.

title: Karen Silk: Securing the future, the role of the repo market
locator: Linked speech, pp. 2–9 on repo and the OCR implementation framework
summary:
Silk explains how government bond-backed repo helps distribute cash and collateral, supports trading in securities and transmits the policy rate through wholesale markets. She says the market has grown internationally and in New Zealand. As settlement cash declines from elevated levels, a well-functioning repo market can reduce the quantity of cash the RBNZ must provide while preserving rate control. The speech introduces the role of regular liquidity provision and reports that term operations can lend at OCR plus 10 basis points for seven and 28 days.

Silk points to scope for deeper activity, stronger transparency and resilience. Her discussion distinguishes observed market growth from the potential benefits of further development. Researchers should track effects on money-market spreads and settlement separately from any change in the target policy rate.

questions.question: How stable are short-term spreads as settlement cash declines?
questions.evidence: Compare local repo rates, volume and collateral with facility use and balances over time.

questions.question: How do global repo stresses spill over to New Zealand?
questions.evidence: Look at cross-currency funding, foreign demand for local government bonds and domestic funding spreads around stress episodes.

questions.question: Which market changes would improve transparency?
questions.evidence: Assess trade reporting, eligible collateral and the diversity of participant trading activity.

title: Governor’s Welcoming Address at the Dinner Commemorating 30th Anniversary of FAST
summary:
The address, delivered by Deputy Governor Marzunisham Omar for Governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour, sets out Bank Negara Malaysia’s plans to update debt-market infrastructure. FAST moved issuance and tendering electronically. The address reports that the domestic bond and sukuk market was about RM2.35 trillion at end-June 2026 and that more than RM377 billion was raised in the corporate bond market from January 2025 to June 2026. These figures describe a market stock and cumulative fundraising, respectively.

BNM expects FAST+ and the next-generation scripless depository to support issuing, settling and holding tokenised debt. It announced a planned soft launch for SSDS+ on 25 September.
