Mild policy restraint, higher longer-term rates and continued productivity gains could help disinflation. She viewed the June and July releases as encouraging but too volatile to establish a trend. The AI buildout could lift core goods prices in the short run. Collins was comfortable with the July hold and wanted evidence of durable progress. Her outlook depends in part on avoiding fresh supply shocks and keeping expectations anchored.

questions.question: Which inflation measures would show that supply shocks are fading?
questions.evidence: Compare energy and tariff-exposed categories with the broader core distribution and long-horizon expectations.

questions.question: Where is mild monetary restraint visible in the economy?
questions.evidence: Compare mortgage and consumer borrowing, bank lending to firms and the sensitivity of business spending to long yields.

questions.question: What would make the productivity channel stronger than AI-related input pressure?
questions.evidence: Use industry productivity, costs and goods prices to compare AI-exposed sectors with industries further from the buildout.

title: Ninth District businesses continue to grapple with high costs
locator: July General Business Survey write-up, cost, profit and hiring figures and sampling note.
summary: This August release summarises July responses from 905 Ninth District businesses. More than half reported lower profits than a year earlier and about 43% reported raising retail prices by at least 5%. Contacts attributed higher costs to several sources including tariffs and materials, with some reluctant to pass them through. Less than half were hiring and many of those were replacing leavers. Six-month sentiment was mixed. The survey used a convenience sample, heavily weighted towards Minnesota. It provides a timely account of pressures on responding firms. Its percentages do not represent national estimates.

questions.question: How do cost pressures translate into margins by sector?
questions.evidence: Compare respondents’ input exposure, price changes and operating margins with administrative data.

questions.question: Are tariffs separable from regional demand or weather effects?
questions.evidence: Match business locations and industry inputs to tariff changes and regional travel and spending patterns.

questions.question: Could the employment signal reflect sampling composition?
questions.evidence: Reweight the responses and compare them with independent job openings and payroll data.

title: Monetary Council decision, 25 August 2026
locator: Rate table and paragraphs on domestic inflation, risk premia and the policy decision.
summary:
The Monetary Council cut its base rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%, with the overnight deposit and lending rates declining by the same amount to 4.50% and 6.50%. The Council said July inflation of 1.2% was lower than expected and core inflation fell to 1.9%. Food and tradables inflation eased while bank and telecommunications repricing contributed to higher market services prices. Preliminary GDP was up 1.7% from a year earlier in Q2. The Council cited weaker inflation and stable domestic risk premia as room for the cut.

The Council described positive real rates and FX stability as helpful in anchoring expectations. It identified fiscal plans, views on euro adoption and the external market environment as future influences on the domestic risk assessment, and deferred judgement on the next rate path to the September Inflation Report.

questions.question: Was the July inflation undershoot concentrated in a few categories?
questions.evidence: Compare the June forecast and realised component contributions, including services affected by earlier voluntary restrictions.

questions.question: How did the cut affect financing without destabilising the forint?
questions.evidence: Track loan and deposit pricing, then examine timed EUR/HUF and local rates around the decision separately.

questions.question: Which fiscal and external conditions would constrain the next move?
questions.evidence: Compare the next report’s risk scenarios with government budget releases, euro-area rates and domestic spreads.

title: Minutes of the August 2026 Monetary Policy Board meeting
locator: Meeting held 11 August. Minutes released 25 August. Considerations for monetary policy and decision.
summary:
The minutes set out what the Board considered before holding the cash rate at 4.35% in August. The discussion balances persistent above-target inflation against the tightening already in place and evidence that housing and domestic spending were slowing. Members discuss the prospect that inflation risks could warrant another increase and the value of observing how the previous moves transmit. Measures of potential supply and longer-horizon expectations are important to that calculation.

The text describes the arguments that could justify an increase or a pause rather than committing the Board to a fixed path. The distinction matters for investors assessing what might cause repricing. Announcing the minutes on 25 August offered a later opportunity for markets to learn about the discussion, whereas the rate and quarterly forecasts were already public on 11 August.

questions.question: Did the minutes reveal a different threshold for action from the statement?
questions.evidence: Read the two texts side by side, then compare the meeting-dated OIS price around the 25 August release.

questions.question: How much policy restraint was already reaching investment and housing?
questions.evidence: Compare mortgage cash flow and loan approvals with business investment and market yields.

questions.question: Are persistent price pressures showing up in medium-term expectations?
questions.evidence: Compare horizon-specific surveys with inflation compensation and business pricing intentions.

title: David Jacobs: The Road to Ample
locator: Demand for reserves, Graphs 8–12 and Conclusion
summary:
Jacobs describes the RBA’s transition toward reserves driven by banks’ demand rather than past asset purchases. As pandemic-era bonds run off, the RBA’s weekly full-allotment repo operations can expand if money-market rates create an incentive for lenders to obtain reserves. The amount of reserves can then react to demand while the asset side shifts from long-term bonds toward short-term repo. Jacobs says a smooth transition depends on the ability to supply liquidity flexibly rather than a fixed reserve target.

If official repo activity grew enough to affect functioning in private markets, the RBA could use additional liquidity instruments, such as FX swaps or purchases of short-term government securities. Existing overnight and intraday facilities remain in the toolkit even as open repo is phased out under the new approach. Graphs distinguish past usage and illustrative projections. The speech concerns how the RBA implements its cash rate target and why private liquidity management still matters.

questions.question: What observable markers indicate demand for reserves is starting to bind?
questions.evidence: Compare the effective cash rate and market repo rates with RBA facility use, eligible collateral and settlement balances.

questions.question: Could larger official repo activity crowd out private liquidity?
questions.evidence: Monitor private turnover, rates and collateral use alongside open market operations.

questions.question: What would indicate an FX swap injection is an implementation operation?
questions.evidence: Check announced purpose, size and tenor against cash-rate guidance and central bank asset runoff.

title: Schweigaard lecture: Ten questions and answers about monetary policy — Ida Wolden Bache
summary:
Bache explained why the policy rate can contain inflation even when some individual prices rise in response to higher financing costs. Rents are one possible cost channel. She argued that weaker consumption and investment and a stronger exchange rate dominate for aggregate Norwegian inflation over time. She also emphasised identifying the effect of rate changes separately from the tendency for rates to rise when inflation is already high.

Comparing Scandinavian economies, she distinguished Norway’s floating exchange rate and independent policy setting from the close connection between Danish rates and euro area policy. The speech explains the mandate, its interaction with employment and the adjustment mechanism. Uncertainty about the size and timing of effects remains part of the policy problem.
locator: Sections 6–7 and the chart comparing Scandinavian rates

questions.question: How large is the rent cost channel over different horizons?
questions.evidence: Compare rental resets and landlord financing with contraction in overall demand.

questions.question: Which source best identifies exogenous policy surprises?
questions.evidence: Review Norges Bank’s cited evidence with time-stamped market data.

questions.question: How do Norwegian rate changes affect the krone when rates change abroad?
questions.evidence: Compare relative short rates, exchange rates and risk measures.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Financial Conditions (July 2026)
locator: Official bulletin, monetary aggregates and loans and investments paragraphs.
summary:
The CBC reports July declines in daily-average M1B and M2 of 0.71% and 0.09% from June. Growth from a year earlier nonetheless measured 7.34% and 7.42%, respectively, with net foreign capital outflows contributing to slower annual growth. The measure of loans and investments rose 9.07% from a year earlier, primarily because of claims on government and public enterprises. The broader adjusted financial institutions measure, including life insurer activity and certain reclassified loans, rose 7.40%.

The release gives reasons for measuring both funding and asset composition and distinguishing monthly changes from year-over-year comparisons. Lower deposits and larger public-sector claims can coexist. The release covers July balances and is not an announcement of a new rate or liquidity operation.

questions.question: Did outflows affect specific types of deposit funding disproportionately?
questions.evidence: Compare FX and domestic deposit components with portfolio flow and currency settlement data.

questions.question: How much of claims growth reflects public rather than private financing?
questions.evidence: Compare the report’s sector breakdown with issuance and loan origination measures.

questions.question: How sensitive are the reported rates to definition changes or valuation?
questions.evidence: Check total and adjusted series and differences between cost-basis and reported market exposures.

coverageLimitation: The analysis uses the official HTML bulletin. The linked workbook was not independently reviewed.

title: Consumer Price Developments in July 2026
locator: Linked joint MAS release, Charts 1–2 and Outlook
summary:
The joint release reports MAS core inflation at 2.0% year on year in July, up from 1.6% in June. Headline CPI rose to 2.2% from 1.9%, though the headline index was down 0.2% on the month. The difference between the monthly and annual rates shows why analysts should compare both horizons and inspect the components. The charts show measured rates and percentage-point contributions and distinguish the coverage of core from all items.

The report cites higher global input costs alongside potentially slower domestic unit labour cost growth and a dampening effect from subsidies. It projects both core and headline inflation to average 1.5–2.5% in 2026. A large renewed disruption to food or energy supply and stronger demand spillovers from global technology investment are upside scenarios. An abrupt global tightening and weaker AI investment could reduce growth and price pressure. These are release-date forecasts rather than realised future outcomes.

questions.question: How much of the annual increase reflects a change in base rather than current momentum?
questions.evidence: Compare month-on-month core and headline levels and contribution changes over several months.

questions.question: Which imported costs are reaching service and food prices?
questions.evidence: Align import values, energy tariffs and disaggregated consumer prices with each other.

questions.question: Could domestic wage costs offset energy disinflation later?
questions.evidence: Check nominal wages and services productivity alongside subsidy implementation.

title: Chicago Fed Survey of Economic Conditions — August 2026
locator: August release PDF, activity and cost-pressure charts, index construction note and official release schedule.
summary: The Seventh District survey’s overall activity index fell from +11 to +5. The release PDF described growth as near trend. Manufacturing activity remained positive at +20, though it slowed, and the nonmanufacturing index reached −2. Current and expected hiring balances weakened, and the 12-month capital-spending expectation index stayed negative despite improving. Both labour and nonlabour cost-pressure indexes fell. The indexes summarise how many contacts rated conditions above or below their usual experience. Their levels measure the breadth of responses within this survey.

questions.question: Is the divergence between manufacturing and services broad based?
questions.evidence: Cross-check subsequent district and national business surveys by sector and respondent mix.

questions.question: Do weaker hiring plans appear in realised employment?
questions.evidence: Compare regional payrolls, hours and vacancies with the survey’s hiring balance.

questions.question: What explains lower cost-pressure breadth?
questions.evidence: Compare local supplier costs and wages with the survey’s responses to assess whether disinflation is durable.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
title: Turkish lira liquidity management: resumption of one-week repo auctions
locator: Press release 2026-35 and CBRT’s 17 September MPC minutes, paragraph 26. The short release provides no quantities or new policy-rate decision.
summary:
The CBRT said it would resume its one-week repo auctions, which had been suspended on 1 March. The release addresses the operating framework for Turkish lira liquidity. The September committee summary confirms the August announcement and the dates.

The immediate monetary-policy research question is how the availability of one-week funding changes effective funding costs and the placement of overnight market rates inside the operating corridor. Auction details and market series are needed to measure those effects.

questions.question: Did the one-week auction resumption shift the composition of central-bank funding?
questions.evidence: Compare auction allotments, maturities and outstanding overnight facilities around the first auction.

questions.question: How did the distance between the overnight market rate and the policy rate change?
questions.evidence: Use timestamped overnight and policy series and account for calendar-related liquidity shifts.

questions.question: How quickly did banks adjust lira deposit or commercial loan offers?
questions.evidence: Compare weekly bank-rate distributions with lira liquidity and loan composition around the implementation date.

title: Productivity and inflation dynamics
locator: Staff Working Paper No. 1,201; authors’ abstract. Review limited to the abstract.
summary:
Ludovica Ambrosino, Jenny Chan and Silvana Tenreyro distinguish a temporary improvement in the level of productivity from a lasting rise in its growth rate. A temporary improvement lowers marginal costs and raises potential output in their account. It places downward pressure on the price level during adjustment before inflation returns to target.

A lasting improvement raises expected permanent income, potentially lifting investment, consumption and the natural real interest rate. Inflationary pressure can result under some monetary policy responses if demand rises before the productive capacity arrives. For an open economy, the transmission also depends on the sector affected. These are conditional mechanisms from a staff paper.

questions.question: How should policymakers tell a temporary improvement in productivity from a persistent rise in its growth rate?
questions.evidence: The authors assign different marginal-cost, spending and real-rate channels to those shocks.

questions.question: How early would investment and consumption respond to an expected increase in productive capacity?
questions.evidence: The abstract identifies the timing of anticipated demand versus realised supply gains as a determinant of inflation pressure.

questions.question: Which affected sectors would matter most for an open economy’s inflation response?
questions.evidence: The authors say the sectoral incidence of the shock and the composition of demand matter.

title: The German economy — Monthly Report, August 2026
summary:
The Bundesbank assessed that Germany remained on a recovery path despite higher energy costs. The second-quarter flash estimate showed real GDP growth of 0.2% quarter on quarter. Revised first-quarter growth was 0.4%. Because the revisions arrived in late July, the Bundesbank’s June forecast had not incorporated the stronger preceding activity.

Exports helped sustain industrial production and sales. Manufacturing capacity was still low, and higher borrowing costs and uncertainty limited equipment investment. Construction recovered partly because of weather-related catch-up, and household consumption was likely to have grown only modestly amid softer labour conditions and higher prices. The report distinguishes the shift in measured GDP from the breadth and durability of the recovery.
locator: Sections 1 and 2, with GDP figures and revisions

questions.question: How much of the estimated recovery reflects statistical revisions?
questions.evidence: Compare GDP vintages, employment and state-of-business surveys.

questions.question: Can stronger export demand support investment?
questions.evidence: Compare foreign equipment orders, utilisation and financing costs.

questions.question: How long will construction catch-up last?
questions.evidence: Compare starts, permits and real spending with weather impacts.

title: Rebecca Williams: The Inflation Outlook
locator: 20 August SIFA Conference listing and linked slides 2–8. Slides are the source; no Q&A transcript reviewed.
summary:
The linked slides used for Williams’s SIFA Conference talk reprise the July Monetary Policy Review. They explain the committee’s consensus to raise the OCR to 2.50% and its view at that time that some further withdrawal of stimulus was likely, with timing dependent on pricing behaviour, demand and incoming data. The slides distinguish lower crude and refined petrol prices from levels before the conflict, and show easing in some domestic financial conditions alongside a recovery projection.

The material records the presentation’s use of the committee’s July assessment. The RBNZ listing explicitly says the event would cover insights already contained in the July review. For an August communication archive, it shows how the bank presented that existing assessment to market participants. An event study would need evidence of the remarks and first public timing, and should account for the fact that the underlying decision and projections were already public.

questions.question: Did anything beyond the published slides become public?
questions.evidence: Check any official transcript or released Q&A and compare it with the July statement.

questions.question: How did fuel assumptions evolve between July and the talk?
questions.evidence: Compare contemporaneous Dubai crude and refined petrol prices with the charts and underlying forecast assumptions.

questions.question: Did eased mortgage and FX conditions point to stronger demand?
questions.evidence: Check dated lending and consumption indicators, separating mortgage pricing from currency effects.

title: Policy rate unchanged at 1.75 per cent
summary:
The Board held the policy rate at 1.75%. Summer growth and inflation had exceeded the June forecast, raising concern that supply shocks would lift underlying inflation. At the same time measured inflation remained low, unemployment high and companies’ pricing plans subdued. Some international supply disruptions had eased. The Board judged the overall outlook little changed and continued to see a possible increase later in the year.

The policy response around the hold was state contingent. A larger, more persistent rise in inflation would warrant tightening. The August update assessed the incoming news without publishing fresh forecasts.
locator: Decision text and note on the August Monetary Policy Update

questions.question: Is the upside surprise seasonal or persistent?
questions.evidence: Compare travel services, tax-adjusted CPIF and pricing survey data.

questions.question: How much spare capacity is left?
questions.evidence: Compare vacancies, unemployment and capacity with the forecast.

questions.question: Was later-year tightening already priced?
questions.evidence: Retrieve timestamped Swedish OIS around the release.

title: Loan Prime Rates for 20 August 2026
locator: PBOC-authorised National Interbank Funding Center statement, two published lending benchmarks and effective period.
summary: The authorised announcement put the one-year loan prime rate at 3.00% and the five-year-plus rate at 3.50%, with both valid until the next fixing. The quoted tenors are distinct references for lending rather than realised borrowing rates or a complete funding curve. The fixing identifies the published references; assessing how a bank passes them through calls for separating contract pricing and changes in bank margins, credit risk and borrower composition. The brief source gives no forecasts, decision rationale or release-window repricing.

questions.question: Did effective rates change for new short- and long-tenor borrowing?
questions.evidence: Compare bank loan originations by tenor, collateral and borrower segment with the corresponding published benchmark.

questions.question: How far do the benchmarks transmit into stock rather than only new loans?
questions.evidence: Track floating reset dates, fixed shares and refinancing costs across vintages.

questions.question: Where would any release surprise appear first?
questions.evidence: Compare expectations known before the fixing with subsequent movements in onshore swaps and loan rates on separately timed releases.

title: Governing Board minutes – August 6 monetary policy decision
summary:
All five voting members supported keeping the overnight interbank rate at 6.50%. The account distinguishes policy views within that vote. One member discussed a neutral stance, noted uncertainty about potential GDP and argued that slack was secondary for choosing the stance during potential supply shocks. Another emphasized that transmission was still helping disinflation and that the exchange rate suggested room to absorb changes in conditions abroad.

A separate argument for a hold was that it addressed persistent inflation components and external risks while leaving flexibility to reassess easing inflation pressure. The individual views are presented without identifying speakers in the discussion section.
locator: Minutes, monetary-policy discussion and Votación, official printed pp. 11–14. Decision August 6, minutes released August 20.

questions.question: How sensitive are conclusions about slack to potential-output revisions?
questions.evidence: A member noted that a lower estimate of potential GDP would imply a smaller gap. Compare the activity data available to the Board and different real-time potential-output estimates before relying on slack as a rate catalyst.

questions.question: What would establish that monetary transmission is continuing rather than fading?
questions.evidence: A member linked disinflation to ongoing transmission. Compare contemporary credit conditions, core components and the timing of prior rate changes to test how demand is responding.

questions.question: How much protection could the exchange rate offer against an external tightening shock?
questions.evidence: A member cited the exchange rate as evidence of a buffer. Examine timestamped peso, overnight-indexed swap and US-rate data around prior external surprises, controlling for simultaneous Mexican releases.

coverageNote: Review covers the policy discussion and voting section, excluding the full statistical annex.

title: Quarterly Financial Report – Second Quarter 2026
summary:
The Bank reported second-quarter net income of C$298 million and first-half net income of C$479 million. It retained the earnings to reduce its accumulated deficit. Higher term and overnight repo activity supported year-over-year interest revenue despite lower interest generated by investments.

During the first half the Bank continued purchases through term and overnight repos and Government of Canada treasury bills. The report presented these operations in its account of assets and deposit balances.
locator: Management overview, financial position and financial results. Fiscal data to June 30; the publication is dated August 19.

questions.question: How did the composition of the Bank's short-term assets change as settlement balances declined?
questions.evidence: The financial-position discussion connects the change in deposits with investments and repos. Compare the detailed statements and the Bank's settlement-balance series to assess the maturity mix and the potential implications for funding-market liquidity.

questions.question: How much of the net-income improvement came from higher repo volumes?
questions.evidence: The income discussion attributes higher interest revenue in part to repos. Reconcile repo volumes, rates and investment maturities in the quarterly notes to separate effects of earning assets from interest expense.

questions.question: How persistent could the accumulated deficit be under different funding costs?
questions.evidence: The Bank retained net income to reduce that deficit. Use the report's balance-sheet notes and maturity schedule to test net-income scenarios and the point at which remittances could resume.

coverageNote: Review covers management commentary and financial highlights. The underlying statements are unaudited.

title: Minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee Meeting, 3–5 August 2026
summary:
The August minutes show that all six members favoured retaining the repo rate at 5.25%. Their reasons illuminate the conditions behind the neutral stance. Nagesh Kumar cites stronger capacity utilisation and investment despite risks from weather, trade and energy. Poonam Gupta points to an improved oil assumption and a marginally lower inflation forecast, while judging that a case for a hike could emerge if inflation proved persistent. Sanjay Malhotra sees little evidence of widespread inflation so far and would wait for better evidence on where inflation is settling.

The minutes explain the timing problem. A hold kept room to respond to adverse supply shocks while evidence on second-round effects developed. Indranil Bhattacharyya’s statement describes the value of communicating the conditions for future moves in an uncertain environment. Gupta cites about US$90 per barrel as a reasonable assumption for the fiscal year using oil futures available then. This is a forecasting assumption, and the minutes themselves are a later release about an earlier decision.

questions.question: Which inflation components would cause members to converge on a hike?
questions.evidence: Compare individual reaction conditions with forward revisions, diffusion and survey expectations.

questions.question: How sensitive is the difference between the June and August forecasts to the oil assumption?
questions.evidence: Use the published model assumptions to compare effects from oil, weather and other forecast changes.

questions.question: Did publication of individual views change market pricing beyond the meeting-day decision?
questions.evidence: Compare OIS quotes around the minutes release, isolating other scheduled announcements.

locator: Member vote and individual statements, including Gupta paragraphs 47–52, Malhotra paragraphs 53–57 and the discussion of framework guidance.

title: MAS introduces measures to strengthen Singapore’s competitiveness as an asset management hub
locator: Paragraphs 1–8, programme, tax and work-pass measures
summary:
MAS describes measures aimed at expanding Singapore’s asset-management ecosystem. It cites growth in industry assets to nearly S$7 trillion and highlights a planned investment programme for hedge fund managers that establish or deepen local operations. MAS expects local prime brokers, service providers and investment teams to benefit if the programme draws a larger cluster of firms. The package also proposes a tax exemption for qualifying performance-linked fund-management returns and a specialist work-pass track for senior investment professionals. The industry figures in the release are reported context for the announcement.

For macro research, the distinction is between assets administered in Singapore and capital devoted to domestic assets. Hosting more managers can change financing, collateral and service demand without implying an equivalent change in net investment flows. The release outlines policy commitments and aims, with programme details, realised take-up and market impacts left to later evidence.

questions.question: Does manager relocation bring new investment capital or move existing mandates?
questions.evidence: Compare changes in assets under management, domicile and asset location with launch and relocation disclosures.

questions.question: Which funding and brokerage services would face greater demand?
questions.evidence: Monitor prime-broker activity, custodian services and local fund formation.

questions.question: What criteria will determine participation and scale?
questions.evidence: Check subsequent MAS programme documents for eligibility, mandate terms and allocations.

institution: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: FOMC minutes — 28–29 July 2026 meeting
locator: Staff Economic Outlook; Participants’ Views; Committee Policy Actions and recorded vote.
summary:
Minutes released on 19 August show the Committee held the federal funds target range at 3.50–3.75% at its July meeting. Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari and Lorie Logan preferred a 25-basis-point increase. Most participants expected new data to help them assess inflation persistence. The staff projected lower headline inflation as gasoline prices fell and saw inflation around 2% in 2028. Participants placed greater weight on upside inflation risks, including the prospect that repeated energy and tariff shocks could change expectations and pricing.

Demand and supply effects from AI investment were both relevant. Participants noted that strong investment in data centres and related inputs could lift demand and prices before any wider productivity gains expanded supply. Some saw those prices as concentrated in a few categories, while others already saw broader pressure. Resilient consumption and stable employment supported a waiting decision, although some noted low job-finding and strains on lower-income households. The Desk review attributed much of the earlier rise in nominal yields to higher expected policy rates and reported little change in inflation compensation. Those observations refer to the interval before the July meeting. The minutes give no market move at their August release.

questions.question: What would make the July dissent the majority view?
questions.evidence: Compare the next core PCE measures, price breadth, inflation expectations and workforce indicators with the evidence the minutes identify. Separate a fresh commodity-price increase from wider pass-through.

questions.question: How much of a tighter path was already priced before the minutes?
questions.evidence: Use meeting-dated fed funds futures, two-year Treasury yields and inflation swaps around the 19 August release. Distinguish changes to expected policy rates from a shift in inflation compensation.

questions.question: When could AI investment tighten financial conditions through credit?
questions.evidence: Use segment-level capital spending, financing disclosures and banks’ or private lenders’ exposures to test how a reassessment of AI-linked earnings might affect funding and demand.

title: BI-Rate Held at 5.75%: Strengthening Stability, Supporting Economic Growth
summary:
Bank Indonesia held the BI-Rate at 5.75%, with the Deposit Facility at 4.75% and Lending Facility at 6.50%. The bank described rupiah stability and keeping inflation inside its 2.5% ± 1 percentage point corridor as objectives. The release anticipated above-10% primary money growth as part of maintaining adequate liquidity while other tools addressed volatility from abroad.

The bank expanded eligibility for a 12.5% hedging-swap premium reduction. In addition to qualifying portfolio inflows, the measure opened eligibility to qualifying foreign loans by banks and foreign direct investment, with the new transactions due to take effect in the second week of September. It also anticipated macroprudential liquidity incentives to redistribute liquidity and support lending. The release ties the FX intervention and hedging measures to stabilisation, while reserve and credit measures aim to preserve domestic funding.

questions.question: Did broader eligibility lower all-in funding costs for eligible borrowers?
questions.evidence: Compare swap pricing including the premium incentive with alternatives at matched tenor.

questions.question: Did the change alter the composition of foreign flows?
questions.evidence: Distinguish portfolio flows, foreign borrowing and FDI alongside new eligible hedging transactions.

questions.question: Did money-market liquidity reach smaller lenders?
questions.evidence: Compare transaction depth, INDONIA and facility usage by participant type after implementation.

locator: Release 28/162/DKom, decision and policy-mix measures 1–3.

title: Who Moved the Career Ladder? AI and Youth Employment in Korea
locator: Bank of Korea Issue Note 2026-19 publication summary, worker- and industry-level findings and identification caveats.
summary:
The authors use pension subscriber and labour-force survey data to study young workers during the spread of AI. They report that high-exposure industries accounted for 268,000 of a 285,000 fall in youth employment between June 2022 and June 2026. The losses were stronger in industries using AI for automation. Exposure associated with augmentation showed no comparable pattern. They also observe fewer entrants and more exits, meaning a hiring-only explanation misses one margin. Some industries where youth employment declined still added employees in their fifties.

The public research summary explicitly cautions against treating exposure as identification of causation. Reversing pandemic hiring, preferences for experienced workers, changing training and remote work also matter. The proposed focus is supporting pathways into experience and skills as technology changes, rather than mechanically preserving existing posts. This is staff research about structural labour markets.

questions.question: Can the estimated exposure correlate with labour demand changes that predate AI diffusion?
questions.evidence: Test pre-existing trends by sector and occupation and compare actual AI adoption with exposure scores.

questions.question: What explains the split between new entry and exits?
questions.evidence: Compare suitably matched worker transitions and training histories using cohort data.

questions.question: Does use of AI for augmentation help young workers build experience?
questions.evidence: Measure subsequent wages, retention and promotions in firms with different adoption patterns.

coverageLimitation: Analysis covers the public summary. The full issue-note appendix and robustness exhibits were not independently verified.

title: Monthly Business Survey — Start of August 2026
summary:
The August survey suggested a slowing pace of activity in industry and services in July, with respondents expecting a pickup in August. July manufacturing utilisation stayed at 76.7%. Technology, defence and energy-related industries were stronger. Order books were comparatively high in aerospace and some equipment categories, while some other firms expected seasonal or catch-up effects rather than sustained demand. Market services still reported a generally adverse cash position.

Input and selling price rises became less widespread. Close to 11% of industrial firms reported supply difficulties, with more severe constraints in aerospace. The bank estimated 0.2% third-quarter GDP growth using the survey and other indicators, while stressing weather and geopolitical uncertainty. That estimate was a nowcast rather than a published outturn.
locator: Survey overview and Sections 1–4

questions.question: Is an industrial rebound visible beyond catch-up effects?
questions.evidence: Compare sector output, orders and prior-month shutdowns.

questions.question: Where are supplier constraints most likely to persist?
questions.evidence: Check component delivery times and backlogs in aerospace and equipment.

questions.question: How fragile are cash positions?
questions.evidence: Compare working capital, payment delays and costs for weaker service sectors.

institution: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
title: Introducing trimmed imports and exports
locator: Research Working Paper 26-08, official summary and reported forecast comparisons.
summary: The authors introduce trimmed measures of US import and export growth. They aim to isolate components that improve forecasts of aggregate trade from volatile series with weak predictive content. The official summary reports better out-of-sample errors at medium horizons, particularly four to 12 months, with reductions up to 15% in some comparisons. The figures describe a forecast evaluation. The realised trade flow still includes the trimmed items, and large temporary changes in those items can matter for a quarter’s national accounts.

questions.question: Which components are repeatedly trimmed?
questions.evidence: Inspect the algorithm and the weights across estimates and test whether the same industries drive improvements.

questions.question: Do the gains survive new tariff regimes?
questions.evidence: Re-estimate sequentially with data vintages and compare errors before and after changes in trade policy.

questions.question: Does the trimmed signal improve GDP forecasts?
questions.evidence: Test how its use affects net-export nowcasts alongside actual shipments and inventory data.

coverageNote: The author conclusions and headline forecast evidence come from the Bank’s working-paper summary. Detailed tables and implementation were not reviewed.

title: End-July 2026 GIR settle at US$103.3B; BOP posts US$1.5-B deficit in July 2026
summary:
The BSP reported a July balance-of-payments deficit of US$1.5 billion and a cumulative January–July deficit of US$5.3 billion. It attributes the cumulative deficit to merchandise trade and foreign portfolio outflows, partly cushioned by remittances, government borrowing, services trade and inward direct investment.

End-July gross international reserves were revised to US$103.3 billion from US$104.7 billion at end-June. The BSP attributes the decrease to factors including its net FX operations, the government’s reserve-related flows and valuation effects, partially offset by foreign investment income and higher gold valuations. Its reserve-coverage measures were 6.7 months of relevant imports and payments and about 3.7 times short-term external debt on a residual-maturity basis. The two ratios use different denominators. The release separates movements in the reserve stock from the overall balance-of-payments flow.

questions.question: How much of the monthly reserve loss can be traced to FX transactions?
questions.evidence: Reconcile net reserve transactions, market valuation, investment income and government account movements.

questions.question: Is the year-to-date external deficit narrowing because of durable improvement?
questions.evidence: Compare trade volumes, prices, financing and remittances over the same seasonal windows.

questions.question: What if short-term external repayments rose?
questions.evidence: Use a residual-maturity schedule to test changes in the reserves-to-debt ratio under alternative flows.

locator: Dated release text and notes 1–2. The BSP page is rendered dynamically; the publisher’s dated indexed version supplies the release text.

title: Overseas Filipino Remittances: June 2026 release table
summary:
The BSP release table records June personal remittances at US$3.388 billion, up 1.8% from June a year earlier, and cash remittances through banks at US$3.039 billion, up 1.7%. January–June cash remittances reached US$17.149 billion, 2.4% above the corresponding prior-year period. The seasonally adjusted personal remittance series rose 0.4% month on month in June.

Personal and cash remittances cover different flows. The source defines personal remittances more broadly, including certain non-cash transfers and net compensation. The peso value reaching households can move differently from these dollar totals, so household purchasing power depends on conversion rates and prices. The 2026 table rows are labelled preliminary.

questions.question: Do the monthly data signal sustained acceleration or a calendar effect?
questions.evidence: Compare longer runs of the seasonally adjusted personal series across vintages.

questions.question: How much purchasing power did these inflows represent for households?
questions.evidence: Convert by period exchange rates and deflate using an appropriate consumer price series.

questions.question: How concentrated is remittance growth across sources?
questions.evidence: Compare origin countries, channels and overseas employment data to identify common vulnerabilities.

locator: BSP release annex dated 17 August in the archive filename. 2026 June monthly/cumulative rows and the personal, cash and seasonal adjustment definition notes.

title: Reserve Bank provides update on LSAP sales
locator: Release of 14 August, paragraphs on NZGB sale and LGFA divestment
summary:
The release sets out operational details following the MPC’s 8 July decision to fully unwind the Large Scale Asset Purchase portfolio by 30 June 2027. The RBNZ and New Zealand Debt Management agreed to bring forward a NZ$141 million sale of April 2029 government bonds to 15 June 2027, combining it with the planned sale on that day for a total of NZ$576 million. The release describes a transfer to the government debt manager. It does not quantify any net bonds offered to public investors.

The Bank also reports NZ$392 million in Local Government Funding Agency securities maturing after June 2027 and intends to prioritise the agency’s regular repurchase tenders for divestment. The details matter for analysis of bond supply and relative spreads. Assessing the market effect requires tracking how the counterparties finance or manage the tender and what changes in privately held duration, not treating the headline amount as an immediate open-market sale.

questions.question: How much duration actually returns to private investors after the schedule change?
questions.evidence: Reconcile the transfer with government refinancing, cancellation and issuance plans by maturity.

questions.question: Is there an effect on LGFA spreads when bonds become eligible for repurchase?
questions.evidence: Match tender dates and lines with individual bond prices, turnover and matched government yields.

questions.question: Did the operational details change expectations beyond the July MPC decision?
questions.evidence: Compare the July guidance with information available before the August release and dated spread changes.

title: Monetary Policy Report – Summer 2026
locator: Scope: official landing-page headline forecast, approval date and data cutoff. Full linked PDF, boxes and chartbook require a separate review.
summary: The CNB summer forecast sees inflation close to the 2% target in 2026, a temporary rise to 3% at the start of 2027 and a subsequent return near target. Its baseline is consistent with broadly stable short-term market interest rates, while growth is expected to slow a little in 2026 and pick up the following year. The report was approved on 13 August and largely uses information through 24 July. These projections describe the staff baseline supporting the policy discussion and do not specify a binding rate path.

questions.question: Which components drive the temporary 2027 inflation pickup?
questions.evidence: Use the report’s decomposition, inspecting headline, core and regulated or administered series with separate units.

questions.question: How sensitive is the baseline to a stronger energy shock?
questions.evidence: Compare the report’s risk scenario with the assumptions for foreign prices, the koruna and household demand.

questions.question: What signals would overturn the baseline of stable short rates?
questions.evidence: Compare subsequent CNB forecast vintages, revisions and the narrative around the underlying risks.

title: Minutes of the 6 August Bank Board meeting
locator: CNB publication calendar dated 14 August and full minutes for the 6 August meeting. The accompanying background report is separate.
summary:
The Board considered current policy appropriate following June’s increase and unanimously held the two-week repo rate at 3.75%. Members noted that volatile food and administered energy prices had kept headline inflation below target while services and core prices remained elevated. Some cited a stronger koruna and elevated longer-term yields as sources of restriction.

The Board discussed fast growth in genuinely new mortgages before tighter rules on investment mortgages and amid concern over higher mortgage rates. The discussion also acknowledged that persistent credit growth could increase financial risks. Members distinguished the possible timing shift in originations from evidence of a lasting boom.

questions.question: Did mortgage growth persist after the new rules took effect?
questions.evidence: Separate genuinely new loans from refinancing and split investment mortgages from owner-occupier loans across policy dates.

questions.question: How much of the headline inflation undershoot came from temporary components?
questions.evidence: Compare item contributions with services and trimmed price indicators, accounting for administrative energy measures.

questions.question: How much restriction came from the exchange rate and the long end of the curve?
questions.evidence: Compare a monetary conditions index with separate bank rates, currency and yield-curve drivers.

title: Economic and Financial Developments in Malaysia in the Second Quarter of 2026
summary:
Bank Negara Malaysia reported that GDP growth strengthened to 6.0% year on year, from 5.4% in the first quarter. Seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter growth was 2.5%. BNM links the expansion to steady income and policy support for households, investment activity and exports. It identifies technology-related electrical and electronics exports and services as areas of sustained strength, with a rebound in LNG and other manufactured shipments adding support.

Headline inflation climbed to 1.9% as fuel costs increased. Core inflation eased to 1.9% from 2.1%, with BNM pointing to jewellery, watches and rent among the drivers. BNM observed that higher producer costs were mostly upstream and reported limited pass-through across broader consumer prices. The share of items with monthly price increases rose to 45.5%, near the stated historical average, with an April rise followed by moderation. The growth, inflation level and diffusion figures are separate measures.

questions.question: How much of the stronger GDP reading reflects a sustained trend in domestic demand?
questions.evidence: Compare seasonally adjusted consumption and investment by component with export and import volumes.

questions.question: Are upstream costs starting to reach consumer categories beyond fuel?
questions.evidence: Compare producer and retail price series and update the monthly CPI diffusion measure.

questions.question: Does stronger technology demand create durable income growth locally?
questions.evidence: Examine employment, value-added shares and net exports in the segments seeing the strongest capital spending.

locator: Release sections on quarterly activity, inflation and currency conditions; embargo dated 14 August 2026.

title: Trial of Government of Canada securities settlement fail fees
summary:
The Collateral Infrastructure and Market Practices Advisory Group and the Canadian Depository for Securities announced a September 8 start for the first stage of a fee trial on settlement fails in Government of Canada bonds and treasury bills. The stage was scheduled to last at least 18 months.

The trial calculates indicative fees and supplies fail statistics and participant reports. A subsequent decision by the Canadian Fixed-Income Forum would be needed to activate payments.
locator: Bank-hosted market notice, trial mechanics and decision authority.

questions.question: Which issues or tenors account for the most persistent fails during the trial?
questions.evidence: The first stage makes statistics available on Government of Canada bond and bill fails. Use CDS fail counts and auction issue identifiers to test whether settlement risk clusters in collateral relevant to pricing or hedging.

questions.question: Do participants change settlement behaviour when they receive indicative invoices?
questions.evidence: The notice specifies that reports and indicative fees are available during the first stage. Compare failures and indicative invoice exposure around implementation while accounting for seasonal settlement patterns and issuance.

questions.question: How would a decision to activate payments affect repo spreads for scarce collateral?
questions.evidence: The forum retained authority for any subsequent decision on actual payments. Compare security-level repo quotes and fails before and after any future activation to assess the prospective cost of financing short positions.

coverageNote: Joint market infrastructure notice hosted by the Bank. The notice describes trial design.

title: The mysterious US economy — Tom Barkin
locator: Prepared remarks on demand resilience, the low-hire and low-layoff labour market, and persistent inflation.
summary: Tom Barkin explored why consumption, business investment and a low unemployment rate had persisted through an extended series of shocks. The speech links resilience to employment, wealth gains among asset holders and changes in spending behaviour. Weak sentiment and lower real income point to the risk that resilience is uneven. The unemployment rate can stay low when both demand for new hires and growth in the labour force slow. Barkin judged that much of the observed productivity improvement followed the post-pandemic labour squeeze through firms’ operational changes. He left room for additional AI gains. These mechanisms affect his reading of inflation persistence and labour-market slack. The speech does not identify a fixed next move.

questions.question: How dependent is consumption on households with asset gains?
questions.evidence: Compare spending growth and liquid savings by income and wealth, controlling for changes in wages and credit.

questions.question: Does the low-hire, low-layoff pattern raise the risk of a rapid unemployment change?
questions.evidence: Use transition rates out of unemployment and changes in labour-force growth to examine that scenario.

questions.question: How can productivity sources be disentangled?
questions.evidence: Compare timing of operational changes and AI adoption with output per hour at the industry level.

title: Rate decision August 2026
summary:
Norges Bank held at 4.25% in August. Inflation had been below its June projection but remained above target. Capacity utilisation was near normal and softening. The krone had recovered some of its earlier weakness and was broadly in line with the June assumption. The committee still saw a restrictive stance as necessary and judged it was too early to infer a material change in the inflation path.

June guidance had indicated an increase would probably be needed at one of the upcoming meetings. The committee did not prepare new forecasts for August, and was due to reassess them in September. The decision to wait illustrates the balance between high existing inflation and a potentially softer outlook.
locator: Press release and committee deliberations

questions.question: Was lower inflation driven by temporary components?
questions.evidence: Compare CPI-ATE, energy and domestically produced prices with June assumptions.

questions.question: How much slack does registered unemployment capture?
questions.evidence: Compare the labour force survey, vacancies and regional contacts.

questions.question: What did the hold mean relative to pre-announcement rates?
questions.evidence: Compare NOK forwards and OIS around the release.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
title: Fatih Karahan’s briefing on Inflation Report 2026-III
locator: Written briefing, including inflation developments, monetary policy and medium-term projections. The official remarks feed dates the speech 13 August. The associated Q&A is outside this review.
summary:
Governor Fatih Karahan attributed weaker demand and relatively contained core goods inflation to the tight policy stance while highlighting geopolitical supply shocks. He said the Bank would continue to use its tools to support price stability. The briefing reported gross reserves of USD 185 billion as of 12 August, up from USD 155 billion on 27 March.

The CBRT raised its year-end 2026 inflation forecast to 28%. The new path put year-end inflation at 15% in 2027 and 9% in 2028 before converging to the 5% medium-term target. These are official conditional projections. The briefing describes demand, pricing and geopolitical risks around the path.

questions.question: Which assumptions contributed most to the 2026 forecast revision?
questions.evidence: Compare vintage projection tables, energy and food assumptions and the inflation forecast decomposition in the two reports.

questions.question: Is weaker domestic demand limiting the pass-through from imported costs?
questions.evidence: Compare producer-to-consumer price pass-through by tradable category with retail volumes and import price measures.

questions.question: What drove the increase in gross reserves?
questions.evidence: Distinguish valuation changes, FX transactions, swaps and other balance-sheet flows before drawing conclusions about reserve adequacy.

title: Christopher Kent: The Restrictive Stance of Monetary Policy
locator: Graphs 1–3 and discussion of transmission and offsets
summary:
Kent assesses financial conditions as somewhat restrictive after three cash-rate increases in 2026. He notes that lending and deposit rates moved up, scheduled mortgage payments were near their 2024 peak relative to disposable income, and the Australian dollar had strengthened by around 5% on a trade-weighted basis since the start of the year. Exchange-rate appreciation affects imported prices and the demand for domestic production. Kent also observes that since May some market-implied future rate expectations had eased, reducing some wholesale borrowing rates.

His neutral-rate comparison places the cash rate near the upper end of the range of central estimates. He stresses that those estimates are uncertain and can adjust slowly to changes in the economy. Resilient investment and global demand, including spending linked to AI, can offset some of the drag on household demand. The speech’s market significance is the distinction between the current cash rate and the full set of conditions that determine restraint.

questions.question: How far have mortgage resets affected aggregate spending already?
questions.evidence: Compare the timing of scheduled payments and consumption across households with different debt exposure.

questions.question: What is driving the trade-weighted AUD move?
questions.evidence: Compare changes in domestic and overseas rate expectations with export prices and global risk indicators.

questions.question: Is an apparent increase in neutral robust across different methods?
questions.evidence: Compare the models in Graph 3 and assess the sensitivity to rate and activity assumptions.

institution: Banco Central de Reserva del Perú
title: August 2026 monetary program – Reference rate maintained at 4.25%
summary:
The central bank announced that its board maintained the monetary-policy reference rate at 4.25% in the August program. The Bank's separate official daily series displays the level around the August 13 meeting.

The central bank's short public announcement confirms the action. A full review of the decision rationale and projections would require the detailed program materials.
locator: Central bank's decision-day post and its daily reference-rate series PD12301MD.

questions.question: What did the local-currency yield curve price before the release for August and the next meeting?
questions.evidence: The BCRP confirms the unchanged 4.25% benchmark. Compare the release time with local rates or quotes on both sides of the announcement so pre-release expectations can be distinguished from the policy action.

questions.question: Which inflation or activity inputs did the full statement identify as decisive?
questions.evidence: The public post confirms the choice of rate and points to the August program. Read the official monetary-program presentation and dated underlying CPI, expectations and activity inputs to see which arguments could shape the subsequent rate path.

questions.question: How does the August wording compare with September once both statements are available?
questions.evidence: The headline confirms the August policy action but gives limited rationale. Use the August release as the baseline and compare its risk paragraph with September's official publication to distinguish changing data from changing guidance.

coverageNote: Based on the official announcement and rate series. The policy PDF was inaccessible during review.

title: Measuring foreign and domestic macroeconomic uncertainty and their impact on the New Zealand economy
locator: Publication overview, methodology and key findings
summary:
The RBNZ analytical note constructs separate measures of foreign and domestic macroeconomic uncertainty and estimates their associations with the New Zealand economy. The two series move together to a substantial degree. The authors interpret that co-movement as consistent with foreign developments contributing to domestic uncertainty. For both categories, estimated responses imply weaker GDP and a higher CPI after an uncertainty increase.

This pattern raises a policy trade-off because the inflation and activity implications point in different directions. The estimated effects belong to the authors’ identification method and sample. Co-movement alone leaves open how a specific international disruption reached New Zealand, and responses to a particular episode can differ by source and duration. The publication is research on shock transmission, useful for framing how to test whether local market moves reflect external uncertainty.

questions.question: Can foreign uncertainty be separated from coincident global commodity and demand shocks?
questions.evidence: Compare model responses under alternative controls and around externally dated episodes.

questions.question: Which components explain the estimated CPI increase?
questions.evidence: Examine import prices, the exchange rate and other disaggregated CPI components around identified shocks.

questions.question: How stable are these responses across regimes?
questions.evidence: Compare estimates before and after major exchange-rate, inflation and financial conditions changes.

title: China Monetary Policy Report, Q2 2026
locator: PBOC executive summary. Report released on 12 August according to the PBOC-affiliated Financial News; Suzhou government mirror posted 13 August.
summary:
The PBOC’s second-quarter report describes maintaining a moderately loose stance under a more uncertain external backdrop. It cites 4.7% year-on-year GDP growth in the first half. It pairs ample system liquidity and reduced financing costs with targeted tools for innovation, smaller firms and other preferred sectors. It describes adding overnight reverse repos and narrowing the temporary repo and reverse-repo band from 70 to 50 basis points. It also reports a cut of 25 basis points to the rate on structural monetary tools. That is a change in facility pricing, while the narrower operating band concerns short-end implementation.

The bank reports a first-half average DR001 of 1.31%, a June new corporate loan rate near 3.0%, and a new mortgage rate near 3.1%. It reports the corporate rate about 20 basis points below its prior-year level, while the mortgage rate was broadly flat. Those outcomes suggest looking separately at financing terms by borrower class when assessing transmission. The outlook keeps operations and fiscal coordination flexible and supports orderly moves in the managed RMB float. The summary supplies no market pricing around publication.

questions.question: Does structural relending change financing costs for otherwise comparable firms?
questions.evidence: Match loan originations by borrower risk, location and sector with receipt of programme funding.

questions.question: How do the sources of lower short-end volatility differ at tax dates and ordinary days?
questions.evidence: Compare official operations, government cash flows and DR001 under the wider and narrower operating bands.

questions.question: Does the gap between corporate and mortgage-rate movements indicate different policy transmission?
questions.evidence: Compare changes in loan pricing, margins and borrower or property mix across the two markets.

coverageLimitation: Analysis uses the official executive summary. The full report’s charts and appendices were not independently verified.

title: The Italian economy in brief, No. 8 — August 2026
summary:
The August reference pack puts different measures of borrowing costs side by side. Table 38 gives monthly-average gross benchmark yields. The Italian ten-year yield rose from 3.73% in June to 3.88% in July, and the three-year yield rose from 2.90% to 3.06%. The table uses daily MTS data and benchmark securities. Chart 39 uses daily ten-year spreads relative to German government bonds, a separate measure of relative credit and liquidity conditions.

Chart 37 compares marginal borrowing benchmarks with the average effective cost and residual maturity of existing debt. Only maturing or newly issued debt is priced immediately at new funding conditions. These observations describe the level and term structure of yields, without attributing them to a particular event.
locator: Charts 37–39, especially Table 38 and definition notes

questions.question: How much of the benchmark move was common across Europe?
questions.evidence: Compare daily BTP–Bund spreads and matched swap yields.

questions.question: How quickly will refinancing increase the interest bill?
questions.evidence: Map issuance and maturities to loan coupons and effective debt costs.

questions.question: Which curve segment shows a larger funding shift?
questions.evidence: Compare auction rates, liquidity and yields by tenor.

coverageLimitation: Focused review of the public funding sections. Other sections are not summarised here.

title: Statement on Monetary Policy, August 2026
locator: Overview forecast table and Outlook, including conditioning assumptions and historical forecast bands. Selected chapters reviewed.
summary:
The August projections describe a period of below-trend growth, an increase in unemployment and inflation declining gradually toward the target midpoint. The overview table shows CPI inflation falling from 3.9% in June 2026 to 2.6% in December 2027, with unemployment rising from 4.4% to 4.7% over the same dates. The staff expect some relief from energy-related costs and a reduction in domestic capacity pressures as restrictive financing restrains demand. Stronger activity among trading partners supports the growth outlook even with weakness in domestic household spending.

The cash-rate assumption comes from financial-market pricing on 5 August. The forecast also holds the trade-weighted exchange rate at its 5 August level. Neither assumption describes what the Board promises to do. The trimmed-mean inflation fan chart uses historical forecast errors, with a wide range by the end of the projection. Uncertainty around the conflict and the global AI investment cycle matters for the path of import prices, export demand and capacity pressures.

questions.question: What is most important to the projected disinflation, easing input costs or spare capacity?
questions.evidence: Compare the staff’s decomposition of trimmed-mean inflation with changes in energy and labour indicators as data arrive.

questions.question: Is the 5 August market path still a reasonable conditioning benchmark?
questions.evidence: Compare the dated OIS curve with subsequent market pricing, keeping the assumptions separate from the Board’s decision.

questions.question: How much could weaker domestic demand be masked by resilient exports?
questions.evidence: Use disaggregated activity data to test the drivers of the growth forecast.

title: Monetary Policy Board decision: cash rate held at 4.35%
locator: Opening assessment and Decision
summary:
The Board held its cash rate target at 4.35% after three increases earlier in 2026. The release says financial conditions had tightened through higher money-market rates and yields and through exchange-rate appreciation. Housing and household spending showed signs of slowing, while business borrowing and investment remained strong. Trimmed-mean inflation was still elevated and little changed from the March quarter. The initial Middle East conflict effect on inflation had been smaller than expected, with evidence of fuel-cost pass-through and domestic capacity pressure still present.

The hold gave the Board time to assess how earlier tightening was working. The Board described the policy setting as somewhat restrictive and retained the option to raise the rate if upside inflation risks materialised. Stronger trading-partner activity associated with AI investment was helping offset some of the global energy shock. Weak domestic productivity meant Australia’s capacity to absorb stronger demand was limited. These were reasons to pay attention to the composition of growth even while aggregate demand was slowing.

questions.question: Was the hold already priced and did the conditional tightening language affect later meetings?
questions.evidence: Check Australian OIS and futures before and after the published decision time, accounting for the simultaneous forecast.

questions.question: How persistent was the domestic component of inflation?
questions.evidence: Compare domestically exposed services and the trimmed mean with fuel prices and firm-level selling-price intentions.

questions.question: How far had financial tightening reached household demand?
questions.evidence: Compare mortgage payments, new housing borrowing and spending with business credit and investment activity.

title: Copom minutes – 280th meeting
summary:
The minutes give Copom's reference inflation projections of 5.1% for 2026, 3.8% for 2027 and 3.2% for the first quarter of 2028. The scenario used the Focus survey interest-rate path and a falling Brent futures path for the second half of 2026. The committee judged the risk balance to be skewed upward.

Members described continued low unemployment, slowing employment growth and real pay growth above productivity. They unanimously judged that de-anchored expectations required greater and longer monetary restriction than would otherwise be appropriate.
locator: Minutes of the August 4–5 meeting, risk scenario paragraphs 5–12 and Table 1. Release dated August 11.

questions.question: How sensitive are the reference projections to the assumed paths for crude and the Selic rate?
questions.evidence: The minutes set out both market-based assumptions. Use alternative oil and rate scenarios with the committee's published inflation model to test forecasts that could alter the expected Selic path.

questions.question: To what extent could real wage growth above productivity sustain services inflation?
questions.evidence: The labour section compares real wage growth and productivity. Compare official wage, productivity and services inflation indicators at comparable frequencies before treating wage growth as a forward inflation signal.

questions.question: What evidence would convince the committee that expectations are re-anchoring?
questions.evidence: Members identify persistent de-anchoring as requiring longer and greater restriction. Compare the Focus distribution with indexed-bond measures adjusted for liquidity and risk premia to test whether anchoring extends beyond surveys.

title: Summary of Opinions at the July 30–31 Monetary Policy Meeting
locator: Policy summary §§I–II, emphasis on transmission lags and conditions for adjustments. An edited account of July opinions.
summary:
Opinions published after the July meeting indicate differing views on timing. One assessment supported holding while testing whether June's hike would affect domestic activity and inflation with a lag of about one to one and a half years. Other comments found that negative short real rates, favourable bank lending and underlying inflation approaching 2% still made the direction of further hikes appropriate. A more forceful view pointed to upside price risks and the possibility of a faster pace than markets expected if conditions called for it.

Participants considered the drag of higher crude oil and the support of technology-related demand. Wages, pricing behaviour and longer-term expectations mattered for whether inflation would remain near target. The Bank’s document is an edited set of remarks rather than a count of preferences by stance. It gives no new voted decision on the August publication date.

questions.question: Where would earlier hikes first appear in bank-intermediated credit?
questions.evidence: Compare new loan rates, quantities and term changes in mortgage and firm borrowing.

questions.question: What could bring forward the next adjustment?
questions.evidence: Compare sector-level price pressure and wage data with evolving guidance and separately observe the market-implied schedule.

questions.question: Can the relative weight of inflation and lag concerns be inferred by member?
questions.evidence: Consult subsequent named speeches and vote records in addition to this unattributed document.

institution: Banco Central de la República Argentina
title: Monthly Monetary Report – July 2026
summary:
In its July release series, the central bank reported that real seasonally adjusted transactional M2 rose 1.8% in July. Real time deposits fell 0.4%, and the broader M3 measure edged down. The report estimated real monetary base growth of 0.2%, with net foreign exchange purchases partly offset by operations involving the Treasury and secondary-market trades.

The report also described proposed charter amendments that would make preserving the value of money the central objective and bar new temporary advances to the Treasury. It presented these measures as elements of a draft. Separately, real seasonally adjusted peso credit to the private sector grew 1.2%, led by commercial loans.
locator: Official release, executive summary and linked report. Figures are from the August 7 publication vintage.

questions.question: Why did transactional money expand while the broader money measure fell?
questions.evidence: The report records rising transactional M2 and declining real time deposits. Break down the BCRA monetary tables by inflation adjustment, currency, demand deposits and time deposits to tell whether depositors are shortening maturity.

questions.question: How large were the offsetting effects of foreign exchange and Treasury transactions on the base?
questions.evidence: Net currency purchases supported the base while other operations partly offset them. Use the central bank's daily balance sheet and the Treasury cash timetable to distinguish potentially reversible operations before assessing peso funding.

questions.question: How would the draft restrictions change the balance-sheet channels through which the bank funds the Treasury?
questions.evidence: The report describes a proposed ban on temporary advances. Read the submitted bill and balance-sheet notes to establish which liabilities and asset transfers would be restricted and what changes would require enactment.

coverageNote: Review covers the executive summary. The draft charter provisions are identified separately from enacted rules.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Interbank Call Loan and Commercial Paper Markets (July 2026)
locator: Sections I–II, overnight rates and turnover, primary and secondary paper observations.
summary:
In July the weighted overnight call-loan rate averaged 0.824%, up 0.001 percentage points, while interbank turnover and average daily balances rose. Longer private funding showed a different pattern. For commercial paper of one to thirty days, the preliminary primary average fell 8 basis points to 1.87% while the secondary average rose 14 basis points to 1.68%. The figures describe aggregates in markets with different issuer, maturity and transaction mixes, so the difference cannot by itself measure a bank or issuer premium.

The same publication shows a decrease in the amount of commercial paper outstanding even as overall short-term bills rose. That distinction matters if using turnover or outstanding amounts to diagnose funding pressure. The release reports July outcomes on 7 August and announces no change of monetary-policy setting.

questions.question: Does the divergence in commercial paper survive a maturity and issuer match?
questions.evidence: Compare matched primary and secondary observations by rating and remaining tenor.

questions.question: Did larger interbank turnover reflect broader conditions or calendar effects?
questions.evidence: Compare daily data on rates, turnover and borrower mix at similar month-ends.

questions.question: Which securities explain the increase in bills outstanding?
questions.evidence: Use the issuance table and change in component stocks to separate commercial paper from other bills.

coverageLimitation: The official release text was checked. The separate detailed table file was not independently reviewed.

institution: Banco Central de la República Argentina
title: Santiago Bausili – Second-quarter Monetary Policy Report opening remarks
summary:
BCRA President Santiago Bausili said monthly inflation averaged 2.2% in the second quarter, down from 3.0% in the first. June headline inflation was 1.9%, and the BCRA's underlying index was 1.6%. He attributed the moderation partly to fading seasonal, administered-price and fuel pressures and argued that it also extended more broadly.

He said the second-quarter monetary policy orientation had remained unchanged. The President reported US$13.337 billion in foreign-exchange purchases through July 31 and described a recovery in demand for transactional money from May.
locator: Prepared opening remarks, sections III and IV on prices and monetary policy.

questions.question: Which categories drove the difference between headline and underlying June inflation?
questions.evidence: Bausili cites 1.9% headline and 1.6% on the Bank's underlying index. Compare the BCRA's underlying index weights with INDEC CPI contributions to assess how much of disinflation could persist as seasonal effects unwind.

questions.question: How should foreign-exchange purchases be reconciled with growth in peso demand?
questions.evidence: The remarks discuss reserve purchases and a recovery in transactional money demand. Reconcile BCRA reserve transactions, intervention and real deposit aggregates before attributing peso funding conditions to changes in liquidity.

questions.question: What data would test Bausili’s account of limited second-round effects?
questions.evidence: He attributes part of the disinflation to weaker pass-through and fading transitory influences. Compare time-stamped sector CPI, exchange rates and administered-price decisions to estimate the breadth and speed of pass-through.

coverageNote: Review covers the President’s published opening remarks.

title: Monetary policy announcement – August 6, 2026
summary:
The Governing Board unanimously held the overnight interbank target at 6.50%. From the first half of June to the first half of July, annual headline inflation declined from 3.55% to 3.10% and core inflation fell from 4.12% to 3.95%. The Bank projected a more gradual disinflation path and convergence to 3% in the fourth quarter of 2027, with inflation risks still skewed upward.

The Bank reported a second-quarter rebound after a first-quarter contraction. It assessed the economy as still having slack and viewed growth risks as tilted down.
locator: Official statement pp. 1–2, activity, forecast table, risk balance and decision.

questions.question: How much of June-to-July disinflation reflected temporary non-core price moves?
questions.evidence: Headline inflation fell more than core between the stated fortnightly observations. Compare fortnightly CPI contributions and monthly seasonal patterns to test how much disinflation can persist.

questions.question: Which core components account for slower expected convergence?
questions.evidence: The decision retained an upside-skewed risk balance and projected convergence in Q4 2027. Use forecasts and actual services and merchandise inflation to distinguish slower trend disinflation from volatile monthly releases.

questions.question: How did the changes in the peso and local yields discussed by the Bank predate the release?
questions.evidence: The announcement compares prevailing market conditions with the preceding policy decision. Compare independently time-stamped TIIE swaps and peso quotes around the publication before attributing any move to the decision.

institution: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
title: Monetary policy and productivity — Alberto Musalem
locator: Full prepared remarks, the investment case for easing, inflation trade-off and closing judgment.
summary: Musalem considers whether monetary policy can foster productivity by supporting investment and innovation. He sees potentially large cumulative gains if a policy change raises long-run productivity. He argues that this possibility provides weak grounds for deliberately accepting more inflation. The payoff from easier money is uncertain, financing conditions differ by borrower, and persistently high inflation can make planning and investment harder.
