He describes himself as optimistic about AI while treating future productivity gains as uncertain for current policy. The remarks set out a framework for the trade-off, rather than an assessment of a near-term market move.

questions.question: Which productivity investments are actually sensitive to policy rates?
questions.evidence: Compare investment by firm financing structure, internal cash flow and exposure to long-term funding costs.

questions.question: Would faster productivity show up in inflation before it changes expected returns?
questions.evidence: Track unit costs and utilisation, then separate demand generated by the buildout from subsequent supply gains.

questions.question: What would demonstrate a persistent investment effect from easing?
questions.evidence: Test exogenous financial-condition changes against capital deepening and productivity over sufficiently long horizons.

title: Economic Bulletin Issue 5, 2026
summary:
The bulletin’s overview records the 23 July hold. Conditions had tightened slightly since the June increase. June headline inflation declined to 2.8% from 3.2% in May and inflation excluding energy and food fell from 2.6% to 2.4%. Services also eased, although the full effect of higher input costs remained uncertain.

Survey information suggested some recovery in services after the shock and resilience in manufacturing, helped by inventory-building and defence outlays. Job postings continued to fall even while unemployment was near historical lows. The outlook combined downside growth risks with upside inflation risks if disruption persisted. A sustained resolution or lower pass-through could instead reduce inflation.
locator: Overview and sections on economic activity, inflation and financing conditions

questions.question: Which input shocks had not yet reached selling prices?
questions.evidence: Compare purchasing costs, inventory and consumer price components.

questions.question: Was manufacturing strength mostly precautionary stockbuilding?
questions.evidence: Compare orders, production and inventories.

questions.question: Are labour market indicators pointing to more slack?
questions.evidence: Compare vacancy, hiring and unemployment measures.

coverageLimitation: The economic overview is covered. Separate boxes and the long-form article are outside this note.

title: CNB Bank Board keeps the two-week repo rate at 3.75%
locator: Decision page, rate paragraph and accompanying meeting materials.
summary: The Board kept its two-week repo rate at 3.75%, its discount rate at 2.75% and its Lombard rate at 4.75%. The short decision notice records the instrument settings and points to the statement, press conference and minutes for the rationale. The unchanged rate can be analysed as a discrete release and the subsequent explanation as a separate communication event.

questions.question: Were short-term markets already pricing a hold?
questions.evidence: Compare timed CZK forward rates and the koruna in a window around the decision.

questions.question: How did the statement qualify the unchanged headline rate?
questions.evidence: Read the decision notice alongside the statement and forecast, recording their different publication times.

questions.question: How much are unchanged policy settings transmitted to deposit and loan rates?
questions.evidence: Compare CNB bank-rate series and longer-maturity market rates by borrower and tenor.

title: Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee, 3–5 August 2026
summary:
The MPC unanimously kept the repo rate at 5.25% and retained a neutral stance. The standing deposit facility stayed at 5.00% and the marginal standing facility and Bank Rate at 5.50%. June headline CPI had risen to 4.4%, primarily from food and fuel, while core inflation was steady at 3.9% over May and June. Excluding precious metals, the resolution puts core inflation in a 2.3–2.5% range over those months. The committee saw limited spread of price pressures so far and was watching whether higher input costs would move into other prices.

The MPC projected 6.7% real GDP growth and 5.0% CPI inflation in fiscal 2026–27, with inflation reaching 5.9% in Q3. The decision weighs domestic consumption, infrastructure and credit growth against weather risks and uncertainty about oil and trade. A weaker monsoon could raise food prices while hurting rural demand. The committee held while seeking evidence on the makeup and persistence of inflation.

questions.question: Is the evidence of limited cost pass-through consistent across sectors?
questions.evidence: Compare CPI diffusion, firm selling-price surveys and wage measures with input costs.

questions.question: What happens to consumption if the weaker monsoon reduces rural income?
questions.evidence: Compare rainfall, agricultural production and rural spending using consistent regional coverage.

questions.question: Which upcoming data can change the expected repo path?
questions.evidence: Compare policy-sensitive OIS across dated releases and identify shocks from contemporaneous survey expectations.

locator: Resolution paragraphs 2 and 4–17; charts 1 and 2 correspond to the growth and inflation projections stated in the text.

title: Minutes of the 21 July Monetary Council meeting
locator: Published 5 August at 2 p.m. Section 1 records the 21 July discussion and vote. Section 2 contains background charts.
summary:
The minutes show that every member present supported the sole proposal to cut the base rate by 25 basis points to 5.75%. Members saw inflation and the outlook as more favourable than in the June baseline. They assessed domestic financial markets as relatively stable despite a weaker forint as energy prices rose and judged that lower risk premia had persisted.

The discussion acknowledged uncertainty linked to the renewed US–Iran conflict and stressed continued assessment of external conditions. The minutes identify a collective agreement on the proposal and selected arguments raised by members. They offer limited evidence about how members would have voted on alternatives.

questions.question: Which CPI items and forecast assumptions enabled the cut?
questions.evidence: Use the June report and real-time component observations discussed in the minutes.

questions.question: Did lower domestic risk premia cushion the forint during the energy shock?
questions.evidence: Compare FX and sovereign spread changes with energy prices and comparable regional currency moves.

questions.question: Were real rates still restrictive after the reduction?
questions.evidence: Compare policy rates adjusted for matched-horizon inflation expectations with household and corporate credit conditions.

title: Indonesia’s Economy Grows 5.29% in Second Quarter of 2026
summary:
Bank Indonesia reported 5.29% year-on-year real GDP growth in the second quarter, following 5.61% in the previous quarter, and kept its full-year forecast range at 4.9–5.7%. It attributes Q2 growth primarily to domestic spending. Household consumption grew 5.06%, reflecting in part school holidays and religious holidays. Government consumption grew 15.97%, with salary timing and programme procurement contributing. Investment and exports grew, supported by vehicle investment, public and private projects and trade partner demand.

On the production side, Bank Indonesia cited strength in manufacturing, trade, construction, information and communication, and accommodation and food services. The release separates activity realised in Q2 from its forecast of ongoing domestic demand support. The timing of salaries, school holidays and government purchases matters when using a single quarter to judge underlying demand.

questions.question: How much consumer growth survives adjustments for calendar and fiscal effects?
questions.evidence: Compare seasonally adjusted consumption, retail activity and government payments with the same quarter’s raw levels.

questions.question: Is investment demand broadening outside vehicle purchases?
questions.evidence: Review gross fixed capital formation by asset type and separate projects financed by the public sector.

questions.question: Which export industries contributed to real output and local demand?
questions.evidence: Compare trade weights and production volumes with import intensity and domestic value added.

locator: Release paragraphs on GDP, expenditure components, production sectors and annual outlook.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Foreign Exchange Reserves as of the End of July 2026
locator: Release’s reserve total, three drivers and portfolio exposure note.
summary:
The CBC reported reserves of US$594.27 billion at end-July, US$2.88 billion below the previous month. It attributed changes to investment returns, valuation changes in non-dollar reserve currencies and interventions to smooth volatile capital flows. It separately reported holdings of securities and Taiwan dollar deposits by foreign portfolio investors of US$1,663.1 billion. That stock can inform exposure work. It is a different measure from actual portfolio outflows.

Reserve valuation, investment income and trading can offset one another. The net decline therefore does not identify the direction or size of all official foreign exchange transactions. The report concerns the balance at the end of July, which is distinct from the report date of 5 August.

questions.question: How much of the change in reserves was transactional after allowing for valuation?
questions.evidence: Compare published net FX purchases and sales alongside currency movements and reserve income estimates.

questions.question: Which flows were most associated with currency volatility?
questions.evidence: Separate net foreign equity turnover, realised outward remittance and forward hedge adjustments.

questions.question: How liquid were FX markets when the bank intervened?
questions.evidence: Review spot and forward liquidity indicators, trading volumes and the timing of unusually large flows.

title: Copom reduces the Selic rate to 14.00%
summary:
The Copom reduced the Selic target by 25 basis points, from 14.25% to 14.00%, describing the resulting policy setting as still restrictive. Its reference projection placed inflation at 3.2% in the first quarter of 2028.

The committee described uncertainty around geopolitical effects on oil and possible El Niño effects. It flagged de-anchored expectations, persistent services inflation and a potentially weaker exchange rate among upside risks.
locator: Committee statement, inflation risk assessment and decision. Official comunicado 45.693 records the meeting decision.

questions.question: What makes the post-cut rate restrictive under alternative neutral-rate estimates?
questions.evidence: The committee reduced the nominal rate while calling the ensuing stance restrictive. Compare estimates of the real neutral rate with a maturity-matched expected real Selic path to assess how much restraint remains after the cut.

questions.question: Does services persistence reflect labour markets or broader pricing behaviour?
questions.evidence: Persistent services inflation appears in the upside risk discussion. Compare wage and vacancy indicators with price diffusion, regulated prices and commodity-sensitive services to test when the committee might see sustained disinflation.

questions.question: How sensitive is the Q1 2028 inflation projection to exchange rates and oil?
questions.evidence: The release discusses a potentially weaker currency and geopolitical commodity-price uncertainty. Use the Copom reference assumptions and alternative Brent and real paths to separate local inflation effects from the external drivers.

coverageNote: The official statement was reviewed from its published text as indexed. The linked site requires JavaScript to display the article in some environments.

title: Board minutes – Policy rate held at 12.00%
summary:
The minutes record four votes to maintain the 12.00% policy rate and three for a 50-basis-point increase. The majority supported a pause to assess earlier tightening. Some members pointed to stable June core inflation and the influence of prices affected by weather and international shocks.

The directors favouring an increase emphasized the risk of broader inflation from El Niño, the limited change in the ex-ante real policy stance relative to a year earlier, and the risks of delaying further tightening. The minutes cited July analyst expectations of 6.6% for December 2026 and 5.0% for December 2027.
locator: Official minutes, opening vote and majority and minority discussion. Published August 5 for the July decision.

questions.question: Which indicators are most informative about the lagged impact of prior rate increases?
questions.evidence: The majority paused to assess transmission from previous increases. Compare monthly credit, lending rates and activity with earlier policy moves to see whether the majority's rationale holds as the data arrive.

questions.question: How does the neutral-rate estimate change the real-rate-gap comparison?
questions.evidence: Supporters of a larger increase cited a broadly similar ex-ante real policy stance to a year earlier. Use the Bank's real neutral-rate research and like-for-like inflation expectations to see how assumptions affect conclusions about existing restriction.

questions.question: Which indicators distinguish a weather-driven relative-price change from general inflation?
questions.evidence: The two sides discussed supply-driven inflation and the possibility that it spreads. Use price diffusion, weather monitoring and inflation expectations to distinguish a sectoral shock from a shift that could affect the nominal policy path.

title: Monetary policy perspective: keeping an open mind — Anna Paulson
locator: Current Conditions, Balance of Risks, Implications for Monetary Policy and footnotes.
summary: Anna Paulson supported the preceding FOMC hold. The labour market looked broadly stable. Lower energy prices had helped June headline PCE, while her estimate of underlying inflation after adjusting for tariff and energy effects was around 2.4–2.8%. She set out two plausible readings of the same economy. Moderate pay growth and weak housing activity pointed to some restraint. Healthy private demand and business investment suggested current settings might prove too loose to bring inflation down promptly. Anchored expectations gave her room to assess which mechanism mattered most. She placed greater weight on inflation risk and remained open to an adjustment once underlying inflation became clearer.

questions.question: How sensitive is the underlying inflation estimate to the tariff and energy adjustment?
questions.evidence: Reproduce the calculation across different affected items and lag structures using the component data.

questions.question: Is weak housing evidence of broad restraint?
questions.evidence: Compare housing turnover and financing costs with consumption growth across income groups and capex outside the AI buildout.

questions.question: Could an apparently steady unemployment rate hide weakening hiring?
questions.evidence: Cross-check job-finding, layoffs and survey perceptions with labour-force growth and labour demand.

title: Monetary Policy Report – July 2026
summary:
The technical staff reported June headline inflation of 6.1%, up from 5.6% in March, and June inflation excluding food and regulated prices of 6.0%. It described pressure from labour and production costs, firm household and public spending, and agricultural disruptions. Peso appreciation partly tempered price pressure.

The staff projected headline inflation of 6.9% at year-end 2026 and 4.3% at year-end 2027, against the 3% target. It also described expansion in consumption and capital-equipment investment. Growth was 2.2% year over year in the first quarter. The staff projected 2.5% growth for 2026 and 1.9% for 2027, with a weaker impulse from some recent demand drivers.
locator: Official release page, inflation outlook and activity overview. July edition published August 4.

questions.question: Which services are most responsive to higher labour costs?
questions.evidence: The report cites labour costs in discussing persistent inflation. Use sector CPI and wage series across services to test which prices could keep inflation high after agricultural disruptions fade.

questions.question: How do household and public spending contribute to the inflation path separately?
questions.evidence: The staff describes both sources of firm demand. Reconcile national accounts demand components and official fiscal execution data before attributing the projected inflation path to private consumption or fiscal support.

questions.question: What exchange-rate pass-through assumptions underpin the return toward target?
questions.evidence: The report cites recent peso appreciation as a partial offset and forecasts lower year-end inflation in 2027. Read the report's model and exchange-rate sensitivity assumptions to identify which peso trajectories materially alter the return toward target.

coverageNote: Review covers the published landing-page overview and figures.

title: Lesetja Kganyago on emerging market resilience
locator: Governor’s lecture, historical comparison, policy reforms in emerging markets and the South Africa section.
summary:
Governor Lesetja Kganyago traced how emerging markets became less vulnerable to repeats of the 1990s crises. He highlighted changes in exchange-rate policy and inflation credibility, as well as steps to limit risky balance-sheet exposures. He used South Africa’s move to a floating exchange rate and inflation targeting as an example of reform and cited a smaller inflation differential with the US over time.

The speech stressed that greater resilience supports stability while long-run growth still depends on fundamentals such as productive capacity and the success of reforms. It is an institutional and historical argument, with no near-term rate announcement.

questions.question: Which reforms most reduced crisis sensitivity?
questions.evidence: Compare external currency mismatch, reserves, debt composition and volatility over policy regime changes.

questions.question: How effective is the floating rand at absorbing external shocks?
questions.evidence: Analyse exchange-rate moves together with inflation pass-through, output and expected rates.

questions.question: What would transform resilience into faster sustainable growth?
questions.evidence: Track productivity, infrastructure and investment alongside peer economies with similar inflation credibility.

title: PBOC Work Conference for the Second Half of 2026
locator: PBOC statement republished by the Shanghai municipal financial authorities, paragraphs on monetary policy and financial services. Meeting held 1 August.
summary:
The central bank’s work conference reported ongoing use of moderately loose monetary policy and described operating priorities for the second half. It listed reverse repos, medium-term lending and government bond operations as tools for supplying liquidity at different tenors. It described the introduction of an overnight reverse repo and a narrower band for temporary overnight operations as refinements to short-end control. The statement reported 7.4% year-on-year growth in outstanding social financing and 8.0% in broad money at the end of June. With targeted tools, the aim was to support demand, innovation and smaller firms while continuing to contain financial risks.

The readout describes how the bank intends to implement the stance. In research terms, quantity of liquidity, level of the operative rate and its distribution to borrowers are distinct. The document also notes more flexible cross-border funding arrangements and an overseas official-sector repo facility. Those facilities relate to access to RMB liquidity. The summary of the conference does not identify any realised repricing or a new economy-wide rate decision.

questions.question: Did the narrower overnight band reduce day-to-day variability in traded funding rates?
questions.evidence: Compare DR001 dispersion and operations around matched month-ends, tax dates and settlement days.

questions.question: How much of the additional funding reached smaller or private businesses?
questions.evidence: Compare eligibility and use of the relending tools with new loan flows, spreads and borrower composition.

questions.question: Are overseas official institutions actively using the repo facility?
questions.evidence: Check official uptake and RMB liquidity indicators onshore and offshore.

title: Outlook for Economic Activity and Prices (July 2026, full text)
locator: Bank’s View and Box 2 on AI demand. Full report released 3 August, following the Bank’s View at the July meeting.
summary:
The July Outlook projected moderate growth in fiscal 2026 at a slower pace than before, because expensive oil weighed on activity while fiscal measures, domestic financing conditions and global AI demand offered support. Growth forecasts were little changed from the previous round and expected to improve from fiscal 2027 as the oil drag faded. The Board expected CPI excluding fresh food to accelerate to well above 2% from the second half of fiscal 2026, then ease toward 2%. Compared with the previous forecast, government measures helped lower the fiscal 2026 CPI forecast.

The report distinguishes that measured CPI profile from underlying inflation, which it expected to approach the 2% objective as wages, pricing behaviour and expectations became more supportive. It judged growth risks generally balanced and warned about upside price risks. Its separate discussion of AI demand matters because the effects can support activity and lift input prices together. The document records the July baseline and policy assessment made public in full in August.

questions.question: How sensitive is the inflation baseline to government mitigation of energy costs?
questions.evidence: Compare forecast assumptions with an unsubsidised energy price scenario and check the CPI component weights.

questions.question: What part of the growth path depends on AI exports and equipment demand?
questions.evidence: Use the report's AI box, trade quantities and sector order data to test concentrations and spillovers.

questions.question: Which measures would confirm inflation near target after temporary costs fade?
questions.evidence: Compare trend inflation, wages and expectations, keeping institutional price changes separate.

coverageLimitation: Analysis draws on the Bank's View and selected sections. Full chart and box verification is incomplete.

title: One-year Euribor rises to 2.855% in July 2026
summary:
The Banco de España reported that the one-year Euribor mortgage reference rate reached 2.855% in July, 0.776 percentage points higher than a year earlier. The observation is the July index reported in August. Its relevance for policy transmission is the connection between money market benchmark rates and the reference rate used in floating-rate mortgage contracts.

The household cash flow effect varies with contract terms and the timing of a reset. The release identifies the benchmark change, without estimating changes in payment burdens or measuring the reaction to a specific central bank announcement.
locator: Press note title, benchmark explanation and chart

questions.question: How much of the mortgage stock resets soon?
questions.evidence: Check outstanding floating-rate loans and the schedule of annual resets.

questions.question: How large is the payment shock across households?
questions.evidence: Compare balances, loan margins and income distributions.

questions.question: How much benchmark repricing reflects forward policy expectations?
questions.evidence: Compare Euribor with matched overnight swap and bank funding rates.

title: Mortgage lock-in: a review of the literature
locator: Working Paper 2026-11, mobility and home-sales evidence, Table 1, policy options and concluding discussion.
summary: The working paper reviews what happens when owners with low fixed-rate mortgages would have to finance a new home at a materially higher rate. Keeping the old mortgage can discourage both a sale and a move, affecting housing turnover and the allocation of labour. The reviewed studies use different data, designs and definitions of a move. The authors distinguish the financing advantage of keeping a particular loan from the direct effect of that loan’s payments on household cash flow. Those mechanisms need different empirical tests and can imply different responses to market rates. The review also examines portability, wider mortgage assumption and a delivery option. Their wider housing and labour-market effects remain open.

questions.question: How much lost mobility is caused by replacing the loan rather than the payment on the old loan?
questions.evidence: Compare households with comparable mortgage costs but different feasible refinancing or assumption terms.

questions.question: Where is the supply response strongest?
questions.evidence: Match listings, sales and rental prices to the distribution of local outstanding mortgage rates and transaction costs.

questions.question: Would portability reduce broader labour-market costs?
questions.evidence: Assess worker mobility, job transitions and lender or investor pricing under a change to mortgage contract terms.

coverageNote: This note focuses on the paper’s discussion of mobility, sales, empirical designs and policy options.

institution: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
title: John Williams on inflation and the policy path — New York Fed interview recap
locator: New York Fed’s published summary of the Reuters interview, including its inflation, conditional policy and transmission passages.
summary: John Williams judged that policy was positioned to support further disinflation in the circumstances he described. He expected tariff and Middle East effects on inflation to diminish over the second half of 2026 and into the following year. The recap also shows the policy condition behind that assessment. A failure to return towards 2% would warrant a response. Williams described financial-market developments as part of transmission to households and firms. The recap provides neither the size of any adjustment nor an estimate of the probability of a particular decision.

questions.question: What would indicate that disinflation had gone off-track?
questions.evidence: Check energy and tariff-exposed categories alongside broad core PCE and household and professional expectations.

questions.question: Which financial-market moves would affect the real outlook?
questions.evidence: Track mortgage rates, corporate spreads and bank credit conditions alongside changes in the expected policy path.

questions.question: How firm was the outlook for an unchanged rate?
questions.evidence: Compare the full interview, adjacent public remarks and meeting-dated OIS to distinguish conditional guidance from any market assumption.

coverageNote: The Bank’s first-party recap is used here. It reproduces selected remarks from the interview.

title: Draft cross-border Crypto Assets Manual consultation
locator: SARB and National Treasury joint statement dated 3 August, including reporting trigger and consultation status. The proposed manual and regulations were still subject to change.
summary:
The SARB and National Treasury opened consultation on a draft manual for cross-border crypto activity to complement April’s proposed Capital Flow Management Regulations. The notice describes proposed authorisation, transaction conditions and reporting for crypto asset service providers. It seeks better surveillance and reduced regulatory arbitrage across entities involved in cross-border activities.

The draft clarifies that transfers from a domestic authorised provider to an offshore provider or a non-custodial wallet can trigger reporting to the Financial Surveillance Department. In the proposal, individuals could externalise crypto assets through authorised providers within their applicable allowance. The statement records the state of the consultation at publication.

questions.question: How would the reporting trigger change the coverage of measured private outflows?
questions.evidence: Compare the proposed categories with exchange-control returns and anonymised flows for authorised providers.

questions.question: Would the rule affect prices or liquidity on domestic crypto platforms?
questions.evidence: Track spreads, premiums and turnover by permitted route across consultation and eventual implementation dates.

questions.question: How well would the proposed reporting cover transfers outside authorised providers?
questions.evidence: Assess the consultation evidence on intermediary and wallet coverage, with explicit limitations for unobservable transactions.

title: Bank lending survey – third quarter of 2026
locator: Official Polish report, executive summary, survey method and sector sections. The study was prepared in July and reported publicly on 3 August.
summary:
NBP’s survey describes easier lending standards for enterprises in Q2, especially for smaller firms, and stronger reported demand across the surveyed credit categories. Banks generally maintained household lending criteria while cutting some margins, with competitive pressure a prominent explanation. They expected tighter household lending standards in Q3 even as demand for consumer and mortgage loans rose, alongside mixed expectations on business lending policy.

The measure summarises the direction and breadth of bank responses weighted by market share. A positive balance for demand describes the survey, while actual lending growth requires the subsequent volumes. The June-quarter readings and banks’ next-quarter expectations have different dates.

questions.question: Did competition reduce the total price of business credit?
questions.evidence: Compare margins, non-interest charges, collateral and annualised borrowing costs from new contracts.

questions.question: Did expected household tightening materialise?
questions.evidence: Compare the next survey and actual approval rates by consumer and mortgage lending segment.

questions.question: What drove the recorded SME credit demand?
questions.evidence: Separate capital investment financing from short-term working capital using loan originations and enterprise surveys.
